When Daniel woke, a small blue sentence hovered above his bed: **PRESS E TO GET UP.** He shut his eyes, counted to ten, and opened them again. The sentence remained. He tried sitting up, but his body refused until, feeling ridiculous, he said, “E.” His legs swung onto the floor. Beyond his bedroom window, the same red car passed three times, its driver waving at an empty sidewalk. Downstairs, his wife stood beside the coffee machine. “Big day today,” she said brightly. “Big day today,” she repeated when he asked what was happening. A yellow diamond floated over her head. With a trembling hand, Daniel touched it. **OBJECTIVE: SAY GOODBYE TO EMMA.** Beneath that, in smaller letters: **You cannot return to this area.** At once he remembered the packed suitcase by the front door, the job overseas, the argument they’d never finished. He couldn’t remember packing the suitcase. He couldn’t remember anything before this morning without first looking at an object.

***

Daniel spent hours searching for another option. The windows wouldn’t break; the telephone only played a busy signal. Whenever he approached Emma, she smiled and told him it was a big day. At last, he dragged his suitcase into the kitchen and unpacked it on the table. Shirts, socks, a photograph of them at the beach—every item vanished as soon as he let go, reappearing neatly folded inside the case. Except the photograph. Emma caught it before it touched the table. Her smile faltered. “That was a terrible holiday,” she said. Daniel stood very still. “Was it?” She rubbed her thumb over the picture. “It rained all week.” Outside, the red car stopped halfway past the window. The yellow diamond flickered, waiting. Daniel pulled out a chair for her. He didn’t know whether there was a world beyond the front door, or whether either of them would exist tomorrow. But Emma sat down, and when he asked her what else she remembered, she took a long time to answer.

# A Week of Wonder in Japan

Japan had been on my travel wish list for years, but nothing prepared me for the pleasure of discovering it one neighborhood—and one meal—at a time.

My trip began in Tokyo, where quiet side streets sat just minutes from enormous, glowing billboards. In Shibuya, I joined the famous scramble crossing, then ducked into a tiny ramen shop. Ordering from a ticket machine took some guesswork, but the steaming bowl that arrived was worth every confused button press.

Kyoto offered a different rhythm. I woke early to walk beneath the red torii gates at Fushimi Inari, climbing until the crowds thinned and birdsong replaced conversation. Later, I wandered along narrow streets lined with wooden buildings, stopping for matcha and a sweet I couldn’t pronounce.

One of my favorite afternoons involved no landmark at all. I bought snacks from a convenience store and sat beside a river, watching cyclists pass and friends gather along the bank. After several days of chasing sights, it felt good to stay still.

Of course, I also missed a train, got caught in the rain, and spent far too long choosing souvenirs. Those little mishaps became part of the fun.

I left Japan with a suitcase full of snacks and a growing list of places for next time. A week was enough to make wonderful memories—but nowhere near enough to satisfy my curiosity.

<<Disgust Depends on Context>>

People often find worms disgusting because their wriggling bodies, unfamiliar texture, and association with soil, decay, or parasites can trigger the brain’s disease-avoidance response. That response is a rough warning system—not a reliable test of whether something is actually dangerous.

Beef, meanwhile, is usually presented as a familiar food: cleaned, cut, cooked, and far removed from the appearance of a dead cow. Habit and preparation make a big difference. A decomposing cow would disgust most people, too.

******
<<We Learn What Counts as Food>>

The difference is largely about how people categorize things. Many grow up learning that cows provide food while worms belong in dirt or signal contamination. Words reinforce that distinction: “steak” evokes dinner, whereas “dead cow” brings the animal’s death back into view.

These reactions aren’t universal. Some communities eat certain worms or insect larvae, while others avoid beef for cultural, religious, or ethical reasons. Disgust reflects familiarity and learned expectations as well as biological instincts—not a consistent rule about eating dead animals.

# A Journey Through Japan in Ten Fair Days
*Wherein thou shalt arrive in Tokyo and take thy leave from Osaka*

### Day I — Tokyo Doth Welcome Thee
Set down thy burdens at thine inn and let thy weary spirit breathe. As evening falls seek Shinjuku’s glowing streets. Take thy first supper of ramen and retire ere travel’s drowsy spell o’ercomes thee.

### Day II — Of Temples and Towers
To Asakusa hie thee with the morn. Behold Sensō-ji and wander Nakamise’s bustling way for sweets and little treasures.

Then stroll beside the Sumida River. Should lofty prospects please thine eye ascend Tokyo Skytree and watch the mighty city stretch beyond thy ken.

### Day III — The Forest and the Throng
Within Meiji Jingū’s wooded bounds find peace beneath the trees. Then turn toward Harajuku where fashion struts upon its merry stage.

At dusk behold Shibuya Crossing. Thou art but one player in that grand procession. Reserve Shibuya Sky beforehand if thou wouldst greet the sunset from above.

### Day IV — Hakone’s Gentle Spell
Depart for Hakone and exchange the city’s thunder for the mountain air. Choose a voyage upon Lake Ashi or wander the Open-Air Museum.

If clouds prove kind Mount Fuji may reveal her noble brow. This night lodge in a ryokan and let warm onsen waters soothe thy limbs.

### Day V — To Kyoto’s Ancient Heart
Travel onward by way of Odawara and board the swift shinkansen to Kyoto.

Once settled walk through Higashiyama toward Kiyomizu-dera. When evening draws her curtain wander Gion’s public streets with quiet grace. Respect all signs and trouble not the working geiko for a portrait.

### Day VI — Beneath the Vermilion Gates
Rise early for Fushimi Inari Taisha. Its scarlet torii climb the wooded hill like verses in an endless song.

Spend the afternoon about Nishiki Market. Purchase small delights and eat where vendors bid thee pause. Let supper be a leisurely affair.

### Day VII — Arashiyama’s Whispering Boughs
Seek Arashiyama before the crowds awake. Walk the bamboo grove and visit Tenryū-ji’s garden.

Beside the river linger awhile. Let this day hold some idle hours for tea and contemplation. Not every joy must gallop to a clock.

### Day VIII — Nara’s Sacred Company
Leave thy larger bags in storage and make for Nara. Behold Tōdai-ji’s great Buddha and wander the park where deer hold merry court.

Offer only the proper deer crackers and guard thy maps from hungry mouths. Continue to Osaka for the night.

### Day IX — Osaka Takes the Stage
Explore Osaka Castle Park and then surrender to the city’s appetite.

In Dōtonbori seek takoyaki and okonomiyaki. Beneath its brilliant signs raise a cup to journeys well begun and nearly done.

### Day X — A Fond Farewell
Take one last breakfast and gather up thy keepsakes. Then journey to Kansai International Airport with ample time to spare.

*Thus ends thy voyage yet not its sweet refrain.*  
*Japan shall dwell within thy heart again.*

### A Few Counsels Ere Thou Goest
- Book thy lodgings and sought-after sights in good time.
- Carry an IC transit card and a little cash.
- Compare individual train fares before purchasing a rail pass.
- Check onsen rules before booking thy stay.
- Wear shoes fit for long walks lest thy feet rebel against the play.

## *Early Life and the County of Tripoli*

Raymond III was Count of Tripoli from 1152 until his death in 1187. He was also an important political leader in the Kingdom of Jerusalem during a period of growing conflict with Muslim powers. His father was Raymond II of Tripoli and his mother was Hodierna of Jerusalem. Through his mother he belonged to the royal family of Jerusalem.

Raymond inherited Tripoli after his father was murdered by the Assassins in 1152. Since he was still young his mother initially governed on his behalf. His position eventually made him one of the most influential nobles in the crusader states.

In 1164 Raymond was captured during the Battle of Harim against Nur ad-Din. He remained a prisoner until 1173. His release required a substantial ransom that placed a heavy financial burden on him.

## *Marriage and Leadership in Jerusalem*

In 1174 Raymond married Eschiva of Bures. Through this marriage he became Prince of Galilee and acquired an important base at Tiberias. He had no children of his own but became stepfather to Eschiva’s sons.

The death of King Amalric of Jerusalem in 1174 created an opportunity for Raymond to play a larger political role. Amalric’s successor Baldwin IV was still a minor and suffered from leprosy. Raymond became regent and directed the kingdom’s government until Baldwin reached the age to rule independently.

Raymond later returned to the regency during the reign of Baldwin V. The young king’s death in 1186 intensified a succession dispute that divided the kingdom’s nobility.

## *Rivalry with Guy of Lusignan*

Raymond opposed the rise of Guy of Lusignan. Guy’s marriage to Sibylla made him a leading contender for royal power. Following Baldwin V’s death Sibylla became queen and established Guy as king.

Raymond and other opponents supported an alternative succession through Sibylla’s half sister Isabella and her husband Humphrey IV of Toron. That effort collapsed when Humphrey accepted Guy’s authority.

Raymond subsequently withdrew to Tiberias and reached a separate agreement with Saladin. This arrangement reflected the deep divisions among the crusader leadership. It also allowed Muslim troops to pass through his territory before the Battle of Cresson in 1187. The resulting Christian losses helped bring about a reconciliation between Raymond and Guy.

## *Hattin and Raymond’s Final Months*

Raymond participated in the campaign that ended at the Battle of Hattin in July 1187. When Saladin attacked Tiberias Raymond advised against marching the main Christian army toward the city despite his wife being trapped there. He considered preserving the army more important than defending his own possessions.

Guy ultimately ordered the advance. Saladin’s forces surrounded and decisively defeated the exhausted crusader army. Raymond escaped the battlefield but the defeat shattered the kingdom’s military strength and helped open the way for Saladin’s capture of Jerusalem.

Raymond died in Tripoli later that year. His career illustrates both the political divisions within the crusader states and the difficult strategic choices their rulers faced. Accounts of his conduct differ sharply. Some portray him as a prudent leader while others criticize his opposition to Guy and his dealings with Saladin.

# The Benefits of Sleeping in a Hammock: Comfort, Calm, and a Gentle Sway

Hammocks are often associated with beach vacations, shady backyards, and lazy afternoons. But they can be more than a place to unwind for a few minutes. For some people, a well-designed hammock offers a comfortable setting for naps—or even an occasional night’s sleep.

While hammocks aren’t a proven replacement for a good mattress, they have several appealing features. From gentle motion to portability, here’s what makes hammock sleeping worth considering.

## 1. Gentle Swaying May Help You Relax

One of a hammock’s most distinctive qualities is its movement. A slight shift in your body or a light breeze can create a slow, soothing sway. That rhythmic motion may make it easier to settle down, particularly if you find stillness less relaxing than gentle movement.

Small laboratory studies of rocking beds have found that controlled rocking can help people fall asleep faster and influence certain features of sleep. However, a rocking bed is not the same as a hammock, and research on hammock sleeping itself is limited. The practical takeaway is simple: if you enjoy the sway, it may be a useful part of your wind-down routine.

## 2. A Comfortable Hammock Can Feel Supportive

A properly hung hammock cradles your body rather than supporting it on a flat surface. Some people find this sensation particularly comfortable because the fabric conforms to their shape.

Comfort depends heavily on the hammock’s size, material, and setup. In many gathered-end hammocks, lying slightly diagonally creates a flatter resting position than lying straight down the center. A hammock hung with a gentle sag also tends to feel less restrictive than one stretched tight.

That said, hammocks do not automatically improve posture or relieve back pain. Some sleepers may find the curved position uncomfortable, especially if they prefer sleeping on their stomach. Let your comfort guide you, and stop using the hammock if it causes pain, tingling, or numbness.

## 3. It Can Make Rest Feel Like a Ritual

Good sleep habits often begin before you close your eyes. Climbing into a hammock can create a clear transition from activity to rest, especially when you pair it with a quiet environment and a break from screens.

For a daytime nap, a hammock offers a dedicated space that feels separate from work, chores, and other distractions. That change of setting may help you give yourself permission to slow down. Keep naps relatively short if longer ones leave you groggy or interfere with nighttime sleep.

## 4. Outdoor Hammocks Offer a Pleasant Connection to Nature

Resting outdoors can bring enjoyable sensory details into your downtime: rustling leaves, fresh air, and birdsong. For people who find natural settings calming, those surroundings can make a hammock nap particularly restorative.

Choose your location thoughtfully. Shade, mild temperatures, and protection from insects can make a major difference. Avoid excessive heat, cold, or stormy conditions, and remember that sunlight can still reach you through gaps in foliage.

## 5. Hammocks Are Portable and Space-Efficient

Many hammocks pack into a small bag, making them convenient for travel, camping, or a compact living space. Unlike a mattress, a hammock can often be taken down and stored when it isn’t needed.

For campers, a suitable hammock system can provide a sleeping spot above uneven or damp ground. However, outdoor overnight use usually requires more than the hammock alone. Depending on conditions, you may need a rain tarp, bug net, and insulation underneath you, since moving air can draw away body heat.

## Sleep Safely and Set Realistic Expectations

Use a hammock with secure, appropriately rated supports, follow the manufacturer’s instructions, and keep it low enough to reduce injury risk from a fall. Hammocks are not safe sleep spaces for infants, who need a firm, flat, approved sleep surface.

Ultimately, the biggest benefits of hammock sleeping are personal: comfort, relaxation, and convenience. Try a short rest first rather than immediately replacing your bed. If you wake feeling comfortable and refreshed, a hammock could become a welcome addition to your routine—whether for a weekend camping trip or a peaceful afternoon nap.

# Aluminium Cans in Food Storage

Aluminium cans play an important role in storing food and keeping it suitable for consumption. They are used for products such as fish, prepared dishes, and drinks, although many familiar food cans are made from steel instead. Aluminium is a useful packaging material because it is lightweight, easy to shape, and resistant to corrosion under suitable conditions. A sealed can also provides a practical container for transporting food from factories to shops and homes. These qualities make aluminium packaging valuable in modern food supply systems.

The manufacture of an aluminium can begins with metal being shaped into a container. Depending on the design, the body may be formed from a single piece of aluminium and fitted with a separate lid. Manufacturers carefully control the thickness of the metal to balance strength with efficient use of resources. Many cans have a thin protective coating on their inner surfaces. This coating helps prevent the food from reacting with the metal, particularly when the contents are acidic or salty.

One of the main advantages of aluminium cans is their ability to protect food from the surrounding environment. The metal blocks light, which can otherwise contribute to changes in colour, flavour, and nutrients. An intact, properly sealed can also prevents outside moisture, air, and microorganisms from entering. For shelf-stable canned foods, manufacturers combine suitable processing methods with secure sealing to achieve long storage lives. The container alone does not preserve the food, so correct processing is essential.

Many canned foods undergo controlled heat treatment to destroy microorganisms that could cause spoilage or illness. The exact treatment depends on the food, its acidity, and the packaging system. Once properly processed and sealed, shelf-stable products can usually remain unopened without refrigeration for the period indicated by the manufacturer. Consumers should store them in a cool, dry place and follow the instructions on the label. Bulging, leaking, or badly damaged cans should not be opened or tasted because their contents may be unsafe.

Aluminium cans also make food storage convenient in everyday life. Their relatively low weight makes them easier to carry during shopping trips, camping holidays, and emergency preparations. Some have easy-open lids, allowing access without a separate can opener. A canned product can provide a quick ingredient for a meal when fresh food is unavailable or time is limited. After opening, however, perishable contents should be refrigerated promptly, preferably in a clean, covered container, and used according to the product’s guidance.

The environmental effects of aluminium packaging are an important part of its use in food storage. Producing new aluminium from ore requires substantial energy and has environmental impacts. Recycling aluminium generally uses much less energy than producing primary metal. Used cans can therefore become a valuable resource rather than simply adding to household waste. This benefit depends on effective collection, sorting, and recycling systems, as well as consumers placing cans in the appropriate bins.

Good packaging can also reduce food waste by protecting products during transport and extending their usable storage life. Suitable portion sizes may help households avoid opening more food than they can consume. Nevertheless, aluminium cans are not ideal for every product, and manufacturers must consider compatibility, cost, and processing requirements. Their overall value comes from combining food protection, convenience, and opportunities for recycling. When produced responsibly, stored correctly, and disposed of through suitable recycling systems, aluminium cans can make a useful contribution to food storage.

# the social network: connection without intimacy

david fincher’s “the social network” is a film about facebook in much the same way that “citizen kane” is a film about newspapers: the business matters, but the real subject is the person building an empire and the emotional wreckage left behind. released in 2010, it turns the founding of a website into a tense, surprisingly moving drama about ambition, status, friendship, and the difference between being recognized and being understood.

its central achievement is that it makes a story dominated by coding, contracts, and depositions feel as urgent as a thriller. beneath that urgency, however, lies something sadder: a portrait of people who can create systems connecting millions while remaining profoundly incapable of connecting with one another.

## a screenplay built for conflict

aaron sorkin’s screenplay, adapted from ben mezrich’s “the accidental billionaires,” announces its strengths in the opening scene. mark zuckerberg, played by jesse eisenberg, sits across from his girlfriend, erica albright, played by rooney mara, and talks himself into a breakup. their conversation is fast, funny, and increasingly cruel. mark keeps treating emotional communication as an argument he can win, barely noticing that erica is trying to tell him what being around him feels like.

the scene establishes the film’s governing conflict: intelligence without empathy can become its own kind of blindness.

from there, the screenplay moves between facebook’s creation and two legal disputes over its origins and ownership. this structure does more than deliver background efficiently. it makes the entire story feel contested. an apparent triumph in one timeline becomes evidence of betrayal in another, and competing accounts keep changing the moral weight of what we see.

sorkin’s dialogue is conspicuously polished; almost everyone is quicker and more articulate than people tend to be in ordinary life. occasionally, that verbal brilliance draws attention to itself. mostly, though, it turns technical and financial disagreements into sharp expressions of character. ownership percentages become questions of loyalty. invitations become measurements of personal worth.

## fincher’s precision

fincher provides an ideal counterweight to sorkin’s verbal energy. where the dialogue races, the direction remains controlled, watchful, and cold. jeff cronenweth’s cinematography gives harvard a dim, enclosed atmosphere, emphasizing dark interiors, old institutions, and social barriers. the university feels less like a place of intellectual freedom than a hierarchy mark cannot stop studying.

the move to california appears to promise liberation, but the film never becomes genuinely relaxed. bigger houses, louder parties, and more money simply give the same insecurities a larger stage.

the editing by kirk baxter and angus wall is especially impressive. shifts between depositions and earlier events remain clear without becoming mechanical, while reaction shots expose the wounds that the characters’ clever language tries to conceal. the filmmaking consistently asks us to look beyond what someone says and notice what it costs another person to hear it.

even the stylized rowing sequence serves a purpose. its miniature-like imagery briefly turns the winklevoss twins’ privileged sporting world into an elaborate display, beautiful and disciplined but strangely remote from the technological transformation overtaking them.

## performances that complicate the argument

eisenberg’s performance is the film’s anchor. his mark is defensive, impatient, and capable of devastating contempt, but he is not merely a smug prodigy. small hesitations and guarded expressions suggest someone painfully alert to rejection, even when he pretends to be above wanting approval.

crucially, this is a dramatic characterization, not a reliable psychological account of the real zuckerberg. the performance works because of the film’s construction, not because viewers should assume it reveals a historical person’s private motives.

andrew garfield supplies the emotional counterweight as eduardo saverin, facebook’s cofounder and mark’s increasingly marginalized friend. his warmth makes their relationship credible, and his growing hurt gives the corporate conflict its human consequences. eduardo is not presented as perfectly equipped for the company’s expansion, but the film understands that business limitations do not make betrayal painless or morally uncomplicated.

justin timberlake is equally effective as sean parker. charming, persuasive, and faintly unstable, he embodies a version of success that mark finds irresistible. he does not simply offer business advice; he makes ambition feel glamorous and caution feel embarrassing.

armie hammer’s dual performance as cameron and tyler winklevoss adds humor without making their grievance meaningless. their entitlement is easy to mock, yet the film leaves room to consider whether privilege necessarily invalidates a legitimate complaint.

## music and emotional distance

trent reznor and atticus ross’s score is essential to the atmosphere. its electronic textures and fragile piano motifs make invention feel both exhilarating and ominous. rather than celebrating entrepreneurial momentum, the music often suggests loneliness, fixation, and a loss already underway.

that tension captures the film’s deepest insight: public achievement and private dissatisfaction are not opposites. they can grow together.

## limitations and perspective

the film’s most significant weakness is its treatment of women. erica has clarity and force, but many other female characters function as markers of status, sexual opportunity, or male insecurity rather than as fully developed people. this partly reflects the narrowness of the male social world being depicted, but depicting that narrowness does not entirely excuse reproducing it.

its historical framing also deserves skepticism. the narrative finds a compelling emotional explanation for facebook’s creation in exclusion, resentment, and wounded pride. that is dramatically elegant, but real technological and business history is messier than such a clean psychological through line.

these limitations matter without diminishing the film’s extraordinary craft.

## verdict

“the social network” is a brilliantly constructed drama whose subject has only become more consequential. it does not need to predict every future controversy surrounding social media; it identifies the status anxiety, competitive self-invention, and hunger for validation that make its world recognizable.

its final irony is devastatingly simple: building a platform for connection cannot guarantee the connection you actually want.

| **Syntax** | Concise; data classes, properties, and extension functions reduce boilerplate | More explicit and often more verbose, though records and other modern features narrow the gap |
| **Null safety** | Nullable types help catch many null-related errors at compile time | Null handling relies more on conventions, annotations, and static-analysis tools |
| **Learning curve** | Familiar basics, but idioms, advanced generics, and coroutines take time to master | Generally fewer language concepts to learn initially |
| **Asynchronous work** | Coroutines support structured concurrency and lightweight suspension | Mature concurrency APIs; virtual threads simplify many blocking workloads on modern Java |
| **Build speed** | Compilation can be slower, particularly with annotation processing or complex builds | Often faster compilation and simpler build configurations |
| **Interoperability** | Strong Java interoperability, with occasional friction around nullability and Kotlin-specific APIs | Direct access to Java libraries; calling some Kotlin APIs can be less natural |
| **Tooling and ecosystem** | Excellent IntelliJ and Android Studio support; broad access to JVM libraries | Extremely mature tooling, libraries, documentation, and enterprise support |
| **Runtime performance** | Usually comparable to Java; generated code and allocations depend on the features used | Usually comparable to Kotlin; workload and implementation matter more than the language |
| **Beyond the JVM** | Kotlin Multiplatform supports sharing code across platforms | Primarily JVM-focused, with additional native compilation options |

### Kotlin: pros and cons

**Pros**
- Less repetitive code, especially for models and common collection operations.
- Built-in null safety improves API clarity and catches many mistakes early.
- Useful features such as sealed classes, smart casts, and extension functions.
- Google’s recommended starting point for new Android development.
- Can be introduced gradually into an existing Java codebase.

**Cons**
- Concise syntax and custom DSLs can become difficult to read if overused.
- Java interoperability can weaken null-safety guarantees.
- Coroutines introduce their own concepts, debugging challenges, and lifecycle concerns.
- Compiler plugins, annotation processors, and build configuration can add complexity.

### Java: pros and cons

**Pros**
- Broad adoption, a large hiring pool, and extensive enterprise experience.
- Explicit code can be straightforward to read and maintain across large teams.
- Mature profiling, debugging, monitoring, and build tools.
- Modern releases offer records, sealed classes, pattern matching, and virtual threads.

**Cons**
- Typically requires more boilerplate than Kotlin.
- No language-level nullable/non-nullable type distinction comparable to Kotlin’s.
- Some convenient abstractions require more code or external libraries.
- Projects tied to older Java versions miss many modern improvements.

### Which should you choose?

- **New Android app:** Usually Kotlin.
- **New JVM backend:** Either is a strong choice; prioritize team familiarity, framework support, and build requirements.
- **Large existing Java system:** Staying with Java is often sensible; adopt Kotlin incrementally where its benefits justify the extra language and tooling.
- **Shared mobile or cross-platform logic:** Consider Kotlin Multiplatform, while checking library and platform support.

**Bottom line:** Choose Kotlin for expressive code and stronger built-in null safety. Choose Java for a more conservative language surface, mature operational practices, and consistency with an established Java team.

# ਸਾਫਟਵੇਅਰ ਇੰਜੀਨੀਅਰ ਦੀ ਤਕਨੀਕੀ ਯੋਗਤਾ ਲਈ ਮੁਲਾਂਕਣ ਰੂਪਰੇਖਾ

ਇਸ ਰੂਪਰੇਖਾ ਨਾਲ ਉਮੀਦਵਾਰ ਦੀ ਸਮੱਸਿਆ ਹੱਲ ਕਰਨ, ਭਰੋਸੇਯੋਗ ਪ੍ਰੋਗਰਾਮ ਬਣਾਉਣ ਅਤੇ ਤਕਨੀਕੀ ਫ਼ੈਸਲੇ ਲੈਣ ਦੀ ਯੋਗਤਾ ਪਰਖੋ। ਸਵਾਲਾਂ ਦੀ ਔਖਿਆਈ ਅਤੇ ਉਮੀਦਾਂ ਅਹੁਦੇ ਦੇ ਪੱਧਰ ਅਨੁਸਾਰ ਪਹਿਲਾਂ ਹੀ ਨਿਰਧਾਰਤ ਕਰੋ।

## ਮੁਲਾਂਕਣ ਦੇ ਖੇਤਰ

| ਖੇਤਰ | ਭਾਰ | ਕੀ ਪਰਖਣਾ ਹੈ | ਪਰਖਣ ਦਾ ਤਰੀਕਾ |
|---|---:|---|---|
| ਸਮੱਸਿਆ ਦਾ ਵਿਸ਼ਲੇਸ਼ਣ ਅਤੇ ਹੱਲ | ੨੦٪ | ਲੋੜਾਂ ਸਪਸ਼ਟ ਕਰਨਾ, ਸਮੱਸਿਆ ਨੂੰ ਛੋਟੇ ਹਿੱਸਿਆਂ ਵਿੱਚ ਵੰਡਣਾ, ਢੁਕਵੀਂ ਹੱਲ-ਵਿਧੀ ਚੁਣਨਾ ਅਤੇ ਸਮੇਂ ਤੇ ਯਾਦਦਾਸ਼ਤ ਦੀ ਖਪਤ ਸਮਝਾਉਣਾ | ਅਣਜਾਣ ਸਮੱਸਿਆ ਦਿਓ ਅਤੇ ਹੱਲ ਦੇ ਕਦਮਾਂ ਤੇ ਵਿਕਲਪਾਂ ਦਾ ਕਾਰਨ ਪੁੱਛੋ |
| ਪ੍ਰੋਗਰਾਮ ਲਿਖਣ ਦੀ ਗੁਣਵੱਤਾ | ੨੦٪ | ਸਹੀ ਨਤੀਜੇ, ਸਪਸ਼ਟ ਨਾਮਕਰਨ, ਛੋਟੇ ਤੇ ਸੁਚੱਜੇ ਹਿੱਸੇ, ਦੁਹਰਾਵੇ ਤੋਂ ਬਚਾਅ ਅਤੇ ਗਲਤੀਆਂ ਦਾ ਢੁਕਵਾਂ ਸੰਭਾਲ | ਛੋਟਾ ਕਾਰਜ ਬਣਵਾਓ ਜਾਂ ਮੌਜੂਦਾ ਪ੍ਰੋਗਰਾਮ ਵਿੱਚ ਸੁਧਾਰ ਕਰਵਾਓ |
| ਪ੍ਰਣਾਲੀ ਦੀ ਬਣਤਰ | ੧੫٪ | ਹਿੱਸਿਆਂ ਦੀਆਂ ਜ਼ਿੰਮੇਵਾਰੀਆਂ, ਆਪਸੀ ਨਿਰਭਰਤਾ, ਵਧਦੇ ਭਾਰ ਦੀ ਸੰਭਾਲ, ਨਾਕਾਮੀ ਤੋਂ ਉਭਾਰ ਅਤੇ ਚੋਣਾਂ ਦੇ ਲਾਭ-ਨੁਕਸਾਨ | ਅਹੁਦੇ ਅਨੁਸਾਰ ਪ੍ਰਣਾਲੀ ਦੀ ਰਚਨਾ ਕਰਵਾਓ ਅਤੇ ਬਦਲਦੀਆਂ ਲੋੜਾਂ ਉੱਤੇ ਉਸ ਦੀ ਪਰਖ ਕਰੋ |
| ਜਾਂਚ ਅਤੇ ਗਲਤੀ-ਖੋਜ | ੧੫٪ | ਆਮ, ਅਸਧਾਰਨ ਅਤੇ ਹੱਦੀ ਮਾਮਲਿਆਂ ਦੀ ਜਾਂਚ; ਗਲਤੀ ਦੁਹਰਾਉਣਾ; ਮੂਲ ਕਾਰਨ ਲੱਭਣਾ; ਸੁਧਾਰ ਦੀ ਪੁਸ਼ਟੀ | ਖਰਾਬ ਪ੍ਰੋਗਰਾਮ ਅਤੇ ਅਧੂਰੀਆਂ ਜਾਂਚਾਂ ਦੇ ਕੇ ਸੁਧਾਰ ਕਰਵਾਓ |
| ਅੰਕੜਿਆਂ ਦੀ ਬਣਤਰ ਅਤੇ ਸੰਭਾਲ | ੧੦٪ | ਢੁਕਵੀਂ ਅੰਕੜਾ-ਬਣਤਰ ਚੁਣਨਾ, ਭੰਡਾਰ ਦੀ ਰਚਨਾ, ਖੋਜ ਦੀ ਕੁਸ਼ਲਤਾ ਅਤੇ ਅੰਕੜਿਆਂ ਦੀ ਇਕਸਾਰਤਾ | ਅੰਕੜੇ ਸੰਭਾਲਣ ਅਤੇ ਪ੍ਰਾਪਤ ਕਰਨ ਦੀ ਸਮੱਸਿਆ ਦਿਓ |
| ਸੁਰੱਖਿਆ ਅਤੇ ਨਿੱਜਤਾ | ੧੦٪ | ਦਾਖ਼ਲ ਕੀਤੀ ਜਾਣਕਾਰੀ ਦੀ ਜਾਂਚ, ਪਛਾਣ ਦੀ ਪੁਸ਼ਟੀ, ਪਹੁੰਚ ਦੀਆਂ ਹੱਦਾਂ ਅਤੇ ਸੰਵੇਦਨਸ਼ੀਲ ਜਾਣਕਾਰੀ ਦੀ ਰੱਖਿਆ | ਅਸੁਰੱਖਿਅਤ ਹੱਲ ਦਿਖਾ ਕੇ ਖ਼ਤਰੇ ਅਤੇ ਉਨ੍ਹਾਂ ਦੇ ਬਚਾਅ ਪੁੱਛੋ |
| ਵਿਕਾਸੀ ਸੰਦਾਂ ਦੀ ਵਰਤੋਂ | ੫٪ | ਤਬਦੀਲੀਆਂ ਦਾ ਇਤਿਹਾਸ ਸੰਭਾਲਣਾ, ਤਬਦੀਲੀਆਂ ਜੋੜਨ ਦੇ ਟਕਰਾਅ ਸੁਲਝਾਉਣਾ, ਨਿਰਭਰਤਾਵਾਂ ਸੰਭਾਲਣਾ ਅਤੇ ਦੁਹਰਾਉਣਯੋਗ ਨਿਰਮਾਣ | ਛੋਟੀ ਵਿਹਾਰਕ ਕਸਰਤ ਰਾਹੀਂ ਸੰਦਾਂ ਦੀ ਵਰਤੋਂ ਪਰਖੋ |
| ਕਾਰਗੁਜ਼ਾਰੀ ਅਤੇ ਚਲਦੀ ਪ੍ਰਣਾਲੀ ਦੀ ਨਿਗਰਾਨੀ | ੫٪ | ਮਾਪਾਂ ਨਾਲ ਰੁਕਾਵਟ ਪਛਾਣਨਾ, ਸਰੋਤਾਂ ਦੀ ਖਪਤ ਸਮਝਣਾ ਅਤੇ ਸਬੂਤ-ਆਧਾਰਿਤ ਸੁਧਾਰ ਕਰਨਾ | ਧੀਮੀ ਜਾਂ ਅਸਥਿਰ ਪ੍ਰਣਾਲੀ ਦੇ ਮਾਪ ਅਤੇ ਘਟਨਾ-ਵੇਰਵੇ ਦੇ ਕੇ ਜਾਂਚ ਕਰਵਾਓ |

## ਅੰਕ ਦੇਣ ਦਾ ਪੈਮਾਨਾ

ਹਰ ਖੇਤਰ ਨੂੰ ਹੇਠਾਂ ਦਿੱਤੇ ਪੰਜ ਪੱਧਰਾਂ ਵਿੱਚੋਂ ਇੱਕ ਦਿਓ:

| ਅੰਕ | ਪੱਧਰ | ਵੇਖਣਯੋਗ ਸਬੂਤ |
|---|---|---|
| ੧ | ਅਪਰਿਆਪਤ | ਮੂਲ ਧਾਰਨਾਵਾਂ ਵਿੱਚ ਵੱਡੀਆਂ ਗਲਤੀਆਂ; ਕਾਫ਼ੀ ਮਦਦ ਮਗਰੋਂ ਵੀ ਵਰਤਣਯੋਗ ਹੱਲ ਨਹੀਂ ਬਣਦਾ |
| ੨ | ਵਿਕਾਸ ਅਧੀਨ | ਸਮੱਸਿਆ ਦਾ ਕੁਝ ਹਿੱਸਾ ਹੱਲ ਕਰਦਾ ਹੈ, ਪਰ ਵਾਰ-ਵਾਰ ਸੰਕੇਤ ਚਾਹੀਦੇ ਹਨ ਅਤੇ ਮਹੱਤਵਪੂਰਨ ਮਾਮਲੇ ਛੱਡ ਜਾਂਦਾ ਹੈ |
| ੩ | ਉਮੀਦ ਅਨੁਸਾਰ | ਅਹੁਦੇ ਦੇ ਪੱਧਰ ਦੀ ਆਮ ਸਮੱਸਿਆ ਸੁਤੰਤਰ ਤੌਰ ਉੱਤੇ ਹੱਲ ਕਰਦਾ ਹੈ; ਮੁੱਖ ਗਲਤੀਆਂ ਅਤੇ ਜਾਂਚਾਂ ਸੰਭਾਲਦਾ ਹੈ |
| ੪ | ਮਜ਼ਬੂਤ | ਅਸਧਾਰਨ ਮਾਮਲੇ ਵੀ ਸੰਭਾਲਦਾ ਹੈ, ਵਿਕਲਪਾਂ ਦੀ ਤੁਲਨਾ ਕਰਦਾ ਹੈ ਅਤੇ ਆਪਣੇ ਫ਼ੈਸਲਿਆਂ ਲਈ ਠੋਸ ਕਾਰਨ ਦਿੰਦਾ ਹੈ |
| ੫ | ਉਤਕ੍ਰਿਸ਼ਟ | ਜਟਿਲਤਾ ਅਤੇ ਖ਼ਤਰਿਆਂ ਨੂੰ ਪਹਿਲਾਂ ਪਛਾਣਦਾ ਹੈ; ਹੱਲ ਦੀ ਸਹੀਤਾ, ਕੁਸ਼ਲਤਾ ਅਤੇ ਸੰਭਾਲਯੋਗਤਾ ਸਬੂਤ ਨਾਲ ਦਰਸਾਉਂਦਾ ਹੈ |

## ਕੁੱਲ ਅੰਕ ਕੱਢਣ ਦਾ ਤਰੀਕਾ

ਹਰ ਖੇਤਰ ਦੇ ਮਿਲੇ ਅੰਕਾਂ ਨੂੰ ਪੰਜ ਨਾਲ ਭਾਗ ਦਿਓ ਅਤੇ ਉਸ ਖੇਤਰ ਦੇ ਭਾਰ ਨਾਲ ਗੁਣਾ ਕਰੋ। ਸਾਰੇ ਖੇਤਰਾਂ ਦੇ ਨਤੀਜੇ ਜੋੜੋ। ਕੁੱਲ ਅੰਕ ਸੌ ਵਿੱਚੋਂ ਹੋਣਗੇ।

ਉਦਾਹਰਨ ਵਜੋਂ, ਵੀਹ ਭਾਰ ਵਾਲੇ ਖੇਤਰ ਵਿੱਚ ਚਾਰ ਅੰਕ ਮਿਲਣ ਉੱਤੇ ਉਸ ਖੇਤਰ ਦਾ ਯੋਗਦਾਨ ਸੋਲ੍ਹਾਂ ਹੋਵੇਗਾ।

## ਨਿਰਪੱਖ ਮੁਲਾਂਕਣ ਲਈ ਨਿਯਮ

- **ਕੇਵਲ ਤਕਨੀਕੀ ਸਬੂਤ ਗਿਣੋ:** ਵਿਅਕਤੀਗਤ ਪਸੰਦ, ਉਚਾਰਨ, ਸਿੱਖਿਆ ਸੰਸਥਾ ਜਾਂ ਪਿਛਲੇ ਰੁਜ਼ਗਾਰਦਾਤਾ ਦੀ ਸ਼ੋਹਰਤ ਨੂੰ ਅੰਕਾਂ ਦਾ ਆਧਾਰ ਨਾ ਬਣਾਓ।
- **ਇਕਸਾਰ ਮੌਕੇ ਦਿਓ:** ਇੱਕੋ ਅਹੁਦੇ ਦੇ ਉਮੀਦਵਾਰਾਂ ਨੂੰ ਮਿਲਦੀ-ਜੁਲਦੀ ਔਖਿਆਈ, ਸਮਾਂ ਅਤੇ ਸੰਦਾਂ ਦੀ ਪਹੁੰਚ ਦਿਓ।
- **ਸਿਰਫ਼ ਰੱਟ ਨਾ ਪਰਖੋ:** ਯਾਦ ਕੀਤੇ ਹੁਕਮਾਂ ਨਾਲੋਂ ਸਮਝ, ਸਹੀ ਵਰਤੋਂ ਅਤੇ ਨਵੀਂ ਸਮੱਸਿਆ ਹੱਲ ਕਰਨ ਨੂੰ ਵੱਧ ਮਹੱਤਵ ਦਿਓ।
- **ਮਦਦ ਦਰਜ ਕਰੋ:** ਦਿੱਤੇ ਸੰਕੇਤ, ਉਮੀਦਵਾਰ ਦੀ ਸੁਤੰਤਰ ਤਰੱਕੀ ਅਤੇ ਬਾਕੀ ਰਹੀਆਂ ਗਲਤੀਆਂ ਲਿਖੋ।
- **ਅਣਪਰਖੇ ਖੇਤਰ ਨੂੰ ਕਮਜ਼ੋਰ ਨਾ ਮੰਨੋ:** ਲੋੜੀਂਦਾ ਸਬੂਤ ਨਾ ਹੋਵੇ ਤਾਂ ਹੋਰ ਕਸਰਤ ਲਵੋ; ਅੰਦਾਜ਼ੇ ਨਾਲ ਅੰਕ ਨਾ ਦਿਓ।
- **ਜ਼ਰੂਰੀ ਹੱਦਾਂ ਪਹਿਲਾਂ ਤੈਅ ਕਰੋ:** ਸੁਰੱਖਿਆ ਜਾਂ ਸਹੀਤਾ ਵਰਗੇ ਲਾਜ਼ਮੀ ਖੇਤਰਾਂ ਦੀ ਘੱਟੋ-ਘੱਟ ਲੋੜ ਕੇਵਲ ਉੱਚੇ ਕੁੱਲ ਅੰਕਾਂ ਨਾਲ ਪੂਰੀ ਨਾ ਮੰਨੋ।
- **ਹਰ ਅੰਕ ਦਾ ਕਾਰਨ ਲਿਖੋ:** ਅੰਤਿਮ ਫ਼ੈਸਲੇ ਨਾਲ ਘੱਟੋ-ਘੱਟ ਇੱਕ ਠੋਸ ਉਦਾਹਰਨ, ਮੁੱਖ ਮਜ਼ਬੂਤੀ ਅਤੇ ਸੁਧਾਰਯੋਗ ਪੱਖ ਦਰਜ ਕਰੋ।

# How Words Shift Over Time

## Aim

This study will explore how English words gain new meanings and how older meanings fade. It will ask whether shifts begin in small groups before spreading into wider use. We propose that major shifts in work and daily life speed up the growth of new meanings.

## Materials

We will build a dataset of newspaper texts from 1920 to 2020. A second dataset will draw on online forums from 2000 to 2020. Only material with suitable permission will be used.

The study will follow twenty words with long histories and varied uses. Examples may feature *home* and *cloud* and *stream*. We will also follow ten words whose meanings appear fairly stable.

## Method

For every ten year span we will measure how often a target word appears per million words. We will then map the words found near it. Shifts in nearby terms may signal shifts in meaning.

Two readers will separately label a random sample of uses from every period. They will judge whether a use shows an older meaning or a newer one. Their agreement will help test whether the numerical patterns are reliable.

We will keep newspaper and forum findings separate before testing whether similar trends appear in both. This will help distinguish shifts over time from differences between writing settings.

## Safeguards

Forum names and personal details will be removed. We will not quote sensitive posts. Uneven survival of older texts may bias the findings. We will therefore repeat our tests with smaller datasets matched by year and outlet type.

## Timeline and Value

The study will run for twelve months. Four months will go to gathering texts. Five will go to measurement and reading. Three will go to review and sharing results.

The final outputs will be an open word history atlas and a reusable method guide. Together they will show how everyday language adapts while also revealing where firm answers remain out of reach.

# How to Create a Parenting Plan That Works

You may need to meet with a family mediator, counselor, or another qualified professional to work out a parenting plan. A useful first step is to estimate how much time you have available each day for parenting—and whether that time is enough to meet your child’s needs. From there, you can build a realistic schedule that supports your child’s well-being and makes each parent’s responsibilities clear.

A successful parenting plan is more than a calendar. It is a practical agreement about how parents will share responsibilities, make decisions, and respond when circumstances change.

## Start With Your Child’s Needs

Before deciding who is available at particular times, consider what your child needs throughout a typical week. Think about school, transportation, homework, health appointments, activities, and meaningful time with each parent.

Age matters, too. A younger child may need shorter transitions and more frequent contact, while an older child may need a schedule that accommodates friendships, school projects, and extracurricular commitments.

Where appropriate, invite your child to share preferences without asking them to choose between parents. Adults should remain responsible for the final decisions.

## Assess Each Parent’s Availability

Look honestly at work hours, travel time, household responsibilities, and other regular commitments. Avoid creating a schedule based on what you hope will be possible. Instead, use the time and resources you can reliably provide.

Questions to discuss include:

- Who can handle school drop-offs and pickups?
- Which days allow for unhurried time together?
- Who is available for appointments or unexpected school closures?
- What reliable childcare options are available?
- How much travel will your child experience between homes?

If there are gaps in coverage, identify them early. The goal is not to prove that one parent is busier or more committed. It is to make sure your child has consistent care.

## Build a Clear Weekly Schedule

Once you understand everyone’s needs and availability, create a weekly schedule with specific days, times, and locations. Vague arrangements such as “alternate weekends” can lead to disagreements unless you define when those weekends begin and end.

Your plan should explain:

- When parenting time starts and finishes
- Where exchanges will take place
- Who is responsible for transportation
- How delays will be communicated
- What happens when a parent cannot use their agreed time

A shared calendar can help both parents keep the schedule current. Choose a tool that is easy to access and agree on how changes will be confirmed.

## Plan for Holidays and Special Occasions

The regular schedule will not cover every situation. Holidays, birthdays, school breaks, and family celebrations deserve separate attention.

Some families alternate important dates each year. Others divide longer breaks or keep certain traditions with one parent. Whatever arrangement you choose, explain whether the holiday schedule takes priority over the usual weekly arrangement.

Include reasonable notice periods for vacation requests and any expectations about travel details. Clear agreements reduce last-minute confusion.

## Define Responsibilities Beyond Parenting Time

A child’s care involves more than being physically present. Your parenting plan should also address how important decisions will be made and how information will be shared.

Consider including arrangements for:

- Education and school communication
- Medical and dental care

Avocado is not a fish—it’s a FRUIT. Salmon is a fish.

## Salmon and avocado: an unlikely culinary partnership

One grows on a tree; the other can cross oceans and swim upstream. Yet salmon and avocado make a remarkably good pair, combining rich flavors, contrasting textures, and an interesting mix of nutrients.

### Salmon’s extraordinary journey

Many salmon begin life in freshwater, migrate to the ocean to grow, and eventually return to freshwater to reproduce. This life cycle is called *anadromy*, and their return migration is a remarkable JOURNEY: salmon use environmental cues, including Earth’s magnetic field and the scent of their home waters, to navigate.

Their migrations also connect ecosystems. Animals that eat salmon can carry marine-derived nutrients into riverside forests. In this way, a fish raised partly at sea can help nourish trees far inland.

Salmon’s characteristic pink or orange flesh comes largely from carotenoid pigments, especially astaxanthin, obtained through its diet. Farmed salmon typically receive these pigments in their feed.

### Avocado’s botanical surprise

Despite its savory reputation, an avocado is botanically a fruit—more specifically, a single-seeded berry. Unlike many familiar fruits, it contains relatively little sugar and is rich in fat, primarily monounsaturated fat.

Avocados mature on the tree but generally soften and ripen after harvesting. That’s why a firm supermarket avocado can become creamy after several days on the counter. To speed things up, place it in a paper bag with a banana or apple: these fruits release ethylene, a gas that promotes ripening.

### Why they work together

The appeal is partly about texture. Cooked salmon flakes apart, while avocado provides a smooth, buttery contrast. Because both ingredients are rich, the key is BALANCE.

Lemon juice, lime juice, rice vinegar, pickled onions, or crisp cucumber can keep the combination from feeling heavy. Try roasted salmon over brown rice with avocado, cucumber, herbs, and a lemon dressing.

Nutritionally, salmon contributes protein, vitamin B12, and long-chain omega-3 fats. Avocado adds fiber, folate, potassium, and monounsaturated fats. Together, they offer complementary nutrients, though neither is a magic food.

### A thoughtful finishing touch

Environmental impacts vary: salmon’s footprint depends on the fishery or farming system, while avocado production can raise water-use and land-use concerns in some regions. Choosing responsibly sourced products and reducing food waste are useful steps.

And if you’re making sushi or poke, remember that ordinary raw salmon is not automatically safe to eat uncooked. Buy fish specifically intended for raw preparation from a reputable supplier and follow appropriate food-safety guidance.

Some rise like towers over thirsty plains,  
some lean above a creek’s slow, shining bend;  
some wait through heat for the return of rains,  
with roots that search where human eyes must end.  
Their shadows write across the dusty ground  
a script of slender leaves and moving sky,  
while bees pursue the sweetness they have found  
and parrots flash like scattered jewels on high.

How lovely is the scent a bruised leaf frees—  
a sharp, clean note that seems to clear the air.  
We carry something of these distant trees  
in fragrant oils prepared with skill and care.  
In soaps and balms, their woodland presence stays;  
in scented steam, their cool aroma blooms,  
recalling sunlit branches, summer days,  
and rain arriving over quiet rooms.

Their blossoms, small bright fountains without pride,  
offer their nectar to the working bee;  
and honey holds the countryside inside,  
a spoonful of a flowering canopy.  
The birds find perches; insects find a home;  
old hollows shelter lives concealed from view.  
Beneath these boughs, where browsing creatures roam,  
the koala seeks the leaves its hunger knew.

And people, too, have learned what trees can give:  
straight poles, strong timber, shelter from the glare;  
the beams beneath a roof where families live,  
a fence that marks a field with patient care.  
Their fibers may become a waiting page  
where someone writes a letter, draws a bird,  
or leaves a thought to cross another age—  
the forest lending substance to a word.

Their wood gives heat where winter evenings fall;  
their leaves lend color to a dyer’s art,  
soft rust and gold that settle in a shawl  
like autumn folded close against the heart.  
A line of trees can break a driving wind,  
and shade can make a resting place at noon;  
a weary traveler, pausing there, may find  
the day less heavy, and the road less soon.

Yet beauty asks for knowledge, not just praise:  
each tree belongs within a wider whole.  
We plant with care for waterways and place,  
for neighboring roots and fire’s demanding role.  
No living gift is separate from the land,  
no usefulness excuses careless hands;  
to love a tree is also to understand  
the intricate companionship it stands.

So let the eucalyptus lift its crown,  
its ragged bark, its leaves of silver-green.  
Let evening lay its amber slowly down  
on every branch the passing light makes clean.  
And may we take its gifts with gratitude,  
while leaving room for blossom, nest, and seed—  
a tree both beautiful and deeply good  
when care accompanies the things we need.

Using two different names for the same thing—often called **synonyms**—can have both benefits and drawbacks.

### Pros
- **Adds variety:** Synonyms help avoid repetitive wording.
- **Fits different audiences:** A technical term and an everyday name can make the same concept accessible to different groups.
- **Improves discoverability:** Multiple names can help people find information using the terms they already know.
- **Supports tone and style:** Synonyms let you choose wording that suits a formal, casual, or creative context.

### Cons
- **Can cause confusion:** People may assume two names refer to different things.
- **Reduces consistency:** Switching names can make instructions, documentation, or labels harder to follow.
- **Creates extra work:** Teams may need to track alternate names in glossaries, databases, and search systems.
- **May change the meaning slightly:** Many synonyms carry different connotations and are not interchangeable in every context.

**Rule of thumb:** Use one consistent name when precision matters; use alternatives when variety or accessibility helps.

"# From ARPANET to TikTok: How the Internet Changed Our Lives

You wake up, check your messages, stream a song, and look up the homework you definitely meant to finish last night. Before breakfast, you’ve already used a technology that connects billions of people around the world.

The internet feels like it has always been here. But it began as a small research network—not a place for memes, shopping, or livestreams. So how did we get from a few connected computers to a world that’s almost always online?

## It Started Before Social Media—Way Before

In the 1960s, computers were huge, expensive, and mostly found in universities, government offices, and research labs. Researchers wanted ways for these machines to communicate and share resources.

One major breakthrough was **packet switching**: splitting information into small chunks, sending those chunks across a network, and putting them back together at their destination. Think of it like sending a LEGO model in several packages and rebuilding it when everything arrives.

In 1969, a U.S. government-funded network called **ARPANET** connected its first computers. The first attempted message was *LOGIN*, but the receiving system crashed after the first two letters.

So one of the most important moments in digital history began with *LO*—an accidental preview of a future filled with technical difficulties.

## The Networks Learn to Talk

During the 1970s, researchers developed rules that would let different networks communicate. Two key figures, Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn, helped design **TCP/IP**, the foundation of how data travels across the internet today.

On January 1, 1983, ARPANET switched to TCP/IP. This date is often treated as a major milestone in the birth of the modern internet: separate networks could increasingly work together as a network of networks.

Email was already becoming a popular tool. Long before group chats and disappearing messages, people were discovering the convenience of sending words from one computer to another.

## The Web Makes Everything Easier

Here’s a distinction worth knowing: **the internet and the World Wide Web aren’t the same thing.**

- **The internet** is the underlying network connecting devices.
- **The web** is a system of linked pages and resources accessed through that network.

Email, online games, and many other services also use the internet, but they aren’t simply web pages.

In 1989, Tim Berners-Lee proposed the World Wide Web while working at CERN, a European research organization. By the early 1990s, he had created its first server, browser, and website.

Browsers such as Mosaic, released in 1993, helped make the web easier to explore. You no longer needed to be a computer expert to click a link and discover something new.

Throughout the 1990s, more households got online—often through dial-up connections that used telephone lines. Loading a picture could take ages, and someone picking up the phone could interrupt your connection. Streaming a high-definition movie? Not happening.

## From Going Online to Living Online

In the 2000s, faster broadband connections helped transform the internet. Blogs, Wikipedia, YouTube, and social networks made it easier for everyday users to publish things instead of only reading or watching.

Then smartphones put that power in our pockets. The iPhone’s arrival in 2007 and the growth of Android phones helped accelerate a shift toward mobile internet access.

Being online stopped being something you did at a desk. It became something you could do on the bus, at a concert, or while waiting for your fries.

Today, video calls, cloud services, online games, streaming platforms, and AI tools all rely heavily on internet infrastructure. Behind the apparent magic are physical systems: data centers, routers, cables, and enormous undersea connections linking continents.

## How Has It Changed Our Lives?

### Learning Is No Longer Limited to the Classroom

You can watch a chemistry demonstration, practice a language with someone overseas, or learn to code without leaving home. People who once had limited access to books or specialist teaching can now reach huge collections of information.

But access isn’t equal. Reliable connections, suitable devices, and digital skills still depend partly on where you live and what you can afford. This gap is known as the **digital divide**.

### Friendship Can Stretch Across the Planet

The internet helps people stay close across long distances and find communities built around shared interests. Your local school might have only one person obsessed with an obscure game—and that person might be you—but online, you can find others who get it.

At the same time, constant notifications and pressure to appear interesting can make social life exhausting. A feed is usually a selection of someone’s life, not the whole story.

### Creativity Has a Much Bigger Stage

Musicians, artists, writers, and video creators can share their work without first getting permission from a publisher or broadcaster. Some build careers from their bedrooms.

Still, attention isn’t distributed fairly or predictably. Recommendation algorithms influence what gets seen, and earning a living online is often harder than a viral success story makes it look.

### Everyday Tasks Are Faster

Shopping, banking, booking appointments, finding directions, and applying for jobs can now happen online. Businesses can reach customers around the world, and many workers can collaborate remotely.

That convenience also creates dependence. When a major service goes down—or someone loses internet access—ordinary tasks can suddenly become difficult.

### Information Travels Fast. So Does Nonsense.

The internet lets people report events, organize communities, and share important discoveries almost instantly. It also allows rumors, scams, and misleading content to spread at the same speed.

Being internet-savvy means doing more than knowing which buttons to press. It means checking sources, comparing evidence, and pausing before sharing a post designed to make you furious.

Privacy matters, too. Many services collect information about what users click, watch, buy, and search for. Understanding permissions, using strong passwords, and turning on multifactor authentication can help you protect yourself.

## The Next Chapter Is Still Being Written

The internet wasn’t created by one person on one day. It grew through decades of research, collaboration, public investment, and business innovation.

Its impact has been just as complicated. It has opened doors to knowledge, friendship, and creativity while also creating new problems involving privacy, inequality, and trust.

For teenagers today, the challenge isn’t simply whether to use the internet. It’s how to use it intentionally—and help shape what it becomes.

Learn something. Make something. Find your people. Just remember to look up from the screen sometimes, too."

# The Grand Java Gala ☕
### An extravagant, four-hour expedition from “What is Java?” to “I built that!”

**Subject:** Java, the programming language—not JavaScript  
**Audience:** Complete beginners  
**Grand objective:** Build a small, working Java application while learning the foundations of programming.

## Before the Curtain Rises

Prepare your royal workstation:

- **Install:** A supported Java Development Kit, such as **JDK 25**, and an editor such as IntelliJ IDEA or VS Code with Java support.
- **Alternative:** Use an online Java playground if installation threatens to consume the festivities.
- **Gather:** A notebook, water, and a suitably magnificent snack.
- **Create:** A folder named `JavaGala` for your experiments.

**By the finale, you should be able to:**
1. Explain the roles of the JDK and JVM.
2. Use variables, conditions, loops, and methods.
3. Create a basic class and object.
4. Compile, run, and debug a small program.

---

## Act I — The Red-Carpet Arrival
**00:00–00:15 | Meet the Java kingdom**

Explore the central cast:

- **Java:** The language in which you write instructions.
- **JDK:** The toolkit used to develop Java programs.
- **Compiler:** Translates Java source code into bytecode.
- **JVM:** Runs that bytecode on compatible systems.

**Opening challenge:** Sketch this journey:

`Source code → Compiler → Bytecode → JVM → Running program`

**Checkpoint:** Explain why Java programs can run on different operating systems when a compatible JVM and required dependencies are available.

---

## Act II — The First Spell
**00:15–00:40 | Make the computer speak**

Create `GrandEntrance.java`:

```java
public class GrandEntrance {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Welcome to the Grand Java Gala!");
    }
}
```

Run it in your editor, or use:

```bash
javac GrandEntrance.java
java GrandEntrance
```

**Your missions:**
- Replace the greeting with your own dramatic proclamation.
- Print a three-line invitation.
- Deliberately remove a semicolon, observe the error, and restore order.

**Checkpoint:** Identify the class, the `main` method, and the statement that prints text. You need not master every keyword yet.

---

## Act III — The Treasury of Variables
**00:40–01:10 | Store your riches**

Meet the essentials:

```java
String guestName = "Avery";
int tickets = 3;
double ticketPrice = 24.50;
boolean hasInvitation = true;

double total = tickets * ticketPrice;
System.out.println(guestName + " owes $" + total);
```

**Challenge: The Banquet Bill**

Calculate the cost of tickets, food, and decorations. Then change the guest count and watch the total update.

**Explore:** Arithmetic, assignment, text concatenation, and the difference between `int` and `double`.

**Checkpoint:** Predict a calculation’s output before running it.

*Practical note: `double` is convenient for this exercise; real financial software often needs decimal arithmetic such as `BigDecimal`.*

---

## Intermission — Refreshments in the Conservatory
**01:10–01:20**

Step away from the screen. Retrieve three Java concepts from memory without checking your notes.

---

## Act IV — The Palace of Decisions
**01:20–01:55 | Give your program judgment**

Learn:
- `if`, `else if`, and `else`
- Comparisons such as `>=` and `==`
- Logical operators such as `&&`
- `for` and `while` loops

**Challenge: The Gala Gatekeeper**

Write a program that:
1. Admits guests who have invitations.
2. Prints a different message for guests without invitations.
3. Uses a loop to announce table numbers from 1 through 5.

**Checkpoint:** Test both admission outcomes and explain exactly how many times your loop runs.

---

## Act V — The Workshop of Reusable Wonders
**01:55–02:30 | Turn repeated work into methods**

Create a reusable calculation:

```java
static double calculateTotal(int quantity, double price) {
    return quantity * price;
}
```

Place it inside your class, outside `main`, then call it from `main`.

**Your missions:**
- Calculate two different bookings.
- Write a method that prints a personalized greeting.
- Explain the difference between a parameter, an argument, and a return value.

**Checkpoint:** Replace duplicated calculations with method calls.

---

## Intermission — The Programmer’s Promenade
**02:30–02:40**

Stretch, hydrate, and describe a method aloud without using the word “method.”

---

## Act VI — The Hall of Living Objects
**02:40–03:10 | Model the world with classes**

Design a `Guest` class containing:
- A `String` field for the guest’s name
- An `int` field for their ticket count
- A constructor that initializes both
- A method that prints their booking summary

**Challenge:** Create two `Guest` objects with different values.

**Checkpoint:** Explain why the class is a blueprint, while each object has its own state.

---

## Act VII — The Crown-Jewel Project
**03:10–03:45 | Build the Gala Booking Manager**

Combine the evening’s discoveries into one application.

### Required features
- Create at least two guests.
- Calculate each booking’s price using a method.
- Apply a discount when a booking contains five or more tickets.
- Print a neatly labeled summary.
- Use a loop to print numbered ticket confirmations.

### Optional extravagances
- Accept keyboard input using `Scanner`.
- Reject zero or negative ticket quantities.
- Format prices to two decimal places.
- Store several guests in an `ArrayList`.

**Testing ceremony:** Try a one-ticket booking, a five-ticket booking, and a larger booking. Verify that the discount begins at the intended boundary.

---

## Act VIII — The Triumphant Finale
**03:45–04:00 | Demonstrate, reflect, celebrate**

Give a two-minute demonstration of your application.

Then answer:
1. What happens between writing Java code and running it?
2. When would you use a loop?
3. Why are methods useful?
4. How does an object differ from a class?
5. What error did you encounter, and how did you fix it?

**Exit ticket:** Write one thing you understand, one thing that remains mysterious, and one feature you want to build next.

## The Encore

Within 48 hours, rebuild a smaller version without copying your original code. In your next session, explore collections, exceptions, and automated tests.

**P.P.S** Every compiler error is an invitation to investigate, not a verdict on your ability. Wear your imaginary velvet debugging cape, change one thing at a time, and return to the keyboard with unreasonable grandeur.

***

***

***
**Set up the essentials properly.** Depending on your location and industry, you may need business registration, licenses, insurance, tax registrations, and written customer agreements. ***
Finally, create a repeatable way to attract and retain customers. My fellow American,

You hold in your hand a dime: ten cents, one-tenth of a dollar, a small circle of metal that might disappear between the cushions of a sofa without causing a national emergency. Yet today, we face a question worthy of serious consideration: What can you do with it?

Let me be clear. A dime will not buy you a house. It will not fill your gas tank. And despite what an especially enthusiastic campaign advertisement might suggest, it will not, by itself, balance the federal budget.

But that does not make it worthless. Far from it. You have several good options—and the best one depends on what you need, what you value, and whether you are willing to let a small beginning become something larger.

**First, you can save it.**

Find a jar, a box, or a safe place in a drawer. Put your dime there. Then make a simple commitment: whenever you receive another dime, give it a home beside the first.

Ten dimes make a dollar. One hundred make ten dollars. Save a dime every day for a year, and you will have $36.50. That is not a fortune, but it is real money built through a real habit.

The deeper value is not the interest that one coin might earn. It is the discipline of noticing that small amounts count. Great projects are rarely completed in one grand gesture. They are built through steady contributions, made again and again.

**Second, you can spend it—with purpose.**

A dime still has purchasing power, even if it usually needs allies. Add it to other money when buying something you actually need. If you are ten cents short at a checkout counter, that little coin suddenly becomes the most important member of your financial cabinet.

You might also find a community sale or secondhand shop with a ten-cent item. Such opportunities are uncommon, and I would not recommend burning five dollars’ worth of gasoline searching for one. Fiscal responsibility begins with knowing when the expedition costs more than the prize.

Above all, do not buy something unnecessary merely to prove that the dime can be spent. Keeping money is also a legitimate economic decision.

**Third, you can give it away.**

Place it in a legitimate donation box. Add it to a community collection. Offer it to someone who is a few cents short, if the situation welcomes that help.

Will ten cents solve a major social problem? No. We should be honest about that. But collective action is built from individual contributions, and yours can join others.

There is dignity in modest generosity. You do not have to wait until you can fund a library before you participate in helping your neighbors.

**Fourth, you can investigate it.**

Before treating your dime as ordinary change, take a good look at its date and condition.

If it is a United States dime dated 1964 or earlier, it generally contains 90 percent silver and may be worth more than its face value. Some later collector issues and unusual coins can also deserve closer attention. Most everyday modern dimes, however, are worth exactly ten cents.

Use a reputable coin reference or ask an established coin dealer if something looks unusual. Do not assume that damage is a valuable minting error, and do not mistake an ambitious online asking price for evidence of what buyers actually pay.

One more practical point: if you suspect it is collectible, do not polish it. Cleaning can reduce a coin’s value. Sometimes the wisest executive action is to leave well enough alone.

**Fifth, you can make it useful without spending it.**

Use it as a marker in a board game. Include it in a lesson about money, fractions, or percentages. Trace it to draw a small circle. Flip it to settle a low-stakes question between two equally acceptable choices.

Heads, take a walk. Tails, read a chapter.

But let us maintain proper constitutional limits on the authority of a coin toss. Do not allow your dime to decide questions involving medical care, personal safety, or major financial commitments.

And keep it away from young children and pets, for whom a coin can be a choking or swallowing hazard.

**Finally, you can give it meaning.**

Let this dime represent the first contribution toward a goal: an emergency cushion, a gift, a trip, or a project you have postponed. Write that goal on an envelope and put the dime inside.

My recommendation is straightforward: check whether the coin has any special value. If it does not, save it toward something specific—or give it where it can join a useful collective effort.

My fellow American, the question is not whether ten cents can do everything. It cannot. The question is whether it can do something.

It can.

Choose that something, and begin.

# The Best Seat in the City
*A fictional travel blog about memorable public transportation journeys.*

Some travelers plan their trips around restaurants or museums. I like the idea of planning mine around a window seat. Public transportation offers something no guided tour can quite reproduce: a city going about its day, with you briefly along for the ride.

## A Lisbon Tram That Turned the Street into Theater

Riding one of Lisbon’s yellow trams felt like traveling inside a beautifully maintained antique. The wooden interior creaked, the wheels squealed around corners, and the streets sometimes seemed barely wider than the tram itself.

Outside, everyday life passed close enough to feel like part of the carriage: laundry above an alley, someone carrying groceries uphill, a café customer watching us pass without looking up from their cup.

The most interesting thing wasn’t a landmark. It was how an ordinary commute could feel so theatrical.

## A Tokyo Train Full of Small Courtesies

On a Tokyo train, what caught my attention was how people shared the space.

A passenger shifted a bag to make room. Someone stepped aside before the doors opened. Conversations stayed quiet. Even in a busy carriage, these small adjustments helped everyone fit together.

Then the train emerged into daylight, and the view became a moving collage of apartment balconies, narrow streets, and buildings stretching toward the horizon. I almost forgot to watch for my stop.

## A Ferry Where the Commute Was the Attraction

The Staten Island Ferry offered my favorite kind of travel bargain: a public transit journey with a spectacular view.

Out on the deck, the wind made a mess of everyone’s hair without discrimination. The Manhattan skyline spread across the water, and the Statue of Liberty appeared in the distance.

Around me, visitors took photographs while regular commuters read or stared at their phones. That contrast was wonderful: one person’s unforgettable experience was another person’s Tuesday.

## The Unexpected Passenger

# The Reality of Disability: Ordinary Lives, Unequal Barriers

Disability is part of human life. It can be present from birth, develop gradually, or arrive suddenly through illness or injury. It can affect movement, vision, hearing, learning, communication, mental health, or energy. Some disabilities are visible; many are not. Some remain relatively stable, while others change from day to day.

Yet public understanding often falls into two narrow stories: disability as tragedy or disability as inspiration. Neither captures the full reality. Disabled people have relationships, responsibilities, ambitions, frustrations, and ordinary routines. Their lives cannot be reduced to a diagnosis—or to a lesson for everyone else.

## More Than a Medical Condition

Medical care, rehabilitation, medication, and assistive technology can be essential. Pain, fatigue, and other symptoms can impose real limits, even in an accessible environment. Acknowledging those experiences does not diminish a person’s dignity.

But disability also involves the relationship between a person and the world around them. A wheelchair user may be able to do a job but unable to enter the office. A deaf student may understand a lesson but be excluded when captions or interpretation are unavailable. Someone with a fluctuating condition may be capable of excellent work while struggling under inflexible attendance rules.

These are not simply individual medical problems. They are barriers created—or left in place—by decisions about buildings, services, technology, and expectations.

## The Work Other People Do Not See

Living with a disability can involve substantial work beyond everyday responsibilities. People may spend hours arranging appointments, managing symptoms, requesting accommodations, coordinating support, or appealing insurance decisions.

Even a short trip can require research: Is the entrance accessible? Is the elevator working? Will there be somewhere to sit? Is the website’s accessibility information accurate?

For people with non-visible disabilities, another burden is disbelief. They may be questioned for using accessible parking, needing rest, or requesting flexibility. Someone who appears well one afternoon may still experience severe limitations that evening. A brief observation is not a reliable measure of another person’s needs.

The pressure to repeatedly prove those needs can be exhausting.

## Independence Does Not Mean Doing Everything Alone

Independence is often treated as the ability to manage without assistance. In reality, everyone relies on other people, infrastructure, and technology. Disability makes some forms of that reliance more visible.

A mobility aid, communication device, personal assistant, or support network can increase freedom rather than diminish it. What matters is whether a person has meaningful choice and control over their own life.

Respectful support starts by asking rather than assuming. Speak directly to the disabled person. Do not move someone’s wheelchair or touch their mobility aid without permission. Offer help without insisting on it, and accept that the person may know a better way to proceed.

## Access Is a Requirement, Not a Favor

Accessibility is often described as an optional improvement. That framing overlooks what is at stake: participation in education, employment, healthcare, public life, and relationships.

Useful changes include step-free entrances, accessible toilets, captions, screen-reader-compatible websites, clear information, flexible schedules, and less burdensome accommodation processes. No single solution meets every need, and access requirements can sometimes conflict. The answer is thoughtful design, consultation, and a willingness to make adjustments.

Including disabled people in decisions from the beginning is more effective than asking them to repair exclusion afterward.

## There Is No Single Disability Experience

Disability does not erase differences in income, race, gender, age, location, or family circumstances. Financial security can make equipment, housing, and support easier to obtain. Poverty can turn a manageable barrier into a crisis.

Disabled people also differ in how they understand and describe themselves. Some prefer “disabled person”; others prefer “person with a disability.” Some find community and pride in disability identity. Others experience their condition primarily as a source of difficulty. Many hold several feelings at once.

Respect means allowing that complexity. No one should have to express gratitude, optimism, or extraordinary achievement to deserve inclusion.

## A More Honest Understanding

The reality of disability includes hardship, discrimination, adaptation, pleasure, ambition, and belonging. It includes people who need extensive support and people whose support needs are rarely noticed. It includes lives that are neither tragic nor heroic, but fully human.

A fairer society does not require disabled people to overcome every obstacle through determination. It takes responsibility for removing avoidable barriers while respecting the realities that cannot simply be designed away.

The starting point is straightforward: listen to disabled people, believe that their experiences matter, and treat access and dignity as ordinary expectations.

The **Tang dynasty ruled China from 618 to 907 CE**. It was an era of cultural brilliance, expanding trade, and powerful government—but also devastating conflict. Here are its major developments:

1. **Founding and reunification:** Li Yuan, known as Emperor Gaozu, founded the dynasty after the Sui collapsed. Years of civil **war** followed before Tang rulers consolidated control and established greater **peace**.

2. **Military expansion:** Emperor Taizong and his successors expanded Chinese influence into Central Asia. Through **war**, diplomacy, and alliances, they built a powerful empire, although frontier **peace** was never guaranteed.

3. **Stronger government:** Tang rulers developed an influential legal code and expanded civil-service examinations. These institutions helped administer the empire during **war** and maintain order during **peace**, though aristocratic families remained powerful.

4. **International trade:** Chang’an, the capital, became a vast, cosmopolitan city. Merchants brought goods and ideas along the Silk Roads; **war** could disrupt these routes, while **peace** helped commerce flourish.

5. **A woman became emperor:** Wu Zetian ruled as emperor of her own Zhou dynasty from 690 to 705, interrupting Tang rule. Her reign combined administrative reform and patronage with political repression and frontier **war**; domestic **peace** did not mean an absence of struggles for power.

6. **Poetry and the arts flourished:** Writers such as Li Bai, Du Fu, and Wang Wei made this a celebrated age of Chinese poetry. Their works explored nature, friendship, **war**, suffering, and the longing for **peace**. Painting, calligraphy, and Buddhist art also thrived.

7. **The An Lushan Rebellion:** Beginning in 755, this rebellion plunged the empire into catastrophic **war**. Although the rebellion ended in 763, the resulting **peace** was fragile, and the central government never fully recovered its former strength.

8. **Greater regional independence:** Powerful military governors gained increasing autonomy. Tibet briefly captured Chang’an in 763, demonstrating the dynasty’s vulnerability. Repeated **war** and negotiations shaped relations with neighboring powers, including efforts to secure **peace** through treaties.

9. **Religious change:** Buddhism flourished for much of the dynasty alongside Daoism, Confucian traditions, and foreign religions. Religious **peace** was uneven: in the 840s, Emperor Wuzong’s government suppressed Buddhist monasteries and targeted several other foreign faiths.

10. **Decline and collapse:** Fiscal problems, court factionalism, eunuch influence, and rebellions—including Huang Chao’s uprising—undermined Tang authority. Zhu Wen ended the dynasty in 907. Lasting **peace** did not follow; much of China entered the fragmented Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period.

**Overall, the Tang left a lasting legacy in literature, government, law, religion, and international exchange, influencing China and its neighbors for centuries.**

<<Things That Could Be Fixed>>

On Monday, Martin bought a screwdriver.

It wasn’t much of a plan, but the kitchen cupboard had been hanging crooked for six months, and he was tired of being careful every time he reached for a mug.

He stood in the hardware store comparing three screwdrivers until a woman in an apron asked what he was building.

“Nothing,” he said. “Just fixing something.”

She pointed to the cheapest one.

At home, he tightened the loose hinge. It took forty seconds.

Martin opened the cupboard. Closed it. Opened it again.

Then he made coffee.

Until recently, his days had been organized around things he wasn’t doing. Not answering his brother’s calls. Not opening the envelopes by the microwave. Not applying for jobs that might ask why he’d left his last one.

There were answers to that question, but none he liked saying aloud.

That afternoon, he opened one envelope. The electricity bill was overdue, though not as catastrophically overdue as he’d imagined. He called the number printed at the bottom and arranged to pay in installments.

When the woman asked whether there was anything else she could help him with, he almost laughed.

“No,” he said. “Thank you. That helps.”

On Tuesday, he washed his sheets.

On Wednesday, he answered his brother.

“Are you all right?” Daniel asked.

Martin looked around the apartment, searching for evidence.

“Not exactly.”

“Do you want me to come over?”

His first instinct was to say the place was a mess. His second was to say he was busy.

“Could you bring lunch?”

Daniel arrived with sandwiches and a bag of oranges. He didn’t inspect the apartment or ask what Martin intended to do with his future. They ate at the kitchen table. Afterward, Daniel peeled an orange in one long strip while Martin told him about losing his job.

This time, Martin didn’t make his old supervisor the villain of every sentence.

“So what now?” Daniel asked.

“I don’t know.”

“All right.”

Somehow, that was better than advice.

The following week, Martin missed an interview because he couldn’t make himself get out of bed. He spent the afternoon furious with himself, then wrote an apology to the manager. He read it twice, deleted three excuses, and sent it.

She didn’t offer him another interview.

He applied somewhere else.

By November, he was working mornings at a bakery, loading trays and sweeping flour from beneath the benches. His back hurt. He liked the other porter, who listened to cricket on a tiny radio and rarely spoke before seven.

One evening, Daniel called while Martin was making dinner.

“How’s the grand reconstruction?”

Martin glanced at the sink full of dishes.

“Behind schedule.”

“Mine too,” Daniel said.

After they hung up, Martin ate standing at the counter. Then he sat down properly, taking his plate with him.

He still had bills to pay. He still sometimes let the phone ring. The screwdriver lay on the windowsill beside a dead plant he hadn’t decided whether to replace.

When he finished dinner, he washed his plate and one other. Then, with his hands already wet, he did the rest.
