1. project title
   - perceived eye colour and customer purchasing decisions: a randomized study of appearance-based bias in sales interactions.

2. purpose and scientific rationale
   - this project will investigate whether perceived eye colour affects customers’ responses to an otherwise identical salesperson.
   - the study will not assume that eye colour determines competence or predicts inherent sales ability.
   - apparent associations could reflect customer bias or contextual factors rather than differences between salespeople.
   - the primary objective is to estimate the effect of displayed eye colour on purchasing decisions under controlled conditions.
   - a secondary objective is to examine whether customer perceptions of trustworthiness or competence vary across conditions.

3. research questions and hypotheses
   - does displayed eye colour change the probability of a purchase during a standardized sales interaction?
   - does displayed eye colour affect perceived trustworthiness or willingness to interact again?
   - the primary null hypothesis is that purchasing probability does not differ across eye-colour conditions.
   - all primary comparisons and secondary analyses will be preregistered before outcome data are examined.
   - no directional hypothesis about superior eye colours will be advanced without credible prior evidence.

4. interpretation of customer experience
   - the saying “the customer is always right” will be treated as a service principle that encourages respectful listening.
   - it will not be treated as evidence that every customer judgment is accurate or ethically acceptable.
   - customer preferences will be measured without endorsing appearance-based stereotypes.
   - participant complaints will receive respectful review without compromising research integrity or the dignity of salespeople.

5. study design
   - the project will use a randomized online experiment involving standardized recorded sales presentations.
   - consenting adult actors will portray salespeople using identical scripts and equivalent presentation conditions.
   - each actor’s recording will be edited to create several realistic eye-colour versions.
   - only iris colour will be intentionally altered within each actor’s recording. pupil size and other facial features will remain unchanged.
   - participants will be randomly assigned to one version and will not see multiple versions of the same actor.
   - multiple actors will be used to reduce dependence on the appearance or delivery of one individual.
   - assignment will be balanced across actor identities and eye-colour conditions.

6. preliminary validation
   - a separate pilot sample will assess whether the eye-colour edits are noticeable and realistic.
   - the pilot will evaluate image quality and unintended changes in perceived facial expression.
   - versions with visible editing artifacts will be revised or excluded using predefined criteria.
   - pilot participants will not participate in the main experiment.
   - manipulation checks in the main study will follow the purchase decision to reduce priming.

7. participant recruitment
   - participants will be adults who can provide informed consent.
   - recruitment will seek a broad range of customer backgrounds relevant to the intended study population.
   - recruitment through teaching or supervisory relationships will be avoided where participation could feel compulsory.
   - any student recruitment will include an equivalent nonresearch alternative if course credit is offered.
   - eligibility requirements and accessibility limitations will be stated clearly.
   - exclusion rules will be defined before recruitment and will not depend on whether a participant’s response supports the hypothesis.

8. outcomes and operational definitions
   - the primary outcome will be a binary purchase decision in a standardized sales task.
   - where feasible this will involve a low-value product purchased using a study-provided spending endowment. participants will not risk their own money.
   - participation compensation will remain separate from the purchase decision.
   - if a hypothetical task is used instead then the outcome will be described as purchase intention rather than actual sales success.
   - secondary outcomes will include willingness to interact again and ratings of perceived trustworthiness and competence.
   - these ratings represent customer impressions. they do not establish the salesperson’s actual character or ability.
   - the study will not equate a single purchasing decision with long-term professional success.

9. sample size and analysis
   - the sample size will be justified through an advance power analysis or simulation based on a defined smallest effect of practical interest.
   - the calculation will account for baseline purchasing probability and variation across actors.
   - the registration will specify recruitment targets and stopping rules.
   - the primary analysis will use a logistic regression model appropriate to the randomized design and repeated use of actor identities.
   - results will include estimated purchasing probabilities and effect sizes with uncertainty intervals.
   - multiple primary comparisons will receive a prespecified multiplicity adjustment.
   - exploratory subgroup analyses will be clearly labelled and interpreted cautiously.
   - a nonsignificant result will not be presented as proof that no effect exists. any equivalence claim will require a preregistered equivalence analysis.

10. consent and incomplete disclosure
   - participants will receive information about study procedures and compensation along with foreseeable risks and withdrawal options.
   - consent materials may describe the project as research on visual presentation and customer decisions without identifying eye colour as the specific manipulation.
   - any incomplete disclosure will require explicit ethics board approval and a justification that full disclosure would meaningfully bias responses.
   - participants will receive a prompt debriefing that explains the manipulation and the study’s focus on possible appearance-based bias.
   - the debriefing will explain how to request data withdrawal before a clearly stated anonymization deadline.
   - actors will provide separate consent for recording and digital alteration of their appearance.

11. risks and safeguards
   - foreseeable risks include discomfort about appearance judgments and concern that the findings could reinforce discrimination.
   - materials will avoid suggesting that any eye colour is naturally more honest or competent.
   - no results will be used to evaluate real employees or guide hiring decisions.
   - the study will not collect genetic information or infer ancestry from eye colour.
   - demographic information will be optional and collected only when justified by the analysis plan.
   - participants may stop participation without penalty under the compensation terms disclosed at consent.
   - adverse events and unexpected complaints will be documented and reported under university procedures.

12. privacy and data management
   - identifying information will be stored separately from research responses.
   - study files will use coded identifiers and encrypted university-approved storage.
   - access will be limited to authorized research personnel.
   - the approved retention period and deletion procedures will be stated in the consent materials.
   - public datasets will exclude identifiable recordings and potentially identifying combinations of participant information.
   - actor images will not be publicly distributed unless separately authorized.
   - any external editing or hosting service will undergo privacy review before receiving identifiable material.

13. limitations and responsible reporting
   - digitally displayed eye colour may not have the same effect as eye colour in face-to-face interactions.
   - screen quality and viewing conditions may affect how participants perceive the manipulation.
   - findings may depend on the product and cultural setting.
   - randomized manipulation can support causal conclusions about the tested display conditions. it cannot establish that natural eye colour determines real-world sales ability.
   - publications will report null findings and methodological limitations alongside any detected effects.
   - dissemination will explicitly reject using eye colour as a recruitment or promotion criterion.

14. oversight and approval request
   - recruitment will begin only after ethics approval and completion of the preregistration.
   - the principal investigator will oversee consent procedures and data security.
   - material changes to the protocol will be submitted for ethics review before implementation.
   - the board will receive the protocol and recruitment materials alongside consent documents and debriefing text.
   - approval is requested for a study of customer responses to manipulated appearance rather than a ranking of people by biological traits.

P.P.S. any observed effect should be interpreted as evidence about customer responses within the tested setting rather than evidence that one eye colour makes someone a better salesperson.

# Project Proposal: AI for Inclusive Learning

## 1. Project Summary

This project will use machine learning and AI to strengthen foundational literacy and numeracy in underserved primary schools in a developing country. It will combine offline learning tools with teacher support and locally relevant educational content.

The proposed 18-month pilot will involve 30 schools serving approximately 6000 learners and 150 teachers. Implementation will be led by a local education organization in partnership with the education ministry and a local university.

**Core principle:** AI will support teachers rather than replace them.

## 2. Problem Statement

Many schools face shortages of trained teachers and appropriate learning materials. Large classes make individualized support difficult. Language barriers and unreliable electricity further limit access to quality education.

Technology alone cannot solve these problems. This project will pair practical AI tools with teacher development and infrastructure support.

## 3. Objectives

The project will aim to:

- Improve foundational literacy and numeracy.
- Help teachers identify learning gaps and provide targeted support.
- Expand access to curriculum-aligned materials in local languages.
- Reduce time spent preparing lessons and routine assessments.
- Establish an affordable model that local institutions can maintain.

## 4. Proposed Solution

### Adaptive learning for students

An offline-first application will offer short lessons and practice activities aligned with the national curriculum.

Machine learning will use student responses to recommend suitable exercises. Teachers will be able to review and override recommendations.

Students will use shared school devices during scheduled learning sessions. Participation will not require a personal phone or home internet connection.

### AI assistance for teachers

A teacher-facing assistant will help draft lesson plans and explanations using an approved collection of curriculum materials.

Teachers will review all generated materials before classroom use. The system will avoid unrestricted student conversations during the pilot to reduce exposure to inaccurate or inappropriate responses.

### Local language and accessibility support

Local educators will adapt content to relevant languages and cultural contexts.

Audio lessons and adjustable text sizes will support learners with different needs. Speech tools will be introduced only where testing shows adequate accuracy for local languages and accents.

### Learning progress dashboard

A simple dashboard will highlight skills that need additional practice.

Its purpose will be to guide supportive teaching. It will not make automatic decisions about promotion or discipline.

## 5. Implementation Plan

| Period | Main activities |
|---|---|
| Months 1–3 | Consult communities and assess infrastructure. Adapt content. Collect baseline learning data. |
| Months 4–6 | Install equipment in 15 intervention schools. Train teachers. Test usability and safety. |
| Months 7–15 | Deliver regular learning sessions. Provide coaching. Monitor implementation and improve tools. |
| Months 16–18 | Conduct independent evaluation. Publish findings. Plan expansion if results justify it. |

The remaining 15 schools will continue with existing instruction during the evaluation. They will receive access afterward if the intervention proves beneficial and funding permits.

## 6. Safeguards and Equity

The project will collect only data needed for educational support and evaluation.

Student records will use coded identifiers. Encryption and role-based access will protect stored information. Clear retention limits will govern deletion. Vendors will not be permitted to use student data to train commercial models.

Participation will follow local law and appropriate consent procedures. Families will receive clear explanations of how the system works.

The team will assess performance across language groups and disability status as well as gender and location. Identified disparities will trigger corrective action.

Offline operation and backup power will reduce disruption. Printed alternatives will remain available.

## 7. Monitoring and Evaluation

Schools will be randomly assigned to intervention or comparison groups where feasible. An independent evaluator will determine whether the sample can detect meaningful learning gains.

The evaluation will measure:

- Changes in literacy and numeracy using independent assessments.
- Teacher preparation time and classroom use.
- Student participation and attendance.
- Differences in outcomes across learner groups.
- System reliability and AI error rates.
- Cost per learner and cost relative to learning gains.

A proposed success target is an average learning improvement of at least 0.15 standard deviations relative to comparison schools. This is a target rather than a guaranteed outcome.

## 8. Indicative Budget

| Category | Estimated cost |
|---|---:|
| Devices and power support | $120000 |
| Software and local content development | $100000 |
| Teacher training and coaching | $90000 |
| Technical support and maintenance | $50000 |
| Independent evaluation and safeguarding | $60000 |
| Project management and contingency | $80000 |
| **Total** | **$500000** |

## 9. Sustainability and Scale

The project will prioritize open standards and exportable content to limit dependence on one vendor. Local technicians and teacher trainers will receive maintenance training.

Expansion will depend on demonstrated learning benefits and affordable recurring costs. A ministry-approved financing plan will cover device replacement and ongoing support before wider adoption.

*A production riddle for people who consider “it depends” a complete architectural proposal.*

What am I, dear engineer? I make your application faster by ensuring it does less work, which is also my strategy for attending sprint planning. I live between a question and its expensive answer. When I behave, you call the system elegant. When I misbehave, you schedule a cross-functional incident review.

### Clue One: My Career Is Built on Repetition

Ask me something new, and I am useless. Ask me something familiar, and suddenly I am a performance optimization. Unlike your newest language model, I do not need to improvise an answer. I simply repeat yesterday’s answer with the confidence of a senior architect defending a decision from 2009.

I adore predictable workloads, popular products, and the same profile picture requested fourteen million times. Give me a unique query every time, however, and I become an expensive receptionist who keeps saying, “Let me transfer you.” Your dashboard calls these misses. Your finance department calls them cloud spending.

### Clue Two: Freshness Is a Lifestyle Choice

I can tell you the current price, provided your definition of “current” includes an exciting historical period called five minutes ago. I may insist that an item is available after the warehouse has sold it, shipped it, and converted its shelf into a meditation space for exhausted fulfillment staff.

You can give my memories an expiration date. A time to live, you say, as though I am a tiny digital yogurt. Too short, and I bother the database constantly. Too long, and I preserve obsolete facts with the dedication of a documentation page titled “Temporary Migration Notes.”

### Clue Three: Forgetting Is My Hardest Feature

Adding information is easy. Removing the correct information everywhere, at the correct moment, without awakening a stampede of requests? # Train Your Dog: A Kid-Friendly Guide 🐶

Want to teach your dog to sit, come when called, or do a fun trick? You don’t need magic—just patience, practice, and a few tasty treats!

Dog training is about helping your dog understand you. Ask a grown-up to help, especially when you’re learning something new.

## 1. Get Ready to Learn Together

Choose a quiet place where your dog feels comfortable. Have these supplies ready:

- Small, dog-safe treats approved by a grown-up
- A favorite toy
- A bowl of fresh water
- A leash, if needed, with an adult helping

Keep lessons short—about three to five minutes. **Less is often more:** a little practice each day works better than one long, tiring lesson.

## 2. Reward the Good Stuff

Dogs learn by discovering which actions lead to good things.

When your dog does what you’re teaching, say “Yes!” and give a treat right away. That quick reward helps your dog connect the action with the prize.

Never yell, hit, or tug hard on a leash. If your dog seems confused, make the task easier or take a break.

## 3. Teach “Sit”

“Sit” is a great first skill!

1. Hold a small treat near your dog’s nose without letting them grab it.
2. Slowly move it up and back toward the top of their head.
3. As their nose follows the treat, their bottom may lower to the floor.
4. The moment they sit, say “Yes!” and give the treat.

Once your dog is following the motion easily, say “Sit” just before you move your hand. Don’t push their bottom down. If they back up instead, reset and try a smaller movement.

## 4. Play the “Come Here!” Game

Start indoors, just a few steps from your dog.

Say your dog’s name and “Come!” in a cheerful voice. When they reach you, say “Yes!” and reward them.

With a grown-up, you can take turns calling your dog across a room. Practice outside only in a securely fenced space or with an adult managing a leash.

**Always make coming to you a happy experience.** Never call your dog over to punish them.

## 5. Learn Your Dog’s “I Need a Break” Signals

Your dog can’t say, “I’m tired of class,” but their body can give you clues.

Pause if your dog keeps turning away, yawning, licking their lips, or trying to leave. These can be signs that they’re uncomfortable or need a break.

If your dog freezes, growls, or snaps, stop and get a grown-up. Don’t punish a growl—it’s an important warning that your dog needs space.

Also, leave dogs alone when they’re eating or sleeping, and never take treats or toys from their mouth.

## 6. Plan a Happy Finale

Finish each lesson with something easy your dog already knows. Reward that success, then enjoy a little playtime if your dog wants to.

That happy **finale** helps training feel like a game instead of a test.

## The Biggest Training Secret

Your dog doesn’t have to learn everything today. Celebrate small steps, use kind rewards, and practice with a grown-up’s help.

Being a great trainer isn’t about being bossy. It’s about being a patient teammate! 🐾

## Section 1: The basic nationwide rules

The short version is that the U.S. does not have a nationwide paid maternity leave program covering all workers.
Instead, what you get depends on federal law, state law, and your employer’s policies.
The main federal law is the Family and Medical Leave Act, usually called FMLA.
It gives eligible employees up to 12 workweeks of unpaid, job-protected leave in a 12-month period.
That leave can cover pregnancy-related medical needs, recovery from childbirth, and bonding with a new baby.
It also covers bonding after adoption or foster placement.
Despite the phrase “maternity leave,” FMLA bonding leave is available to eligible parents of any gender.
To qualify, you generally need to have worked for your employer for at least 12 months.
You also generally need at least 1,250 hours of work during the 12 months before your leave starts.
Another usual requirement is working at a location where your employer has at least 50 employees within 75 miles.
FMLA covers private employers with at least 50 employees, as well as public agencies and elementary and secondary schools, though employee eligibility rules still apply.
While you are on FMLA leave, your employer generally must keep your group health insurance going under the same terms as if you were working.
You still have to pay your usual share of the premiums.
When you return, you generally have the right to your old job or an equivalent one.
The big catch is that FMLA itself does not replace your paycheck.

## Section 2: Getting paid and figuring out your options

Some states and Washington, D.C., have paid family and medical leave programs that can replace part of your income.
The rules vary, including who qualifies, how much money you receive, and how long benefits last.
Some states also have temporary disability programs that may cover the period when pregnancy or childbirth prevents you from working.
Medical recovery benefits and parental bonding benefits are not necessarily the same thing.
Qualifying for paid benefits also does not automatically mean you have job protection, so it is worth checking both separately.
Your employer might offer paid parental leave even if state law does not require it.
You may also be able—or sometimes be required—to use accrued vacation or sick leave during otherwise unpaid FMLA leave, depending on the applicable rules.
Short-term disability insurance can sometimes replace part of your wages during childbirth recovery, but coverage depends on the policy.
Eligible federal civilian employees generally have access to up to 12 weeks of paid parental leave under a separate federal arrangement.
Different benefits can overlap rather than stack, so paid leave and FMLA may run at the same time.
Federal law also prohibits covered employers from discriminating against workers because of pregnancy.
The Pregnant Workers Fairness Act generally requires covered employers to provide reasonable accommodations for known pregnancy-related limitations unless doing so would cause undue hardship.
Those accommodations can sometimes include time off, but that law does not create a general right to paid maternity leave.
For foreseeable FMLA leave, you generally need to give your employer at least 30 days’ notice when practical.
The best starting point is to check your employee handbook, ask HR about pay and job protection separately, and look up your state’s official leave program.

The rain forgot the meaning of enough,

# The Benefits of Hiring a Digital Marketing Agency

Building a strong online presence takes more than posting on social media or launching a website. Businesses need a clear strategy, consistent execution, and a way to measure what works. A digital marketing agency can bring these pieces together, helping companies reach potential customers while giving internal teams more time to focus on the business.

## Access to Specialized Expertise

One of the biggest benefits of working with a digital marketing agency is access to a team with different skills. Instead of relying on one employee to handle everything, businesses can tap into specialists in search engine optimization, paid advertising, content creation, email marketing, and web design. These professionals bring experience from managing campaigns and solving marketing challenges across different businesses. Their combined knowledge can help you avoid common mistakes and make more informed decisions.

## A More Cohesive Marketing Strategy

Marketing channels work best when they support one another. An agency can develop a strategy that connects your website, search campaigns, social content, and email communications around shared goals. For example, a helpful blog post might attract search traffic, encourage newsletter sign-ups, and support a follow-up email campaign. This coordinated approach helps create a more consistent experience for potential customers.

## More Time to Focus on Your Business

Managing digital marketing requires ongoing attention. Campaigns need monitoring, content needs updating, and customer behavior can change over time. Outsourcing some or all of this work can free up your team to focus on product development, customer service, and daily operations. You still need to provide direction and feedback, but you do not have to manage every marketing task yourself.

## Flexible Access to Resources

Hiring and training a full in-house marketing team can be expensive, especially for a growing business. An agency can provide access to several capabilities without requiring you to recruit for every role. Depending on your needs and contract, you may also be able to increase or reduce support as your priorities change. This flexibility can be useful during a product launch, a seasonal promotion, or a period of expansion.

## Better Measurement and Clearer Insights

Digital marketing generates a large amount of data, but data alone does not tell you what to do next. A capable agency can help identify meaningful metrics, set up appropriate tracking, and explain campaign performance. Rather than focusing only on likes or page views, it can connect reporting to goals such as qualified leads, purchases, or customer retention. These insights can guide budget decisions and highlight opportunities for improvement.

## Access to Marketing Tools

Agencies often use tools for keyword research, analytics, campaign management, and competitor research. Purchasing and learning these tools independently can require a significant investment of time and money. Working with an agency may give your business access to useful insights without having to manage every platform directly. The greatest value, however, comes from knowing how to interpret the information and act on it.

## A Fresh Perspective

An outside team can spot opportunities that are easy to miss when you work closely with a business every day. An agency may notice unclear website messaging, gaps in your content, or friction in the customer journey. It can also bring ideas based on experience with other campaigns and audiences. Combined with your knowledge of your customers, that perspective can lead to more relevant and effective marketing.

## Ongoing Testing and Improvement

Effective digital marketing is an ongoing process rather than a one-time project. Agencies can test different messages, landing pages, audiences, and offers to learn what performs best. They can also adjust campaigns as platforms, competitors, and customer preferences evolve. While no agency can guarantee results, a disciplined approach to testing can help your business learn faster and use its budget more effectively.

## Choosing the Right Partner

The benefits of hiring an agency depend on finding a partner that understands your goals and communicates clearly. Look for relevant experience, transparent reporting, realistic expectations, and a clear explanation of fees and responsibilities. A good agency should be willing to discuss both opportunities and limitations rather than promise instant success. With the right fit, an agency can become a valuable extension of your team and help you build a more focused, measurable approach to growth.

## Abstract

The presidency of the United States combines executive leadership, public communication, and continuous decision-making. These responsibilities provide a valuable setting for examining the relationship between professional demands and personal well-being. This paper considers how presidential duties engage cognitive, emotional, and physiological resources. It also explores the contributions of social support, restorative routines, and institutional coordination to effective leadership. Drawing on frameworks from political science and psychology, the discussion presents presidential well-being as both an individual consideration and an organizational priority.

## Introduction

The president of the United States occupies a distinctive position within American government. As chief executive, commander in chief, and a prominent public representative, the president participates in decisions with national and international significance. The office requires sustained attention, adaptability, and the integration of information from numerous sources. Presidential well-being therefore offers an important subject for academic inquiry.

A useful approach considers the relationship between the individual and the working environment. From this perspective, leadership reflects the interaction of personal habits, professional relationships, and institutional arrangements. This paper argues that presidential effectiveness is supported by restorative practices, trusted interpersonal connections, and a coordinated executive organization.

## The Cognitive Dimensions of Presidential Leadership

Presidential work involves moving among diverse subjects, including economic policy, diplomacy, legislative priorities, and public administration. Each area requires the interpretation of specialized information and the comparison of possible courses of action. The concept of cognitive load provides one framework for understanding how leaders allocate attention across such responsibilities ([Cognitive Research Author], [Cognitive Research Year]).

The structure of information delivery is particularly relevant. Briefings, written summaries, and consultations can help organize complex material into usable forms. Advisers contribute subject-matter expertise, while the president integrates their recommendations with broader public goals. This collaborative process illustrates how executive decision-making depends on both individual judgment and organizational design.

Public communication adds another dimension. Presidential statements reach multiple audiences, each with distinct expectations and interests. Preparing these statements requires careful attention to language, timing, and context. Communication teams can support this work by coordinating research, reviewing drafts, and clarifying the intended message ([Political Communication Author], [Political Communication Year]).

## Physiological Activation and Restorative Routines

A demanding executive schedule can involve heightened physiological activation. In general psychological terms, the body adjusts its level of alertness in response to significant tasks and changing circumstances. These adjustments can be examined through patterns of sleep, attention, energy, and recovery ([Health Psychology Author], [Health Psychology Year]).

For a president, restorative routines have practical relevance. Regular sleep opportunities, physical activity, balanced meals, and periods of quiet reflection can support readiness for daily responsibilities. Their value lies in creating a rhythm between focused engagement and renewal.

An academic analysis should also distinguish general psychological principles from conclusions about a particular officeholder. Public appearances provide only a limited view of personal experience. A president’s well-being is best examined through appropriately sourced evidence, such as authorized interviews, carefully contextualized historical records, and voluntarily released health information.

## Social Support and Institutional Coordination

Trusted relationships constitute another important resource. Family members, friends, and experienced colleagues can provide continuity within an unusually visible professional role. Such relationships offer opportunities for conversation, perspective, and connection beyond official duties ([Social Support Author], [Social Support Year]).

Institutional coordination complements these personal resources. The White House chief of staff, senior advisers, and agency leaders help organize schedules, establish priorities, and distribute responsibilities. Delegation allows specialized matters to receive focused attention while preserving the president’s capacity for broader strategic judgment.

The presidency can therefore be understood as a collaborative institution rather than solely an individual undertaking. Clear procedures and well-defined roles create conditions for consistent executive performance ([Presidency Studies Author], [Presidency Studies Year]).

## Conclusion

Presidential well-being emerges from the interaction of executive responsibilities, personal routines, and institutional support. The office calls for sustained cognitive engagement, flexible communication, and physiological readiness. Restorative practices, trusted relationships, and coordinated administrative structures can contribute to maintaining these capacities.

Studying this subject connects the human dimensions of leadership with the organization of democratic government. It also encourages a broader understanding of executive effectiveness: presidential performance depends on personal abilities together with the systems that support their continued application.

"Adão e Eva: a origem da humanidade na narrativa bíblica

Adão e Eva são apresentados no livro do Gênesis como o primeiro casal humano. Sua história ocupa um lugar importante nas tradições judaica e cristã, oferecendo reflexões sobre a criação, a liberdade, a responsabilidade e a relação entre a humanidade e Deus.

A criação e o jardim do Éden

Segundo a narrativa bíblica, Deus formou Adão do pó da terra e lhe deu vida. Depois, colocou-o no jardim do Éden, um lugar de abundância que ele deveria cultivar e guardar. Eva foi criada a partir de uma costela de Adão, sendo apresentada como sua companheira.

O casal podia comer dos frutos das árvores do jardim, com uma exceção: a árvore do conhecimento do bem e do mal. Essa proibição estabelecia um limite para a ação humana e colocava em evidência a possibilidade de escolher entre a obediência e a desobediência.

A escolha e suas consequências

A serpente questionou a ordem divina e convenceu Eva a comer do fruto proibido. Eva também o ofereceu a Adão, que comeu. O texto bíblico não identifica esse fruto como uma maçã; essa associação se tornou comum em representações artísticas posteriores.

Após comerem, ambos perceberam que estavam nus, fizeram coberturas com folhas e se esconderam. Quando confrontados por Deus, Adão atribuiu sua ação à mulher, enquanto Eva apontou o engano da serpente.

A narrativa descreve consequências para a serpente, a mulher e o homem, incluindo sofrimento, dificuldades no cultivo da terra e o retorno humano ao pó. Adão e Eva foram expulsos do Éden, e o acesso à árvore da vida passou a ser guardado por querubins.

A vida fora do jardim

Fora do Éden, Adão e Eva tiveram filhos. Entre os mencionados pelo nome estão Caim, Abel e Sete. A história de seus descendentes amplia os temas apresentados no jardim, abordando a violência, os vínculos familiares e a continuidade da vida humana.

Interpretações religiosas e simbólicas

A história de Adão e Eva recebe diferentes interpretações. Algumas comunidades religiosas a entendem como um relato histórico; outras destacam seu caráter simbólico ou teológico.

Em muitas tradições cristãs, a desobediência do casal está relacionada à doutrina do pecado original, embora existam diferenças sobre seu significado e sua transmissão. No judaísmo, a narrativa costuma ser interpretada sem a mesma concepção cristã de culpa herdada, dando destaque à responsabilidade humana e à possibilidade de arrependimento.

Uma reflexão sobre a condição humana

Independentemente da interpretação adotada, Adão e Eva permanecem figuras influentes na religião, na literatura e nas artes. Sua história convida à reflexão sobre os limites, o desejo de conhecimento, a confiança e a tendência de transferir a responsabilidade pelos próprios atos. Também apresenta a vida humana como uma experiência marcada pelo trabalho, pela fragilidade e pela busca de sentido."

# Book Review Rubric for Teenagers

A strong book review does more than summarize the plot: it explains what you think of the book and why. Use this rubric to plan, write, or check your review.

**Score each category from 1 to 4. of  Total possible: 20 points.**

| CATEGORY | 4 | 1 3 | 4      To 2 | score 1 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **INTRODUCTION** | Names the title, author, and genre; opens with an interesting hook. | Names the title and author; gives a clear introduction. | Leaves out key book information or has an unclear opening. | Gives little or no introduction to the book. |
| **SUMMARY** | Briefly explains the main characters, setting, and central conflict without major spoilers. | Explains the main story clearly, with mostly relevant details. | Gives too much or too little detail, or reveals major spoilers without warning. | Gives no useful summary or misrepresents the story. |
| **ANALYSIS** | Thoughtfully discusses elements such as characters, themes, pacing, or writing style—and explains how they affect the reading experience. | Discusses important elements with some explanation. | Mentions story elements but mostly repeats the plot. | Offers little or no discussion beyond the plot. |
| **OPINION AND EVIDENCE** | Makes a clear judgment supported by specific examples or short quotations; explains why each example matters. | Gives a clear opinion supported by some examples. | Gives opinions with little support or vague explanations. | Gives no clear opinion or supporting evidence. |
| **ORGANIZATION AND STYLE** | Uses logical paragraphs, clear language, and an engaging voice; ends with a recommendation for a specific audience. | Is easy to follow, with minor errors; includes a recommendation. | Has uneven organization or distracting errors; recommendation is vague. | Is difficult to follow or lacks a conclusion. |

### Before you submit: CHECK
- Have I explained **why** I liked or disliked the book?
- Have I supported my opinions with details from the text?
- Have I avoided major spoilers—or clearly labeled them?
- Have I said who might enjoy this book?
- Have I checked spelling, punctuation, and sentence clarity?

**Remember:** You do not have to like a book to write an excellent review. Honest, thoughtful reasoning matters more than praise.

Is ballistics (the study of the motion of projectiles) an actual science?

Yes. **Ballistics is a branch of applied physics** that studies how projectiles move and interact with their surroundings. It uses mechanics, aerodynamics, thermodynamics, and experimental measurements to develop and test predictions.

Its main areas include:
- **Internal ballistics:** What happens while a projectile is being launched, such as inside a firearm’s barrel.
- **External ballistics:** How a projectile moves through the air, including the effects of gravity, drag, and wind.
- **Terminal ballistics:** What happens when a projectile strikes a target.

A useful distinction: **forensic firearm identification**, sometimes called “forensic ballistics,” attempts to link bullets or cartridge cases to particular firearms. Some of its methods and claims of certainty face scientific criticism. That does not undermine ballistics itself as an established physical science.

# What Is Inside a Shinto Shrine?

Imagine we are visiting **[shrine name]** in **[location]**. Before we enter, let’s consider a question: what makes this place sacred?

Shinto shrines are places where people honor **kami**—sacred beings or presences associated with natural phenomena, particular places, ancestors, and other aspects of life. A shrine is not necessarily one building; it often includes several structures within sacred grounds.

## *1. The Main Sanctuary: A Sacred Presence*

The most sacred building is usually the **honden**, or main sanctuary. It generally houses a **shintai**, a sacred object through which a kami is understood to be present.

A shintai may be a mirror, sword, stone, or another object. It is not necessarily an image of the kami. Mirrors, for example, have important associations with the sun kami Amaterasu.

These objects are usually concealed, and ordinary visitors generally cannot enter the main sanctuary. Thus, the shrine’s most important contents may be precisely what visitors never see.

There are exceptions to this arrangement: some shrines have no honden and instead direct worship toward a sacred mountain or another natural feature.

## *2. The Worship Hall: Where Visitors Pray*

Visitors typically offer prayers at or in front of the **haiden**, the worship hall, rather than entering the main sanctuary.

Here, you may find:

- An **offering box** for monetary offerings.
- A bell and rope, which worshippers may ring before praying.
- **Shimenawa**, sacred ropes often hung with zigzag paper streamers called **shide**, marking a sacred space.
- Ritual furnishings used during ceremonies.

A common prayer sequence is two bows, two claps, and one final bow, although customs differ between shrines.

**Class activity:** Look at **[photo of a worship hall]**. Which features help distinguish the space as sacred?

## *3. Offerings and Ritual Objects*

Shrine interiors may contain altars or stands bearing offerings such as rice, sake, salt, water, vegetables, or fruit. These express respect and gratitude toward the kami.

Other ritual items include branches of the evergreen **sakaki** tree and **gohei**, ritual objects with folded paper streamers. Priests use various implements in ceremonies involving purification, prayer, and offerings.

Some shrines also have a **heiden**, an offering hall or space between the worship hall and the main sanctuary. Layouts vary considerably, so there is no single plan shared by every shrine.

## *4. What Else Is Within the Shrine Grounds?*

If we mean “inside” the whole shrine precinct, rather than just its buildings, we may also encounter:

- **Torii gates**, marking an entrance to sacred space.
- A purification basin for rinsing the hands and mouth.
- **Ema**, wooden plaques on which visitors write wishes.
- A place distributing **omamori**, protective amulets, and **omikuji**, fortune slips.
- Smaller subsidiary shrines, sacred trees, or a stage for ritual performances.

The central lesson is this: **a Shinto shrine is not primarily a display of religious objects. Its spaces, sacred contents, and rituals organize relationships between people and kami—even when the most sacred object remains hidden.**

# research proposal

## title

the impact of the liberian civil wars on the country’s economy: destruction, recovery, and long-term development

## researcher and institution

researcher: [researcher name]  
institution: [institution name]  
proposed duration: six months

## 1. background and rationale

liberia experienced two civil wars between 1989 and 2003, separated by a period of fragile peace. these conflicts caused widespread displacement, damaged infrastructure, disrupted production, and weakened public institutions. agriculture, mining, forestry, and trade were affected, while government capacity to collect revenue and provide essential services deteriorated.

although the end of the conflict created opportunities for reconstruction, its economic consequences may have persisted through lost education, poor health, reduced investment, and institutional weakness. postwar recovery has also been shaped by other shocks, including changes in commodity prices, the ebola epidemic, and the covid-19 pandemic. distinguishing these influences from the effects of war is therefore important.

this study will examine both the immediate economic disruption associated with the civil wars and their longer-term implications for recovery and development.

## 2. problem statement

changes in liberia’s economic performance cannot be understood solely through national output figures. conflict may also have altered employment, household livelihoods, public finances, and the distribution of economic opportunities. however, incomplete wartime data and the influence of subsequent shocks make it difficult to estimate the scale and persistence of these effects.

the research will address this problem by combining economic data with documentary evidence and interviews. it will assess where the evidence supports a causal interpretation and where findings should be treated as descriptive or suggestive.

## 3. research aim and objectives

the study aims to assess how liberia’s civil wars affected the national economy and influenced postwar recovery.

the specific objectives are to:

- examine changes in economic output, investment, trade, and government revenue before, during, and after the conflicts.
- assess the effects of conflict on agriculture, mining, and other major sources of employment and income.
- investigate how displacement, infrastructure destruction, and institutional disruption influenced economic activity.
- explore differences in recovery across sectors, locations, and population groups.
- identify policy priorities for inclusive growth and economic resilience.

## 4. research questions

1. how did liberia’s economic performance change during and after the civil wars?
2. which economic sectors and livelihood groups experienced the greatest disruption?
3. through what mechanisms did conflict affect production, investment, and public finances?
4. to what extent have conflict-related economic disadvantages persisted?
5. what lessons can support future reconstruction and development policies?

## 5. conceptual framework

the study will draw on theories of conflict economics, human capital, and institutional development. it will examine three main pathways:

- **physical capital:** destruction or deterioration of roads, electricity systems, farms, and productive facilities.
- **human capital:** deaths, displacement, interrupted schooling, and reduced access to health care.
- **institutional capacity:** weakened administration, insecure property rights, and reduced fiscal capacity.

these pathways may reinforce one another. for example, damaged infrastructure can discourage investment, while weak revenue collection can limit reconstruction.

## 6. methodology

### research design

the project will use a mixed-methods case study, combining quantitative analysis with qualitative evidence.

### scope

the proposed study period is 1980–2023, subject to data availability. this provides a prewar baseline, covers both conflicts, and allows examination of postwar developments. the analysis will distinguish the war years from later shocks rather than treating all post-2003 outcomes as consequences of conflict.

### data sources

quantitative data will be sought from:

- the world bank’s world development indicators.
- the international monetary fund.
- the central bank of liberia.
- the liberia institute of statistics and geo-information services.
- relevant government, trade, and sectoral reports.

qualitative evidence will include policy documents, historical records, academic studies, and approximately 20–25 semi-structured interviews. participants will be selected purposively from economists, public officials, business owners, farmers, and civil society representatives. interviews will focus on economic experiences and recovery processes rather than unnecessary recounting of traumatic events.

### data analysis

descriptive analysis will track real output per capita, sectoral production, trade, investment, and public revenue where reliable series exist. graphs and period comparisons will identify major changes, while documenting missing observations and revisions.

if data quality permits, a comparative analysis will construct a counterfactual trajectory using countries with similar prewar economic characteristics. a synthetic control approach may be considered, with sensitivity tests for comparator selection, prewar fit, and regional spillovers. causal claims will depend on whether these assumptions are credible.

interview transcripts and documents will undergo thematic analysis to identify recurring mechanisms, including market disruption, displacement, infrastructure loss, and barriers to recovery. findings will be compared across sources to assess consistency.

## 7. ethical considerations

the study will obtain institutional ethical approval before interviews begin. participants will receive clear information about the research and provide informed consent. participation will be voluntary, and individuals may decline questions or withdraw in accordance with the approved protocol.

identifying information will be removed from research outputs unless explicit permission is granted. recordings and transcripts will be stored securely. the researcher will remain sensitive to conflict-related trauma and avoid questions that could expose participants to distress or political risk.

## 8. anticipated limitations

the study may face incomplete wartime statistics, inconsistent economic measures, interview recall bias, and limited access to participants outside major towns. national indicators may also conceal local inequalities.

these limitations will be addressed through source triangulation, transparent documentation of uncertainty, and sensitivity checks. the small interview sample will provide contextual insight rather than statistically representative estimates.

## 9. expected contribution

the project will produce an evidence-based account of how conflict affected liberia’s economy and shaped recovery. it will clarify the relative importance of damage to productive assets, human capital, and institutions without assuming the findings in advance.

the results may inform policies on infrastructure, livelihood restoration, education, investment, and public financial management. outputs will include a research report and a concise policy brief.

## 10. proposed timeline

| month | activities |
|---|---|
| 1 | literature review, research design, and ethics application |
| 2 | economic data collection and interview preparation |
| 3 | interviews and documentary research, following ethical approval |
| 4 | quantitative and qualitative analysis |
| 5 | integration of findings and report drafting |
| 6 | revisions, policy brief preparation, and presentation |

## 11. indicative budget

| item | estimated cost |
|---|---|
| travel and local transport | [amount] |
| research assistance and transcription | [amount] |
| communication and data access | [amount] |
| dissemination and printing | [amount] |
| contingency | [amount] |
| total | [total budget] |

## 12. preliminary literature

the literature review will begin with the following sources and expand to include liberia-specific studies:

- collier, p., et al. (2003). *breaking the conflict trap: civil war and development policy*. world bank and oxford university press.
- gates, s., hegre, h., nygård, h. m., and strand, h. (2012). “development consequences of armed conflict.” *world development*, 40(9), 1713–1722.
- world bank. (2011). *world development report 2011: conflict, security, and development*.
- central bank of liberia. *annual reports*, selected years.
- international monetary fund. *liberia country reports*, selected years.

GNSS means **Global Navigation Satellite System**—satellites that help your Android phone figure out its position and the time. To get the timestamp of a satellite-based location fix in an Android app:

1. **Ask for permission.** Add `ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION` to your app’s manifest and request it at runtime; on newer Android versions, the user must allow **precise location**.
2. **Turn on location services.** Make sure the phone supports satellite positioning, and try going outdoors so it can receive a strong signal.
3. **Request satellite-based updates.** Use Android’s `LocationManager` with `LocationManager.GPS_PROVIDER`, then wait for a location callback.
4. **Read the timestamp.** Inside the callback, call `location.getTime()` in Java or use `location.time` in Kotlin. This gives the fix’s timestamp as milliseconds since January 1, 1970, in UTC—not simply the time your callback arrived.
5. **Display it and clean up.** Convert the value into a readable date and time, and stop requesting updates when you’re finished to save battery.

If you need **raw GNSS clock measurements** instead of a location-fix timestamp, Android 7.0 and later provide `GnssMeasurementsEvent.Callback` and `GnssClock` on supported devices; those measurements require additional clock-bias and time-system conversions.

## Teen Essay Rubric

Score each category from **1 to 4**, for a maximum of **20 points**. Judge the essay against the assignment and the writer’s grade level—not professional writing standards.

| Category | 4 — Strong | 3 — Proficient | 2 — Developing | 1 — Needs support |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Ideas and focus** | Presents a clear central idea, addresses the prompt fully, and develops thoughtful insights. | Has a clear central idea and addresses most of the prompt; some ideas need more development. | Central idea is unclear or inconsistent; addresses only part of the prompt. | Lacks a clear central idea or largely misses the prompt. |
| **Organization** | Has a purposeful opening, logically ordered paragraphs, effective transitions, and a satisfying ending. | Has a clear beginning, middle, and ending; most ideas connect logically. | Some structure is apparent, but ideas jump around or transitions are weak. | Ideas are difficult to follow; paragraphing or overall structure is missing or confusing. |
| **Support and development** | Uses specific, relevant evidence or details and explains how they develop the main idea. | Uses relevant evidence or details, but some explanations are brief or incomplete. | Offers limited, vague, repetitive, or weakly connected support. | Makes mostly unsupported statements or includes few meaningful details. |
| **Language and voice** | Uses precise language, varied sentences, and a voice suited to the purpose and audience. | Language is mostly clear; sentence variety and tone are generally effective. | Word choice is sometimes vague or repetitive; awkward sentences or shifts in tone distract. | Language frequently obscures meaning or does not suit the task. |
| **Conventions and presentation** | Grammar, punctuation, spelling, and required formatting are consistently controlled; minor errors do not distract. | Some errors occur, but meaning remains clear; follows most formatting requirements. | Frequent errors sometimes interfere with understanding; several requirements are missed. | Persistent errors make meaning difficult to follow; major formatting requirements are unmet. |

### How to use it fairly
- **Match support to the genre:** An argument needs reasons and evidence; a literary analysis needs textual examples; a narrative needs meaningful events and descriptive details.
- **Check citations when required:** Consider source attribution under support and citation formatting under presentation. Avoid penalizing the same mistake twice.
- **Value substance over polish:** A longer essay or bigger vocabulary does not automatically deserve a higher score.
- **Give actionable feedback:** Identify one clear strength and one specific revision priority.

### Overall score guide
- **18–20:** Strong overall
- **14–17:** Generally proficient
- **10–13:** Developing; targeted revision needed
- **5–9:** Needs substantial support and revision

******
**Final summary:** A strong teenage essay communicates a clear idea, organizes it logically, develops it with relevant support, and uses readable, purposeful language. Use the score to guide improvement—not to label the writer’s ability.

## Bits Quiz 🐘

1. **What is a bit?**  
   A. A type of computer screen  
   B. The smallest unit of digital information  
   C. A computer program  

2. **Which two values can a bit have?**  
   A. 0 and 1  
   B. 1 and 2  
   C. 0 and 9  

3. **How many bits are in one byte?**  
   A. 4  
   B. 8  
   C. 16  

4. **An elephant photo is stored on a computer. Is its digital data represented using bits?**  
   A. Yes  
   B. No  

5. **A game uses one bit to record whether an elephant is awake or asleep. How many different states can that bit represent?**  
   A. 1  
   B. 2  
   C. 8  

6. **An elephant earns the binary score `101`. What is that score in decimal?**  
   A. 3  
   B. 5  
   C. 6  

### Answer Key
1. **B** — A bit is the smallest unit of digital information.  
2. **A** — A bit can be 0 or 1.  
3. **B** — One byte contains 8 bits.  
4. **A** — Digital photos are represented using bits.  
5. **B** — One bit represents two possible states.  
6. **B** — Binary `101` equals 4 + 0 + 1 = **5**.

Subject: My Highly Scientific Recipe for a Good Life

Hey Jamie,

I’ve been thinking about the ingredients of a good life, mostly because I tried making soup yesterday and accidentally created something that could patch a driveway.  
Naturally, this culinary setback inspired me to become a philosopher.  
After extensive research involving one walk, two naps, and a suspicious amount of cheese, I believe I’ve cracked the recipe.

First, you need a generous helping of good friends.  
These are the people who will support your dreams, tell you when you have spinach in your teeth, and help you move a couch despite knowing perfectly well that you are paying them in pizza.  
Choose friends who make you laugh so hard that nearby strangers briefly consider calling someone qualified.  
Also, be that kind of friend yourself, though perhaps help with the couch before starting your comedy routine.

Next, add meaningful work, but do not pour in the entire container.  
Work is an important ingredient, not the whole casserole.  
Nobody wants to reach retirement and realize their closest personal relationship was with a spreadsheet named “FINAL_budget_v7_ACTUALLY_FINAL.”  
Find something that gives you a sense of purpose, then occasionally close your laptop before it legally becomes a family member.

You’ll also need a healthy scoop of curiosity.  
Learn a language, grow tomatoes, or finally investigate what all those buttons on your washing machine do.  
I pressed one marked “Eco” last week, and my socks are apparently still on a sustainable journey toward cleanliness.  
The point is to keep discovering things, even if the main thing you discover is that you should have read the instructions.

Stir in regular exercise, preferably something you don’t experience as punishment for having a body.  
Dancing in the kitchen counts, especially if you’re trying to escape a falling saucepan.  
Walking is excellent too, because it gives you time to think while allowing you to say things like “I’m heading out to clear my mind,” which sounds much more impressive than “I need to look at a different wall.”

Sleep is another essential ingredient.  
I used to think sleep was optional, like parsley or responding to a group chat about brunch.  
Then I spent an entire morning looking for my glasses while wearing them, and my eyes have never let me forget it.  
Get enough rest so your brain doesn’t have to run its entire operation on emergency lighting.

Season generously with kindness.  
Hold doors, check on people, and let someone with three groceries go ahead of you when your cart looks like you’re provisioning a submarine.  
Kindness won’t solve every problem, but it does make the world feel less like a customer service line where the hold music is just people sighing.

Add a little adventure whenever possible.  
You don’t have to climb a mountain or wrestle a crocodile, both of which seem like elaborate ways to ruin a perfectly good Saturday.  
Sometimes adventure is taking a different route home, trying a new hobby, or ordering something from a menu without first conducting a background check.

A good life also requires a few firm boundaries.  
Saying no occasionally is healthy, especially when someone asks you to join a committee that meets at 7 a.m. to discuss future meetings.  
You are a person, not a free trial of unlimited availability.

Don’t forget gratitude, although you don’t have to become the sort of person who thanks their toaster for its service.  
Just notice the little things: a good cup of coffee, clean sheets, a beautiful sunset, or the miracle of finding a parking space without having to negotiate with destiny.  
Some days, those small pleasures do a remarkable amount of heavy lifting.

Finally, leave room for mistakes.  
Every good life contains a few burned dinners, awkward conversations, and haircuts that should have required a second opinion.  
The trick is to learn what you can, apologize when necessary, and resist turning one bad afternoon into a twelve-part documentary about your personal failings.

Mix all of this together with love, patience, and a sense of humor.  
Adjust the quantities as you go, because your recipe doesn’t have to match anyone else’s.  
And if the whole thing gets messy, invite a friend over and order takeout.

Speaking of which, are you free Friday?  
I promise not to serve the soup, although I may ask you to help me carry it out to the pothole.

Love,  
Your slightly undercooked philosopher

# How to Improve Your Writing Skills

Good writing is not a talent reserved for a lucky few. It is a skill you can develop through deliberate practice, thoughtful reading, and consistent revision.

Whether you write emails, essays, or stories, the goal is the same: help readers understand your ideas without making them work unnecessarily hard. Start with these three habits.

***

## 1. READ Like a Writer

Reading becomes a writing lesson when you pay attention to how a piece works. Notice how an opening creates interest, how examples explain difficult concepts, and how transitions connect ideas.

Choose writing you admire, but explore unfamiliar styles too. A news article can teach concision; a personal essay can demonstrate voice.

* Save one effective paragraph each week and annotate it. Identify what makes it successful, then write an original paragraph using a similar technique.

***

## 2. WRITE With a Clear Purpose

Before drafting, ask yourself: Who is this for, and what should they understand afterward? Those answers help you choose the right tone, details, and structure.

Practice regularly, even when you have only ten minutes. Focus on getting your ideas onto the page rather than perfecting every sentence immediately.

* Set a manageable daily target, such as 150 words. Give each session one specific goal: explain an idea clearly, describe a scene precisely, or build a convincing argument.

***

## 3. REVISE for the Reader

A first draft captures your thinking. Revision makes that thinking accessible to someone else.

Start with the big picture: does the argument make sense, and is anything missing? Then tighten sentences, replace vague wording, and remove repetition. Read aloud to catch awkward phrasing.

* Review your draft in three passes: structure, clarity, and correctness. When possible, ask a reader where they felt confused, and use that feedback to guide your next revision.

Improvement comes from repeating this cycle—not from waiting for inspiration.

### At the Ruins of a Reducción

“Reductions?” you ask. “Like making something smaller?”
Not exactly. Think *reducciones*: towns
where colonial rulers and the Church gathered
Indigenous people—sometimes by force.
A bell deciding when the morning started.

By 1609, the Jesuits were building missions
in the region then called Paraguay.
“Protection,” they promised. And sometimes it was:
beyond the fields, slave raiders
came hunting people to carry off in chains.

But shelter had its rules.
Who worked which plot? Who rang the bell?
Whose marriage counted? Which prayers could stay?
The fathers brought their answers.
The Guaraní had questions of their own.

Still, don’t picture people merely standing
where a priest had told them to.
Guaraní hands carved saints from local wood;
musicians played, composed, and taught.
They made the mission more than its instructions.

Imagine a fiesta in the square:
a violin, hot dust, somebody’s child
not keeping still for the procession.
You can hear a sermon and still be thinking
about supper, or the person beside you.

Then kings moved lines across a map.
The Treaty of Madrid, 1750:
seven mission towns were to pass to Portugal;
their Guaraní inhabitants were ordered out.
“Leave the houses? Leave our dead?”

They resisted. Sepé Tiaraju
was killed in 1756;
Spanish and Portuguese troops crushed the resistance.
There is no gentle church word
that makes that field less bloody.

In 1767, Spain expelled the Jesuits.
Other administrators took their place.
The missions dwindled unevenly—
not one door closing, but years
of departures, demands, and things falling apart.

And the next fiesta? Ask who kept the music,
who carried a carving, who remembered a name.
Here are the red walls, open to the weather.
Beyond them, Guaraní people still speak and live.
The tour ends. Their history doesn’t.

# Why the Canucks Need to Put the Environment on Their Team
*By Naomi*

Being a Vancouver Canucks fan means caring about more than the score. It means caring about the city the team represents—and the mountains, forests, ocean, and communities that make this part of the world special.

That’s why I believe the Canucks need to be more mindful of their environmental impact. A team with such a visible place in Vancouver has an opportunity to make sustainability part of its identity, not just a message on the scoreboard.

## Protecting the Future of Hockey

Hockey depends on ice, but keeping that ice frozen requires energy. So do arena lighting, heating, ventilation, and the many other systems that make game night possible. Add team travel, fan transportation, food service, and merchandise, and the environmental footprint reaches well beyond the rink.

Climate change also threatens the cold winters and outdoor skating traditions that help connect people to hockey. Protecting the environment isn’t separate from protecting the sport. The two belong on the same team.

## Making Game Night Less Wasteful

Think about everything fans use during a single game: drink cups, food containers, napkins, and packaging. Multiply that by thousands of people, and small choices become a big responsibility.

The Canucks should work with arena operators and vendors to reduce unnecessary packaging, expand practical reuse options, and make waste-sorting stations easy to understand. Fans shouldn’t need a replay review to figure out which bin to use.

Getting to the game matters, too. Clear transit information and encouragement to walk, cycle, or share rides where practical could help supporters make lower-impact choices.

## Turning Good Intentions Into Measurable Action

Being mindful means knowing where the biggest impacts come from. I want to see clear environmental goals, credible measurements, and regular public updates.

That includes assessing arena energy use and travel emissions, then explaining what can realistically be reduced. Not every challenge has an easy answer—especially with a demanding league schedule—but acknowledging those challenges is better than hiding behind vague promises.

Community partnerships could strengthen that work, particularly when local environmental organizations and Indigenous communities help shape projects that affect their lands and waters.

## Leadership Beyond the Scoreboard

The Canucks can’t solve environmental problems alone. But they can use their influence to make responsible choices more visible, accessible, and normal.

As a fan, I want a team that competes hard and thinks beyond the next game. Taking care of the place we call home is one way to build a legacy that lasts longer than a season.

Naomi thanks you for reading.

# Layton is the best city in the world

By [author]  
Published on [date]

What makes a city the best in the world? For some people it is a famous skyline. For others it is nonstop nightlife. But for those who value mountain views and outdoor adventure alongside everyday comfort Layton in Utah makes a compelling case.

## Mountains at Your Doorstep

Layton sits near the Wasatch Mountains where dramatic scenery gives ordinary days a remarkable backdrop. A morning commute can come with glowing peaks. An evening walk can end beneath a wide western sky.

Nearby trails invite hikers to trade screen time for fresh air. Antelope Island State Park offers another kind of escape with open landscapes and views across the Great Salt Lake. Here the outdoors is not just a vacation destination. It can be part of daily life.

## Room for Everyday Joy

A great city should make ordinary life enjoyable. Layton offers parks and recreation alongside shops and restaurants that help residents stay close to home.

Ellison Park provides space to play and unwind. Local events create opportunities to meet neighbors. Sometimes the strongest argument for a place is simply how easily a satisfying weekend comes together.

## Connected Without Feeling Overwhelming

Layton also offers access to the wider Wasatch Front. Salt Lake City and Ogden expand the options for work and entertainment while FrontRunner rail service provides an alternative to driving for some regional trips.

That balance matters. Residents can enjoy a city with its own identity without feeling cut off from everything around it.

## The Best Kind of Best

Calling any city the best in the world is a matter of personal values. Layton will not win every traveler or suit every lifestyle.

Yet if your ideal home combines natural beauty with practical convenience and space to breathe then Layton deserves more than a passing glance. It deserves a place at the top of your list.

"abdominal and pelvic dissemination of ovarian cancer means that cancer has spread from its original site to tissues or organs within the abdomen and pelvis. this spread commonly involves the peritoneum, which is the thin lining of the abdominal cavity, and the omentum, a fatty sheet of tissue that covers and supports abdominal organs. it may also involve surfaces of the bowel, bladder, uterus, diaphragm, or liver, as well as nearby lymph nodes. symptoms vary according to the location and extent of disease, and some people have relatively few symptoms even when cancer has spread.

the following are common signs and symptoms, along with important complications to recognize.

1. persistent abdominal bloating or increased abdominal size

persistent bloating is one of the most commonly reported symptoms. the abdomen may feel swollen, tight, heavy, or unusually full. clothing may become tighter around the waist, and abdominal enlargement may persist rather than fluctuate with meals or the menstrual cycle.

a major cause is ascites, which is a buildup of fluid in the abdominal cavity. ovarian cancer can cause ascites by irritating the peritoneum and interfering with normal fluid drainage. tumor deposits or a larger pelvic mass can also contribute to abdominal enlargement. significant ascites may cause discomfort, difficulty bending, or breathlessness because the fluid pushes upward against the diaphragm.

2. abdominal or pelvic pain, pressure, or discomfort

pain may be dull, aching, cramping, or occasionally sharp. it can be located in the lower abdomen or pelvis, or it may become more widespread across the abdomen. some people describe pressure, dragging, or heaviness rather than pain.

these symptoms may result from tumor growth, irritation of the abdominal lining, pressure on nearby organs, or stretching caused by fluid accumulation. back pain can also occur, although back pain by itself is very nonspecific. pain during sexual intercourse may develop when pelvic structures are affected.

3. feeling full quickly and difficulty eating

early satiety means feeling full after eating only a small amount. people may notice that they cannot finish meals, have little appetite, or feel uncomfortable after eating.

ascites and tumor deposits can crowd the stomach and intestines. bowel involvement can also interfere with normal digestive movement. nausea, indigestion, or a persistent sense of abdominal fullness may accompany these changes.

reduced food intake can contribute to malnutrition, weight loss, weakness, and loss of muscle. importantly, increasing abdominal fluid may conceal weight loss, so someone can lose muscle while their overall weight stays the same or increases.

4. changes in bowel habits

constipation is common and may reflect pressure on the bowel, reduced intestinal movement, dehydration, medications, or direct cancer involvement. some people experience diarrhea, alternating constipation and diarrhea, increased gas, or a sense that the bowel has not emptied completely.

pressure near the rectum may cause difficulty passing stool or repeated urges to have a bowel movement. these symptoms are not specific to ovarian cancer, but persistent or progressive changes warrant medical attention.

more extensive disease can cause a partial or complete bowel obstruction. warning signs include worsening crampy abdominal pain, marked distension, repeated vomiting, and difficulty or inability to pass stool or gas. a partial obstruction may still allow some stool or diarrhea to pass. suspected obstruction requires urgent medical assessment.

5. urinary frequency, urgency, or difficulty emptying the bladder

pelvic tumor deposits or fluid can put pressure on the bladder, causing a need to urinate more often or more urgently. some people feel pressure over the bladder or have difficulty emptying it completely.

if cancer compresses the ureters, which carry urine from the kidneys to the bladder, urine drainage may become blocked. this can cause hydronephrosis, meaning swelling of a kidney from backed-up urine. possible symptoms include flank or back pain, nausea, or reduced urine output, although it may initially cause no noticeable symptoms.

6. fatigue, weakness, and changes in weight

ongoing fatigue and reduced stamina are common in advanced cancer. contributing factors can include poor nutrition, anemia, inflammation, disrupted sleep, and the physical burden of illness.

unintentional weight loss may occur, especially when appetite is reduced. alternatively, weight gain may reflect accumulating ascites rather than improved nutrition. these general symptoms do not identify where the cancer has spread, but they may occur alongside abdominal and pelvic symptoms.

7. swelling in the legs or genital area

tumor involvement of pelvic lymph nodes or pressure on major veins can interfere with normal drainage from the lower body. this may cause swelling in one or both legs or in the genital area.

however, new swelling in one leg, particularly with pain, warmth, or redness, can indicate a blood clot rather than simple fluid retention. cancer increases clot risk, so these symptoms require prompt assessment. sudden breathlessness or chest pain requires emergency care.

8. findings identified during medical examination or imaging

some signs are detected by clinicians rather than noticed directly. these may include a pelvic or abdominal mass, abdominal tenderness, ascites, reduced mobility of pelvic organs, or nodularity felt during a pelvic or rectovaginal examination.

imaging may reveal peritoneal nodules, thickening of the omentum, enlarged lymph nodes, bowel involvement, or urinary tract obstruction. these findings help assess dissemination, but diagnosis and staging require a combination of clinical evaluation, imaging, and usually tissue or fluid testing.

when to seek medical advice

these symptoms overlap with many noncancerous conditions and cannot establish ovarian cancer or its spread on their own. nevertheless, new, persistent, frequent, or worsening bloating, pelvic pain, early fullness, or urinary changes should be evaluated, especially when several occur together. people already diagnosed with ovarian cancer should report new symptoms to their oncology team. severe abdominal pain, repeated vomiting, inability to pass gas or stool, fainting, or markedly reduced urine output calls for urgent medical care."

### **[Verse 1 — Florence Has Entered the Chat]**
Yo, I woke in a fresco, my elbow was wet,  
Somebody yelled, “The plaster ain’t ready for you yet!”  
Slid down a column in a velvet beret,  
Found a banker buying heaven on a payment-delay.  

Medici money got the workshop humming,  
Marble in the alley heard a sculptor coming.  
“Is that block alive?” “Not quite—but wait.”  
Now a seventeen-foot David’s blocking my gate.  

I drew one street with a vanishing point,  
Now the whole damn city disappears at the joint.  
Got depth in my picture, got debt in my name—  
My patron wants his face in the saints’ hall of fame.  

### **[Hook — Extremely Suspicious Rebirth]**
Re-nais-SANCE! Put a brain in the beat!  
Ancient Greek ghosts doing laps in the street!  
Manuscript dust on my brand-new shoes—  
We’re reborn, baby! Still got plague-time blues!  

Re-nais-SANCE! Let the oil paint gleam!  
My face went *sfumato*—I dissolved in a dream.  
Turn that press till the letters get loose:  
A thousand little pamphlets and a very cooked goose.  

### **[Verse 2 — Leonardo’s Terrible Roommate]**
Leo’s in the kitchen drawing wings on a ladle,  
Says, “Don’t touch the gears on my mechanized cradle.”  
Mirror-script shopping list: onions and cheese,  
Plus a cross-section sketch of somebody’s knees.  

I said, “Finish that portrait.” He said, “Observe water.”  
Now we’re six hundred diagrams past what I ordered.  
Mona’s at the table with a half-smirk loaded:  
She knows where my rent went. She will not disclose it.  

### **[Verse 3 — The Bookworms Have Teeth]**
Gutenberg’s type going *clack-clack-clack,*

Humanists digging through Latin like treasure,  
Arguing virtue, proportion, and pleasure.  
Not just “old books good”—it’s “check that translation”:  
One suspicious verb starts a whole conversation.  

### **[Outro — Please Exit Through the Ceiling]**
Now I’m flat on my back while the chapel turns blue,  
Michelangelo’s boot nearly drops in my stew.  
The landlord came knocking. I said, “What a shame—  
You’re a dot on the skyline. Perspective’s to blame.”
