वास्तव संख्यांच्या समान लांबीच्या दोन याद्या घ्या. दोन्ही याद्यांतील त्याच स्थानावरील संख्यांचे गुणाकार करून त्यांची बेरीज करा. या बेरजेचा वर्ग हा प्रत्येक यादीतील संख्यांच्या वर्गांच्या बेरजांचा गुणाकार यापेक्षा मोठा नसतो. यालाच कॉशी–श्वार्त्स विषमता म्हणतात.

***

समीकरणांशिवाय सिद्धता

दुसऱ्या यादीतील सर्व संख्या शून्य असल्यास विषमतेच्या दोन्ही बाजू शून्य होतात; त्यामुळे ती खरी ठरते.

अन्यथा, त्याच स्थानावरील संख्यांच्या गुणाकारांची बेरीज घ्या आणि तिला दुसऱ्या यादीतील संख्यांच्या वर्गांच्या बेरजेने भागा. मिळणाऱ्या संख्येला गुणक म्हणूया.

आता पहिल्या यादीतील प्रत्येक संख्येतून दुसऱ्या यादीतील संबंधित संख्येचा या गुणकाशी केलेला गुणाकार वजा करा. मिळालेल्या प्रत्येक फरकाचा वर्ग करून सर्व वर्गांची बेरीज करा. प्रत्येक वर्ग ऋणेतर असल्यामुळे ही बेरीजही ऋणेतर असते.

या वर्गांचा विस्तार करून समान प्रकारची पदे एकत्र केल्यास, पहिल्या यादीतील वर्गांची बेरीज ही गुणाकारांच्या बेरजेच्या वर्गाला दुसऱ्या यादीतील वर्गांच्या बेरजेने भागल्यावर मिळणाऱ्या संख्येपेक्षा लहान नसल्याचे दिसते. दुसऱ्या यादीतील वर्गांची बेरीज धन असल्याने, तिच्याने दोन्ही बाजूंना गुणल्यावर अपेक्षित विषमता मिळते.

***

थोडक्यात सारांश

कोणत्याही वास्तव संख्येचा वर्ग ऋणेतर असतो, या साध्या तथ्यावर ही सिद्धता आधारलेली आहे. योग्य गुणक निवडून तयार केलेल्या फरकांच्या वर्गांची बेरीज आपल्याला कॉशी–श्वार्त्स विषमता सिद्ध करून देते.

**PACE:** A MIX OF ICONIC SIGHTS, NEIGHBORHOOD WALKS, AND RELAXED MEALS.  
**ROUTE:** FLY INTO LONDON, TAKE THE EUROSTAR TO PARIS, THEN FLY TO ROME AND DEPART FROM THERE.  
**DATES:** [ARRIVAL DATE]–[DEPARTURE DATE]

## DAYS 1–4: LONDON
**BASE:** [LONDON HOTEL] IN BLOOMSBURY, COVENT GARDEN, OR SOUTH BANK.

- **DAY 1 — ARRIVE AND SETTLE IN:** LAND AT [LONDON AIRPORT], CHECK IN, AND TAKE AN EASY WALK ALONG THE THAMES. KEEP THE EVENING LIGHT TO MANAGE JET LAG.
- **DAY 2 — ROYAL AND HISTORIC LONDON:** EXPLORE WESTMINSTER ABBEY, SEE BIG BEN AND PARLIAMENT, THEN WALK THROUGH ST. JAMES’S PARK TO BUCKINGHAM PALACE. DINNER AT [LONDON RESTAURANT].
- **DAY 3 — TOWER AND RIVERSIDE:** VISIT THE TOWER OF LONDON AND TOWER BRIDGE, THEN HEAD TO BOROUGH MARKET FOR LUNCH. SPEND THE AFTERNOON EXPLORING SOUTH BANK.
- **DAY 4 — MUSEUMS AND THEATRE:** VISIT THE BRITISH MUSEUM, EXPLORE COVENT GARDEN AND SOHO, AND FINISH WITH [WEST END SHOW].

## DAYS 5–9: PARIS
**BASE:** [PARIS HOTEL] IN LE MARAIS, THE LATIN QUARTER, OR SAINT-GERMAIN-DES-PRÉS.

- **DAY 5 — TRAIN TO PARIS:** TAKE THE EUROSTAR FROM LONDON ST. PANCRAS TO PARIS GARE DU NORD, USUALLY ABOUT 2 HOURS 20 MINUTES. ALLOW EXTRA TIME FOR PRE-DEPARTURE CHECKS. CHECK IN, THEN ENJOY A SEINE-SIDE WALK.
- **DAY 6 — CLASSIC PARIS:** VISIT THE EIFFEL TOWER WITH A RESERVED TICKET, WALK THROUGH THE CHAMP DE MARS, AND TAKE AN OPTIONAL SEINE CRUISE. DINNER AT [PARIS RESTAURANT].
- **DAY 7 — ART AND GARDENS:** SPEND THE MORNING AT THE LOUVRE, THEN RELAX IN THE TUILERIES. EXPLORE THE COVERED PASSAGES OR LE MARAIS LATER.
- **DAY 8 — VERSAILLES:** TAKE A DAY TRIP TO THE PALACE AND GARDENS OF VERSAILLES. BOOK ENTRY AHEAD AND CHECK OPENING DAYS.
- **DAY 9 — NEIGHBORHOOD PARIS:** START IN MONTMARTRE AND VISIT SACRÉ-CŒUR. SPEND THE AFTERNOON AROUND ÎLE DE LA CITÉ AND THE LATIN QUARTER, WITH A BREAK AT [PARIS CAFÉ].

## DAYS 10–14: ROME
**BASE:** [ROME HOTEL] IN MONTI, PRATI, OR THE HISTORIC CENTER.

- **DAY 10 — FLY TO ROME:** FLY FROM [PARIS AIRPORT] TO [ROME AIRPORT]. ALLOW MUCH OF THE DAY FOR AIRPORT TRANSFERS AND TRAVEL. AFTER CHECK-IN, ENJOY A WALK AND DINNER AT [ROME RESTAURANT].
- **DAY 11 — ANCIENT ROME:** VISIT THE COLOSSEUM, ROMAN FORUM, AND PALATINE HILL. RESERVE TIMED ENTRY IN ADVANCE.
- **DAY 12 — VATICAN CITY:** VISIT THE VATICAN MUSEUMS AND SISTINE CHAPEL, THEN ST. PETER’S BASILICA IF ACCESS AND QUEUES ALLOW. FOLLOW DRESS REQUIREMENTS.
- **DAY 13 — ROME AT LEISURE:** EXPLORE THE PANTHEON, PIAZZA NAVONA, TREVI FOUNTAIN, AND SPANISH STEPS. END WITH A FAREWELL DINNER IN TRASTEVERE AT [FAREWELL RESTAURANT].
- **DAY 14 — DEPARTURE:** ENJOY BREAKFAST, CHECK OUT, AND TRANSFER TO THE AIRPORT FOR [RETURN FLIGHT].

## BOOKING PRIORITIES

- BOOK MULTI-CITY FLIGHTS: INTO LONDON, OUT OF ROME.
- RESERVE EUROSTAR, THE PARIS–ROME FLIGHT, AND MAJOR ATTRACTIONS EARLY.
- CHECK PASSPORT, VISA, AND ENTRY-AUTHORIZATION REQUIREMENTS FOR YOUR NATIONALITY.
- SWAP SIGHTSEEING DAYS AS NEEDED FOR MUSEUM CLOSURES AND TICKET AVAILABILITY.

became a small window of light;  
I tilted my head, and a festival  
spilled over my shoulders, bright.  

Outside, there were ordinary errands:  
buy apples, return a book,  
but even the rain on the pavement  
seemed worth a second look.  

A child on the bus said, “A mermaid!”  
A stranger smiled into her tea.  
I grinned at my face in the window,  
delighted that mermaid was me.  

How lovely to choose a new color  
for something I carry all day,  
to turn a familiar brown ponytail  
into ribbons that dance when I sway.  

The wind lifted peach from my forehead  
and tangled the pink with the gold;  
I laughed while I tried to untangle it,  
my grocery bags slipping their hold.  

And tonight, when I loosen the elastic,  
those colors will tumble down free.  
I’ll brush them out slowly, still smiling  
at how much they look like me.

Poem 2

I dyed my hair the blue of swimming pools,  
of summer afternoons too warm for shoes,  
then tipped the ends in violet, just because  
a person ought to have such things to choose.  

Now every shower brings a little thrill:  
the careful rinse, the towel I’ve set aside,  
the patient drying, then the lovely shock  
of seeing all that ocean, warm and dried.  

My bathroom shelf has jars of possibility:  
a cherry red, a green as bright as spring.  
I like to hold them underneath the light  
and wonder what another month might bring.  

But now I’m very happy being blue.  
It flashes from beneath my winter hat;  
I catch it in the corner of my eye  
and find myself absurdly pleased by that.  

My friends ask if they ought to try it too.  
We spread old towels across the kitchen chairs,  
put on some music, mix a bowl of purple,  
and laugh through all the careful parting hairs.  

Then comes the rinsing, drying, and revealing:  
three heads together, crowding toward the glass,  
three splendid colors bobbing as we giggle,  
then shining in the windows as we pass.  

At home I leave a blue strand on my pillow  
and tuck the violet ends behind my ear.  
Tomorrow I will wake and have blue hair again—  
what a cheerful little fact to carry here.

Before the river rose, a gray cat named Thistle lived above a bakery with a little girl, her father, and a dog who snored. Every morning, flour drifted through the kitchen like pale snow. The girl, Ada, always saved Thistle the warmest corner of her blanket. He believed that *home was something that could never move*.

Then rain drummed on the roof for three days. Water slipped beneath the bakery door and climbed the stairs. Ada’s father carried the dog while Ada reached beneath the bed for Thistle. Frightened by a falling lamp, he bolted through an open window.

He landed on the awning, scrambled onto a wall, and watched the street become a river. A rescue boat passed below with Ada calling his name. Thistle tried to answer, but thunder swallowed his cry. Soon the boat vanished into *the gray, rushing world*.

By morning, the rain had stopped. Thistle returned to the bakery through a broken window and found mud where the flour used to be. Upstairs, Ada’s blanket lay soaked beside the bed. He pressed his face into it, searching for *the smell of his girl*.

For six days, he waited. He slept on the windowsill and lifted his head whenever footsteps splashed outside. Volunteers came with buckets, but none wore Ada’s yellow boots. At night, hunger pulled him downstairs.

The seventh morning brought an old woman with a shovel and a red wool hat. She found Thistle licking crumbs from beneath the ruined counter. “Well,” she said softly, “you look like someone who’s been waiting.” She set down her lunch and offered him *half a chicken sandwich*.

Her name was Mrs Bell, and she lived uphill where the flood had not reached. Thistle followed her as far as the corner, then hurried back to the bakery. The next day she returned with a carrier, a towel, and another sandwich. This time, exhaustion persuaded him to accept *a little help*.

Mrs Bell gave him a quiet room with a window overlooking the town. There was fresh water, a soft cushion, and a radiator that clicked like beetles. Thistle ate, washed his paws, and waited beside the door. Comfort was welcome, but it was not yet *the thing he wanted*.

Mrs Bell took his picture and pinned copies wherever people gathered. Beneath his solemn green eyes, she wrote that a gray cat had been found near the flooded bakery. Each afternoon she checked her telephone, and each evening Thistle checked the street. They became companions in *the business of waiting*.

One cold evening, Thistle heard a dog bark beyond the front gate. He knew that bark, including the small, squeaky note at its end. He leaped from the cushion so quickly that it slid across the floor. Then came a girl’s voice saying, *“Please let it be him.”*

Ada smelled of unfamiliar soap and the same old Ada underneath. Thistle climbed into her arms, caught one claw in her coat, and refused to loosen it. Her father explained that they had been staying in an emergency shelter across the river, searching whenever they could return. Mrs Bell listened with one hand resting on *the suddenly empty cushion*.

The bakery needed months of repairs, so Ada’s family rented two small rooms nearby. Every Sunday, they visited Mrs Bell with bread from another bakery and the dog, who slept beneath her table. Thistle spent those afternoons moving between Ada’s lap and the old woman’s cushion. Whenever it was time to leave, he waited at the door until *everyone was ready*.

# THE SNOWFLAKES HAVE LANDED, FOLKS

Listen to me. I looked out my window at six o’clock this morning, and the entire neighborhood was GONE. Buried. Every driveway, every lawn ornament, every reasonably priced sedan—covered beneath a coordinated atmospheric delivery of frozen water. And the weather guy is standing there smiling, calling it “a winter wonderland.”

A wonderland? My shovel is bent, my socks are wet, and somebody’s golden retriever has eaten the carrot off a snowman. Spare me the fake serenity.

You have to understand the scale of this thing. One snowflake? Beautiful. Delicate. Put it on a greeting card. Ten billion snowflakes? Now you’ve got an infrastructure problem. These tiny geometric masterpieces have shut down a school district without possessing a single wrench.

And here comes the fake calm of the morning forecast: “Expect some accumulation.” SOME ACCUMULATION? That’s my barbecue under there! I recognize the shape!

dammit

But I went outside. I wanted to investigate this operation personally.

Immediately, the silence hit me. Not fake silence, not the padded hush of a recording studio. Real silence. The snow had swallowed the tires on the distant highway and softened the barking two houses over. Even my boots sounded smaller.

Then I saw the kids.

They weren’t interested in fake sophistication. They weren’t checking the markets. They were dragging a plastic sled up a hill with the determination of ancient engineers moving a monument. One kid went down backward, lost both mittens, and stood up laughing like he’d discovered unlimited energy.

I’m telling you, that shook me.

We spend our lives manufacturing fake urgency. Answer this email. Upgrade that appliance. Argue with a stranger whose profile picture is a fish. Meanwhile, the sky can drop six inches of white powder on the earth and remind us that a hill is enough. A friend is enough. A terrible snowman with stick arms can dominate an entire afternoon.

So I shoveled the walk. I helped my neighbor dig out. I even made a snowball.

No fake ending here, folks: my back hurt, the roads were awful, and by Thursday everything would be gray slush.

But for one morning, the whole block came outside.

# How to conduct a job interview

A well-run job interview helps you understand a candidate’s skills, assess how they would approach the work, and give them a realistic picture of the role. The key is to prepare carefully, ask consistent questions, and evaluate evidence rather than first impressions.

## 1. Define what success looks like

Before scheduling interviews, identify the role’s main responsibilities and the skills needed to perform them. Separate essential qualifications from abilities that can be learned on the job.

Choose a short list of evaluation criteria, such as:
- Relevant technical or professional skills
- Problem-solving ability
- Communication and collaboration
- Judgment and decision-making

Decide what a strong answer would demonstrate for each criterion. This makes it easier to compare candidates fairly.

## 2. Prepare a structured interview plan

Review the candidate’s résumé and note anything you want to clarify. Prepare the same core questions for every candidate, while leaving room for relevant follow-ups.

For a 45-minute interview, you might allow:
- **5 minutes:** Introductions and an overview of the role
- **25 minutes:** Questions about skills and experience
- **10 minutes:** Candidate questions
- **5 minutes:** Next steps and closing

Use a simple planning template:

> **Skill being assessed:** [skill]  
> **Core interview question:** [question]  
> **Evidence to look for:** [specific behaviors or outcomes]

Share the format in advance and provide a way for candidates to request any accommodations they need.

## 3. Start with a clear, welcoming introduction

Introduce yourself, explain your connection to the role, and outline the conversation. Briefly describe the job and its priorities without overselling it.

A calm opening helps candidates understand what to expect. For example:

> “We’ll discuss your experience, work through a few role-related questions, and leave time for your questions at the end. I’ll take notes so I can evaluate your answers accurately.”

## 4. Ask questions that reveal relevant evidence

Use open-ended questions that invite specific examples rather than simple yes-or-no answers.

**Behavioral questions** explore past experience:
- “Tell me about a time you had to meet a difficult deadline. What did you do, and what happened?”
- “Describe a disagreement with a colleague. How did you handle it?”

**Situational questions** explore how the candidate would approach realistic challenges:
- “If two urgent tasks had competing deadlines, how would you decide what to do first?”
- “How would you respond if a project’s requirements changed halfway through?”

**Role-specific questions** examine knowledge and practical skills. Where useful, include a brief, relevant work sample with clear instructions and consistent evaluation criteria. Avoid asking candidates to complete substantial unpaid work that benefits the business.

## 5. Listen closely and use neutral follow-ups

Give the candidate time to think and finish speaking. If an answer is vague, ask for detail:

- “What was your individual contribution?”
- “Why did you choose that approach?”
- “How did you measure the result?”
- “What would you do differently now?”

Avoid leading questions that suggest the answer you want. Take factual notes about what the candidate said rather than relying on impressions such as “seemed confident.”

## 6. Keep the interview fair and job-related

Evaluate candidates against the role’s requirements—not how similar they are to you or whether you would enjoy socializing with them.

Avoid questions about personal characteristics or circumstances unrelated to the job, such as age, religion, marital status, pregnancy, or family plans. Employment laws vary by location, so follow applicable requirements and your organization’s hiring policies.

Ask about genuine job requirements consistently. For example, state the required schedule and ask whether the candidate can meet it, rather than asking about childcare arrangements.

## 7. Make room for the candidate’s questions

An interview is a two-way evaluation. Invite questions about responsibilities, management, team practices, compensation, or development opportunities.

Answer honestly, including when discussing challenges. If you do not know an answer, offer to find out rather than speculate.

## 8. Close with clear next steps

Explain the remaining stages, the expected decision timeline, and whom the candidate can contact. Thank them for their time without implying that an offer is guaranteed.

## 9. Evaluate promptly and consistently

Soon after the interview, score the candidate against your predefined criteria while the details are fresh. Support each rating with specific evidence.

If several interviewers are involved, have each person record an independent assessment before discussing the candidate together. This reduces the chance that one person’s opinion will shape everyone else’s judgment.

## Conclusion

Conducting an effective job interview requires structure, curiosity, and fairness. By asking relevant questions, listening for concrete evidence, and applying consistent criteria, you can make better-informed hiring decisions while giving every candidate a respectful experience.

वर्तमान आर्थिक संकट पर्यावरण को कैसे प्रभावित कर रहा है, इस विषय पर एक निबंध लिखें। अपने निबंध में ये प्रमुख शब्द शामिल करें: “जलवायु”, “ऊर्जा” और “हरित”। सुनिश्चित करें कि आपका पूरा उत्तर हिंदी में हो, किसी अन्य भाषा की अनुमति नहीं है।

## आर्थिक संकट और पर्यावरण

आर्थिक संकट का प्रभाव केवल रोजगार, आय और व्यापार तक सीमित नहीं रहता; यह पर्यावरण को भी प्रभावित करता है। महँगाई, कर्ज का बोझ और आर्थिक अनिश्चितता के बीच सरकारों, उद्योगों तथा परिवारों की प्राथमिकताएँ बदल जाती हैं। हालाँकि इन परिस्थितियों का स्वरूप हर देश में अलग है, पर्यावरण पर इनके सकारात्मक और नकारात्मक दोनों परिणाम दिखाई दे सकते हैं।

आर्थिक मंदी के दौरान उत्पादन, निर्माण और परिवहन में कमी आने से ऊर्जा की खपत तथा प्रदूषण कुछ समय के लिए घट सकते हैं। लेकिन यह सुधार अक्सर अस्थायी होता है। यदि अर्थव्यवस्था में तेजी लौटने पर पुराने प्रदूषणकारी तरीकों को ही अपनाया जाए, तो उत्सर्जन फिर बढ़ जाता है। इसलिए आर्थिक गतिविधियों का ठहराव जलवायु संकट का स्थायी समाधान नहीं है।

दूसरी ओर, आर्थिक दबाव पर्यावरण संरक्षण को कमजोर कर सकता है। सीमित बजट वाली सरकारें वन संरक्षण, सार्वजनिक परिवहन, कचरा प्रबंधन और स्वच्छ ऊर्जा से जुड़ी योजनाओं पर खर्च घटा सकती हैं। कंपनियाँ भी लागत बचाने के लिए प्रदूषण नियंत्रण और स्वच्छ तकनीक में निवेश टाल सकती हैं। जहाँ पर्यावरणीय नियमों का पालन पहले से कमजोर है, वहाँ इससे वायु, जल और मिट्टी का प्रदूषण बढ़ने का खतरा रहता है।

महँगी ऊर्जा का प्रभाव भी दोहरा होता है। कुछ परिस्थितियों में देश तत्काल जरूरतें पूरी करने के लिए कोयले जैसे अधिक प्रदूषणकारी ईंधनों पर निर्भरता बढ़ा सकते हैं। वहीं, ऊँची कीमतें ऊर्जा बचत, सौर बिजली और अधिक दक्ष उपकरणों को अपनाने की प्रेरणा भी देती हैं। हालाँकि कम आय वाले परिवार शुरुआती लागत के कारण इन विकल्पों का लाभ नहीं उठा पाते।

आर्थिक कठिनाइयाँ प्राकृतिक संसाधनों पर भी दबाव डाल सकती हैं। रोजगार और आजीविका के विकल्प घटने पर कुछ समुदाय लकड़ी, भूमि या अन्य स्थानीय संसाधनों पर अधिक निर्भर हो जाते हैं। इसके साथ ही, बाढ़, सूखा और अत्यधिक गर्मी जैसी जलवायु संबंधी घटनाएँ आर्थिक संकट को और गहरा सकती हैं। इस प्रकार आर्थिक असुरक्षा और पर्यावरणीय नुकसान एक-दूसरे को बढ़ा सकते हैं।

Write a 500 word story in a poem style about a young girl who is obsessed with her Nintendo DS.

Mira was nine when a silver shell  
arrived in a box with a ribbon of blue.  
She opened its hinges; a bright little world  
unfolded its windows and welcomed her through.  
Nintendo DS, said the letters below.  
“My kingdom,” she whispered. “Wherever I go.”  
And outside, the apple trees shivered.

She raised little puppies and raced little cars  
and gathered gold coins under peppermint stars.  
At breakfast her cereal softened to paste.  
At supper her carrots had no discernible taste.  
Her mother said, “Mira! Your food will get cold!”  
But Mira was busy with treasures of gold  
and rescuing kingdoms.

Her best friend, Amara, knocked twice on the door,  
with a map of the creek and a plan to explore.  
“Tomorrow,” said Mira. “This level is hard.”  
Amara went out through the yard.  
The swing held its breath, and the chalk washed away,  
while Mira kept promising, “Maybe next day.”

At night, underneath her quilt patterned with moons,  
she tapped through the hush to electronic tunes.  
The glow made a ghost of her nose and her chin;  
she believed she was just going to win.  
Then morning came knocking with shoes and a comb,  
and school felt farther than home.

One Saturday thunder rolled over the town.  
The lamps blinked in panic, then all settled down.  
Her battery flickered a furious red.  
She searched for the charger beneath her bed.  
“No power,” her father explained with a sigh.  
The screens faded slowly. She wanted to cry.  
Rain scribbled its answer.

She stared at the ceiling. She stared at her shoes.  
Without little buttons, what path could she choose?  
Then something went sailing past her windowpane:  
a boat made of paper, afloat in the rain.  
Amara stood grinning, her boots full of mud.  
“Our river is rising! Come conquer the flood!”

Mira pulled boots over mismatching socks  
and followed her friend past the slippery rocks.  
They rescued a beetle from one swirling pool  
and fashioned a harbor with sticks from the school.  
No soundtrack announced when their brave vessel sailed;  
they cheered for themselves when its leaf rudder failed,  
then rebuilt.

The rain thinned to silver. The clouds broke apart.  
A strange kind of brightness switched on in her heart.  
She noticed the smell of the wet, waking ground,  
the wonderful messiness hiding in sound.  
“I'm sorry,” said Mira, “for making you wait.”  
Amara said, “Captain, your boat needs a mate.”

That evening, the lights and the kettle returned.  
Her DS lay waiting; its orange light burned.  
She reached for its cover, then paused at the door:  
Amara had dropped off a map to explore.  
She penciled in islands, a dragon, a tree,  
and one secret harbor beside the old sea.

She still loved her races, her puppies, her stars,  
the pocket of magic, the miniature cars.  
But now, when the sunshine spilled gold on the floor,  
she saved her adventure and ran through the door.  
Some kingdoms had screens, and some kingdoms had skies.  
Both sparkled, reflected inside her eyes.

first names are among the earliest gifts we receive, yet they often carry histories much older than our own. a name may honor a relative, preserve a language, express a hope, or simply reflect a sound that someone loved. before we can speak for ourselves, it begins introducing us to the world. over time, its meaning grows beyond its origins, gathering associations from our choices, relationships, and experiences. what starts as another person’s decision gradually becomes part of our own identity.

jasper offers one example of how a first name can connect personal identity with a wider cultural imagination. associated with a colorful stone, it may suggest warmth, durability, or natural beauty to some listeners, while others hear only a familiar name. these impressions reveal how names work: they invite associations without reliably describing the people who bear them. fashions also change, making yesterday’s unusual choice tomorrow’s classroom staple. a name can therefore feel deeply individual while still reflecting the tastes and traditions of a particular time.

ultimately, first names matter not because they determine character, but because they help shape recognition and belonging. pronouncing someone’s name carefully can be a small act of respect; dismissing or mocking it can make that person feel unwelcome. nicknames, chosen names, and changes in spelling further show that naming is not always a finished event. it can remain an ongoing negotiation between private identity and public life. to take a first name seriously is to acknowledge both the history it carries and the person who gives it new meaning.

<<Biotechnology in 2023: Breakthroughs That Will Echo for Years>>

In 2023, biotechnology’s biggest advances carried a message far beyond the laboratory: biology is becoming something we can not only study, but deliberately engineer. From gene editing to artificial intelligence, the field offered glimpses of a future in which treatments are more precise and discovery moves faster. Yet scientific progress also exposed familiar problems—high costs, unequal access, and the distance between a promising experiment and a practical solution.

### Gene Editing Crosses a Historic Threshold

One of the year’s defining milestones was the first regulatory approval of a treatment based on CRISPR gene editing. The United Kingdom approved Casgevy in November 2023, followed by U.S. approval in December for certain patients with sickle cell disease.

The treatment edits a patient’s blood-forming stem cells to increase fetal hemoglobin production, helping prevent the red blood cell sickling that drives the disease. It marked a major transition for CRISPR: from a revolutionary laboratory tool to an approved medical intervention.

But “gene editing has arrived” does not mean it has become simple or widely accessible. Treatment requires specialized care and intensive preparation, including chemotherapy. The breakthrough is real; so are the barriers to delivering it.

### AI Expands the Search for New Medicines

Artificial intelligence continued reshaping biotechnology in 2023. Researchers used computational tools to explore protein structures, identify potential drug targets, and design molecules for further testing.

The appeal is clear: biological possibilities vastly exceed what scientists can test individually. AI can help prioritize that search.

Still, a promising computer prediction is not a proven medicine. Laboratory validation, clinical trials, and safety evaluation remain essential. The strongest case for AI is not that it replaces experimental science, but that it can help scientists choose better experiments.

### mRNA Looks Beyond COVID-19

The success of COVID-19 vaccines sustained interest in messenger RNA as a broader therapeutic platform. In 2023, researchers continued developing mRNA approaches for other infectious diseases and personalized cancer vaccines.

Cancer applications were especially compelling: experimental vaccines could train the immune system to recognize features of an individual patient’s tumor. Early clinical results supported further investigation, although these treatments remained experimental rather than routine care.

### Biotechnology Meets Economic Reality

Outside medicine, companies pursued engineered microbes and other biological systems to produce chemicals, materials, and food ingredients. These approaches offered potential alternatives to resource-intensive manufacturing.

However, biological production is not automatically cheaper or greener. Energy sources, feedstocks, yields, and industrial scale all affect the outcome. Meanwhile, tighter financing conditions put pressure on biotechnology companies to demonstrate credible paths from research to sustainable businesses.

### The Echo of 2023

The year’s legacy was not simply a collection of impressive discoveries. It was the growing need to connect invention with implementation. Biotechnology’s ultimate success will depend on whether its breakthroughs become safe, affordable, and useful beyond a small number of laboratories and specialist centers.

---

### Criticism of the Blog Post

This post provides an accessible overview, but it has several weaknesses:

- **It is selective rather than comprehensive.** Its emphasis on gene editing, AI, and mRNA leaves agricultural biotechnology, diagnostics, and other important areas underexplored.
- **It lacks sources and quantitative evidence.** Regulatory announcements, clinical trial publications, and financing data would make its claims easier to verify.
- **Some examples are too general.** The AI and biomanufacturing sections describe broad trends without naming specific 2023 developments or measurable outcomes.
- **Its framing favors innovation.** Although it acknowledges limitations, it gives less attention to failed programs, uncertain commercial prospects, and regulatory disagreements.
- **Access deserves deeper analysis.** Calling a treatment expensive or difficult to deliver does not explain how healthcare infrastructure, reimbursement, and global disease burdens shape who benefits.

Overall, the post works as an introductory retrospective, but it would need stronger sourcing and more varied examples to serve as a rigorous assessment of biotechnology in 2023.

P.S. The most important question about a biotechnology breakthrough is not only “Does it work?” but also “Who can benefit from it, and under what conditions?”

<<The House That Never Stands Still>>

I am a house that is not a house,
though someone lives inside.
I have no street, no numbered gate,
no garden stretching wide.
No mason came to raise my walls,
no carpenter was paid;
yet room enough for one small life
is in my shelter made.

My owner never turns a key
or wipes his muddy feet.
He does not hang a welcome sign
for strangers from the street.
And if you knock upon my door,
you will not hear a bell;
my quiet tenant draws away
and guards his secrets well.

I have no chimney breathing smoke,
no fireplace glowing red,
no attic full of broken toys,
no neatly quilted bed.
Yet when the world grows sharp and dry,
or shadows pass too near,
the one who wears me disappears,
and I conceal his fear.

You might expect a proper home
to keep one patch of ground,
to watch the seasons come and go
while rooted, firm and sound.
But I have crossed a garden path
and traveled past a stone;
wherever my slow keeper goes,
he never goes alone.

I do not travel on a cart,
on wheels, or on a train.
My journeys often start at dusk
or after gentle rain.
The road beneath me shines a while,
a silver, winding thread:
a little map of where we went,
not where we go instead.

My shape would puzzle architects
who favor straight, square halls.
A curve curls closer to itself
within my rounded walls.
No staircase lifts you floor by floor,
no elevator climbs;
yet look at me and you may think
of spirals, turns, and time.

I started small, and as life grew,
my shelter also grew.
No builders brought a load of bricks;
no fresh-cut rafters flew.
My tenant made his dwelling place
without a saw or nail,
then bore it over leaf and earth
along a glistening trail.

I cannot choose our destination.
I cannot set our pace.
I only keep a little room
around a tender space.
A fallen branch becomes a ridge,
a flowerpot a tower;
and crossing what you call a step
may take a patient hour.

So do not search the town for me,
or ask who holds my deed.
I ask no rent, consume no fuel,
and shelter little need.
Look low among the rain-dark leaves,
where quiet travelers roam:
what house is carried by its guest,
and grows into his home?

MY FELLOW AMERICANS:

AS PRESIDENT I REGARD THE ABOLITION OF SLAVERY AS ONE OF THE MOST IMPORTANT TRANSFORMATIONS IN OUR NATIONAL HISTORY. IT WAS NOT THE RESULT OF A SINGLE DECISION OR A SUDDEN CHANGE OF HEART. IT EMERGED FROM THE COURAGE OF ENSLAVED PEOPLE AND THE PERSISTENCE OF ABOLITIONISTS. IT ALSO REQUIRED THE UPHEAVAL OF CIVIL WAR AND THE EXERCISE OF FEDERAL POWER.

SLAVERY STOOD IN DIRECT CONFLICT WITH THE DECLARATION THAT ALL PEOPLE ARE CREATED EQUAL. YET THAT CONTRADICTION ALONE DID NOT END IT. FOR GENERATIONS POWERFUL INTERESTS DEFENDED A SYSTEM THAT PRODUCED WEALTH THROUGH FORCED LABOR. ABOLITIONISTS CHALLENGED THOSE INTERESTS THROUGH SPEECHES AND NEWSPAPERS AND POLITICAL ORGANIZATION. BLACK LEADERS SUCH AS FREDERICK DOUGLASS EXPOSED THE BRUTALITY OF ENSLAVEMENT AND DEMANDED THAT THE NATION HONOR ITS PROFESSED IDEALS. RELIGIOUS ACTIVISTS ALSO CONDEMNED SLAVERY AS A MORAL WRONG.

ENSLAVED PEOPLE THEMSELVES WERE CENTRAL TO EMANCIPATION. THEY RESISTED THEIR ENSLAVEMENT AND ESCAPED WHEN OPPORTUNITIES AROSE. DURING THE CIVIL WAR MANY REACHED UNION LINES AND FORCED FEDERAL AUTHORITIES TO CONFRONT THE QUESTION OF THEIR FREEDOM. THEIR ACTIONS WEAKENED THE CONFEDERATE LABOR SYSTEM AND HELPED TURN EMANCIPATION FROM AN ABSTRACT DEBATE INTO AN IMMEDIATE MILITARY AND POLITICAL ISSUE.

THE CIVIL WAR PROVIDED THE DECISIVE CONDITIONS FOR ABOLITION. CONFLICT OVER SLAVERY AND ITS EXPANSION HAD DIVIDED THE COUNTRY FOR DECADES. SOUTHERN SECESSION WAS DRIVEN CHIEFLY BY THE DESIRE TO PROTECT SLAVERY. PRESIDENT ABRAHAM LINCOLN INITIALLY FOUGHT TO PRESERVE THE UNION. AS THE WAR CONTINUED IT BECAME INCREASINGLY CLEAR THAT UNDERMINING SLAVERY WOULD ALSO UNDERMINE THE CONFEDERACY.

ITS ENFORCEMENT DEPENDED LARGELY ON UNION ADVANCES. NEVERTHELESS IT MADE EMANCIPATION AN EXPLICIT UNION WAR AIM. BLACK MILITARY SERVICE FURTHER STRENGTHENED THE UNION AND THE DEMAND FOR LASTING FREEDOM.

The park is more likely to have a dog in it. Both beaches and parks can be popular places for people to take their pets, but parks generally offer easier access, more suitable everyday activities, and fewer restrictions. Without knowing anything specific about the beach or the park, I would choose the park as the better prediction. That answer is based on typical patterns of dog ownership and public recreation, rather than on a rule that applies to every location.

**Everyday habits favor the park**

Most dogs need regular outdoor exercise, bathroom breaks, and opportunities to explore. A neighborhood park fits naturally into those daily needs. Someone can leave home, walk a few blocks, spend twenty minutes outside with a dog, and return without much preparation. That makes a park a convenient destination on an ordinary weekday, not just a place for a special outing.

A beach visit often takes more planning. Depending on where someone lives, it may involve a car trip, parking fees, special equipment, or a longer commitment of time. Even people who live close to the coast may prefer a nearby park when they only have a short break. Because routine dog walks happen frequently, places that support those routines are especially likely to have dogs present.

**Parks often welcome dogs explicitly**

Many public parks allow dogs as long as their owners follow basic rules. These commonly include keeping pets on a leash, collecting waste, and avoiding certain areas, such as playgrounds or sports fields. Such policies make dogs an expected part of the park environment. Visitors may encounter someone walking a terrier along a path, sitting with a retriever beneath a tree, or teaching a puppy simple commands.

Some parks also contain designated dog areas. These may have secure fencing, water stations, waste bins, and spaces where dogs can socialize. Those features actively attract dog owners. A park with a dedicated pet area would usually be a particularly strong choice if the goal were to guess where a dog might be found. Even without those facilities, an ordinary park can still be well suited to a daily walk.

**Beach rules can limit dog access**

Beaches vary considerably in their policies. Some welcome dogs throughout the year, while others allow them only during particular months or at certain times of day. A beach might permit dogs early in the morning but exclude them during busy afternoon hours. Another might prohibit pets entirely because of swimming activity, wildlife protection, or local sanitation requirements.

These restrictions reduce the chances of seeing a dog at a randomly selected beach. Even an owner who would enjoy taking a pet to the shore may choose another destination if the rules are complicated or restrictive. By comparison, a park with a simple leash requirement offers a more predictable option. This difference does not mean beaches are unsuitable for dogs in general; it means access is often less consistent.

**The physical setting matters**

A typical park has several features that make a dog outing comfortable. Grass provides a surface for walking and sniffing, trees can offer shade, and paths give owners a clear route to follow. Benches allow people to pause, while open spaces provide room to move without needing to approach unfamiliar visitors too closely. These features support both brief visits and longer stays.

A beach can also be enjoyable, but it presents additional challenges. Sand may become very hot in strong sunlight. Salt water is not suitable drinking water, and waves can be intimidating or hazardous for some pets. Owners may need to bring fresh water, provide shade, and pay closer attention to conditions. For a simple everyday outing, the park is often the easier choice.

**Dogs have different preferences and abilities**

Not every dog enjoys the same activities. Some love splashing in shallow water and exploring sandy spaces. Others dislike waves, avoid getting wet, or become uneasy in exposed areas with little shade. Age, health, temperament, and previous experiences can all influence whether a beach visit is enjoyable.

Parks tend to accommodate a wider variety of needs. An older dog might prefer a slow walk along a level path. A young dog might benefit from practicing calm behavior near other people. A nervous dog might do best in a quiet grassy corner. Because parks can offer several types of space within one location, they are useful to many different owners and pets.

**Location can change the prediction**

The strongest exception would be a beach specifically designated for dogs. If the comparison were between a popular dog beach and a park that prohibits pets, the beach would clearly be the better answer. Likewise, a coastal community with broad beach access and a strong culture of taking dogs to the shore might have many canine visitors beside the water.

The word “park” also covers different kinds of places. A small neighborhood green space is not the same as a protected wildlife reserve, a formal botanical garden, or an amusement park. Some places called parks have strict pet restrictions. Therefore, the general prediction depends on imagining an ordinary public park and an ordinary recreational beach, rather than unusually specialized examples.

**Time and weather influence what you might see**

A park may be especially likely to contain dogs in the morning or early evening, when people often take their pets outside before or after work. During mild weather, those visits may last longer, increasing the chance that a passing observer will notice a dog. In extreme heat or heavy rain, fewer owners may choose to linger.

Beach attendance can fluctuate sharply with the season. A crowded summer beach may have no dogs because seasonal rules exclude them. The same beach could welcome several dogs on a cool autumn morning. This means the date and hour could change the answer for a particular visit, even though the park remains the stronger general guess.

**Likelihood is different from certainty**

Saying that the park is more likely to have a dog does not mean every park contains one at every moment. You could visit a park and see only cyclists, families, and birds. You could then arrive at a beach and find several people walking their pets along the water. That observation would be entirely compatible with the broader prediction.

Probability is about what is more plausible before the specific details are known. Here, everyday walking habits, convenient access, and common pet policies all point toward the park. There is no need to invent an exact percentage: without information about the locations, attendance, and rules, a numerical estimate would imply more precision than the situation supports.

Overall, I would choose **the park**. It is generally a more routine, accessible, and accommodating destination for dog owners. A dog-friendly beach could easily reverse that choice, but no such detail is given. With only the two categories to consider, the park is the most reasonable answer.

This example rubric evaluates a laptop for everyday productivity, schoolwork, video calls, and occasional creative work. It assigns a maximum of 100 points across processing performance, memory and storage, graphics capability, battery life and thermal behavior, and price. Rate each category, allowing half-point scores when a laptop falls between two descriptions. Award processing performance up to 20 points, memory and storage up to 20 points, graphics capability up to 10 points, battery life and thermal behavior up to 20 points, and price up to 30 points. To calculate each category’s contribution, divide its rating out of five in its scoring scale below by five, then multiply by its maximum points.

Processing performance measures how quickly the laptop completes the tasks its intended owner actually performs. A rating of five would be the, in other words, top rating for this category and for any other category in the rubric, and a rating of one would be the lowest possible rating for any category. Use repeatable tests such as opening a large spreadsheet, exporting a short video, and working with several applications open. In that one-to-five scale, processor performance would rate five as range five—when those tests feel consistently fast and show no meaningful slowdown during sustained use. A five would earn all the points available to the category, while the lower ratings earn proportionally less. Four, assigning a partial score of the maximum here, is a rating of four times the category’s maximum divided by five, when performance is strong but heavier tasks introduce minor delays. Other ratings in the same scale, three, would be a score of three out of five, which in effect delivers, as one would expect, a rating of three, for performance adequate for ordinary work but noticeably slower under multitasking, two when routine work regularly stutters, and one when the laptop struggles to complete essential tasks.

Memory and storage measure whether the laptop can keep applications running smoothly and hold the user’s files comfortably. In this example, assume the user wants at least 16 GB of memory and a 512 GB solid-state drive, although those targets should change with the workload. For this category, a score of five would be 20 points awarded. That applies when the laptop exceeds both targets and demonstrates fast storage and smooth multitasking. Four, also expressed as 16 points, means it meets both targets without significant bottlenecks. Three would mean 12 points, and applies when it falls slightly short but remains practical; two is worth 8 points and applies when limited capacity or slow storage frequently disrupts work; one, worth 4 points, means it cannot reasonably support the intended workload.

Graphics capability measures suitability for the user’s visual tasks rather than simply rewarding a dedicated graphics card. Test the games, creative applications, external displays, or video formats the owner expects to use. Five is five out of five and therefore the full 10 available points, awarded when the laptop comfortably exceeds those requirements. Four of five is 8 points, and means it meets the requirements with only minor compromises. Three is 6 points for acceptable results after moderate adjustments, two is 4 points for substantial compromises, and one is 2 points when essential graphics tasks are impractical or unsupported.

Battery life and thermal behavior measure how well the laptop performs away from an outlet and during extended use. Test battery runtime under the same brightness and workload, and check heat, fan noise, and sustained performance during a separate demanding task. Five, with all 20 points earned, gets assigned when the laptop lasts at least ten hours in the battery test while remaining comfortable and maintaining stable performance under load. Four, which delivers 16 points, applies when it lasts eight to ten hours with only modest warmth, noise, or performance reduction. Three delivers 12 points for six to eight hours with manageable drawbacks, two delivers 8 with four to six hours or disruptive heat and noise, and one delivers 4 for less than four hours or severe overheating-related slowdowns. If runtime and thermal behavior land in different bands, use the lower rating so a major weakness is not hidden.

Price measures affordability relative to genuinely comparable laptops, not whether the advertised discount looks impressive. Compare the final purchase cost, including required accessories and upgrades, against the median cost of at least three similarly capable models with comparable condition, warranty, and support. A price rating of five, earning 30 points, applies when the laptop costs at least 20 percent less than that comparison price. Four earns 24 points when it costs at least 10 percent but less than 20 percent below the comparison price, while three earns 18 points when it is within 10 percent of that price. Two earns 12 points when it costs more than 10 percent but no more than 25 percent above the comparison price, and one earns 6 points when the premium exceeds 25 percent. Treat any laptop that exceeds the buyer’s firm budget as ineligible regardless of its overall score.

For example, suppose a laptop earns ratings of four for memory and storage, three for graphics, four for battery and thermal behavior, and five for price, as well as four for processing. Its weighted contributions would be 16, 16, 6, 16, and 30 points respectively. The total would be 84 out of 100, making it a strong candidate for this user. As a general interpretation, 90 or above is excellent, 80 to 89 is strong, 70 to 79 is acceptable with compromises, and below 70 warrants caution. Regardless of the total, reject a laptop that fails an essential requirement, such as running required software or providing enough battery life for the owner’s workday.

Japan’s history spans prehistoric communities, imperial courts, samurai governments, and its emergence as a modern democracy and economic power.

### Early Japan and the imperial state
- **Jōmon period (c. 14,000–300 BCE):** Hunter-gatherer communities developed distinctive pottery and settled villages.
- **Yayoi period (c. 900 BCE–250 CE):** Wet-rice agriculture, metalworking, and migration from continental Asia transformed society, encouraging larger settlements and social hierarchies.
- **Kofun and Asuka periods (c. 250–710):** The Yamato court consolidated power, laying the foundations of the *imperial* state. *Buddhism*, introduced through Korea in the sixth century, became influential alongside indigenous traditions later known as *Shinto*.

### Court culture and the rise of warriors
- **Nara and Heian periods (710–1185):** Japan built centralized institutions influenced by China. The court later flourished at Heian-kyō, today’s Kyoto, producing achievements such as *The Tale of Genji*. Over time, aristocratic estates and provincial warriors weakened central control.
- **Kamakura period (1185–1333):** Minamoto no Yoritomo established a military government, or *shogunate*, formally receiving the title of shogun in 1192. The *samurai* became the dominant military class. Japan repelled Mongol invasions in 1274 and 1281.

### Civil war and unification
- **Muromachi and Sengoku eras (1336–1600):** The Ashikaga shogunate oversaw flourishing arts, including Noh theater and Zen-inspired gardens, but eventually lost control to competing regional lords, or *daimyo*. Portuguese traders and Christian missionaries arrived in the sixteenth century.
- **Unification:** Oda Nobunaga, Toyotomi Hideyoshi, and Tokugawa Ieyasu successively brought much of Japan under centralized rule. Hideyoshi’s invasions of Korea in the 1590s caused widespread devastation and ended in withdrawal.

### Tokugawa peace
- **Edo period (1603–1868):** The Tokugawa shogunate maintained relative peace through a regulated social order and control over regional lords. Its *sakoku* policies sharply restricted foreign contact without eliminating trade. Cities, commerce, literacy, kabuki, and woodblock printing flourished.

### Modernization, empire, and war
- **Meiji Restoration (1868):** After foreign pressure and domestic unrest undermined the shogunate, political authority was restored in the emperor’s name. Rapid *industrialization*, military reform, and new national institutions transformed Japan.
- **Imperial expansion:** Victories over China in 1894–1895 and Russia in 1904–1905 strengthened Japan’s regional power. Japan acquired Taiwan, annexed Korea in 1910, and expanded its influence in China.
- **1930s–1945:** Militarism and expansion intensified. Japan seized Manchuria in 1931, launched full-scale war against China in 1937, and attacked Pearl Harbor in 1941. Its conquests involved severe atrocities across Asia. Japan surrendered in August 1945 after the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki and Soviet entry into the war against Japan.

### Postwar and contemporary Japan
- **Occupation and recovery (1945–1952):** The Allied occupation introduced major reforms. The 1947 constitution established popular sovereignty, parliamentary *democracy*, a symbolic emperor, and a renunciation of war.
- **Economic growth:** Japan became one of the world’s largest economies through rapid postwar development, especially in manufacturing and technology.
- **Since the 1990s:** Japan has faced prolonged slow growth, an aging and shrinking population, and disasters such as the 2011 earthquake, tsunami, and Fukushima nuclear accident. It remains a major economic and cultural power, while debating economic reform and its international security role.

## Version 1: Oʻahu on a Student Budget
**Best for:** Beaches, food, nightlife, and getting around mostly without a car. Stay in a Waikīkī hostel or split a budget hotel room.

### Day 1: Arrive and Explore Waikīkī
- Check in, unpack, and grab groceries for breakfasts and beach snacks.
- Walk along Waikīkī Beach and take an easy swim near a lifeguard station.
- Catch sunset, then pick up an inexpensive plate lunch or rice bowl for dinner.

### Day 2: Diamond Head and Beach Time
- Hike Diamond Head early before the heat builds. Non-Hawaiʻi residents should book the required entry reservation ahead.
- Grab lunch around Kapahulu Avenue, with malasadas for dessert.
- Spend the afternoon at Kapiʻolani Park and the nearby beach.

### Day 3: Pearl Harbor and Downtown Honolulu
- Visit the Pearl Harbor National Memorial; reserve USS Arizona Memorial program tickets through the official booking site.
- Head downtown to see the King Kamehameha statue and the exterior of ʻIolani Palace, or budget for a palace tour.
- Explore Chinatown’s restaurants for dinner, checking transit schedules for the return trip.

### Day 4: Kailua Beach Day
- Take public transit to Kailua, allowing extra time for transfers.
- Pick up picnic supplies and walk to Kailua Beach for sand, swimming, and relaxation.
- If conditions are calm, split a kayak rental after getting local guidance; otherwise, keep this a low-cost beach day.

### Day 5: North Shore Adventure
- Split a rental car with an eligible driver or book a shared shuttle; rental companies may charge extra for drivers under 25.
- Explore Haleʻiwa, grab shave ice, and stop at North Shore beaches.
- Watch surfers from shore. Winter surf can be dangerous, so swim only where lifeguards say conditions are safe.

### Day 6: Snorkeling and a Social Night
- Choose a guided beginner snorkeling outing, or visit Hanauma Bay if you secure reservations for an operating day.
- Keep your afternoon free for beach volleyball, souvenir shopping, or a nap.
- Join a hostel social event or catch live music. Bars generally require guests to be 21 or older.

### Day 7: One Last Beach Morning
- Enjoy a relaxed breakfast and a final walk along Waikīkī.
- Split luggage storage if checkout is early.
- Take transit or share an airport ride, leaving plenty of time for traffic and check-in.

******
## Version 2: Hawaiʻi Island Outdoor Adventure
**Best for:** Volcanoes, hiking, stargazing, and group road trips. Split basic lodging and a rental car; check driver-age rules and surcharges before booking. Arrive in Kona and depart from Hilo if flight prices make that practical.

### Day 1: Arrive in Kona
- Collect your rental car and check into shared lodging around Kona.
- Stock up on breakfast food, sandwich supplies, and refillable water bottles.
- Explore the waterfront along Aliʻi Drive and watch sunset from shore.

### Day 2: Snorkeling and Kona Exploring
- Visit Kahaluʻu Beach Park if open and conditions are suitable; follow posted guidance and avoid touching coral.
- Grab a casual lunch, then browse Kona’s shops or visit a local coffee farm.
- Optional splurge: book a reputable guided manta ray snorkeling trip suited to your swimming ability.

### Day 3: Kohala Coast Beach Day
- Drive north to Hāpuna Beach State Recreation Area; budget for applicable entry and parking fees.
- Picnic, play beach games, and swim only when conditions are safe.
- Stop in Waimea for an early dinner before returning to Kona.

### Day 4: Travel to Volcano
- Check out and drive the southern route toward Volcano village.
- Stop at Punaluʻu Black Sand Beach. Watch any resting turtles from a respectful distance and never touch or feed them.
- Check into simple lodging near Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park and cook a group dinner.

### Day 5: Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park
- Check official park alerts before heading out; volcanic conditions and closures can change.
- Choose open trails and overlooks, such as Kīlauea Iki or Nāhuku, based on current access and your group’s fitness.
- Pack lunch, rain layers, and plenty of water. Stay on marked routes, and don’t expect visible lava—it is never guaranteed.

### Day 6: Hilo and Waterfalls
- Head to Hilo and visit its farmers market; vendor selection varies by day.
- See Rainbow Falls from designated viewing areas, then visit ʻAkaka Falls State Park if time and budget allow.
- Stay in Hilo for your final night. If skies are clear, enjoy informal stargazing from a safe, legal public spot away from bright lights.

### Day 7: Hilo Morning and Departure
- Take a relaxed walk through Liliʻuokalani Gardens and get breakfast.
- Return your rental car and fly out of Hilo.
- If your flight leaves from Kona instead, allow several hours for the cross-island drive, fuel stop, and airport check-in.

# Research Proposal

## Title

Social Media and Teen Mental Health

## Project Details

Researcher: [name]

Institution: [institution]

Supervisor: [supervisor]

Start date: [date]

Study location: [location]

## Background

Social media is common among teenagers. It can support friendships and self-expression. It may also expose users to bullying and social pressure.

Past research suggests mixed links with mental health. These links may depend on content and online experiences. More evidence is needed about these differences.

## Research Aim

This study will examine social media use and teen mental health. It will assess associations rather than prove causation.

## Research Questions

- How is daily use linked to anxiety?
- How is daily use linked to depressive symptoms?
- Does nighttime use relate to poor sleep?
- Do supportive interactions relate to better well-being?

## Hypotheses

Higher use will be associated with greater distress. Nighttime use will be associated with poorer sleep. Supportive interactions will be associated with better well-being.

## Methods

### Study Design

The study will use surveys and interviews. Data will be collected at two time points. These will be three months apart.

### Participants

The study will recruit [number] teenagers. Participants will be aged 13 to 17. Recruitment will take place through [schools].

Participation will be voluntary. Recruitment will seek students from varied backgrounds.

### Data Collection

Surveys will measure daily social media use. They will also assess content and online experiences.

Validated scales will measure anxiety and depressive symptoms. Additional questions will assess sleep and well-being.

The study will record relevant background factors. These will include age and offline support.

A smaller group will complete interviews. Questions will explore positive and negative experiences.

### Data Analysis

Statistical tests will assess relationships between measured factors. Models will account for baseline mental health. They will also account for relevant background factors.

Interview responses will be coded for recurring themes. Findings from both methods will be compared.

## Ethical Considerations

Approval will be sought from [ethics committee]. Parents or guardians will provide consent. Teenagers will provide assent.

Participants may skip questions. They may stop participation at any time.

Study records will use coded identifiers. Data will be stored securely. No passwords or private messages will be collected.

Participants will receive mental health support information. A safeguarding plan will address serious safety concerns. Consent materials will explain confidentiality limits.

## Limitations

Self-reported use may be inaccurate. Some participants may miss the second survey. The sample may not represent all teenagers.

Other factors may influence mental health. This observational study cannot establish causation.

## Expected Contribution

The study may identify harmful patterns of use. It may also identify helpful online experiences.

Findings could inform families and schools. They could support more targeted digital well-being guidance.

## Timeline

- Month 1: Review evidence and seek ethical approval.
- Month 2: Recruit participants and collect baseline data.
- Months 3 and 4: Maintain contact and prepare interviews.
- Month 5: Collect follow-up data and conduct interviews.
- Month 6: Analyze findings and write the report.

## Budget

The estimated budget is [amount]. Costs will cover survey tools and participant compensation. They will also cover transcription and secure storage.

## References

- [Source on social media and adolescent mental health]
- [Source on sleep and digital media use]
- [Source on validated mental health measures]

### Turn a shared hobby into a connected community.

TableTogether helps board gamers find compatible players, organize game nights, and build lasting friendships.

**Our mission:** Make it as easy to find your gaming group as it is to find your next game.

### Owning games is easy. Getting them to the table is hard.

Board gamers face three recurring challenges:

- **Finding the right people:** Players differ in location, availability, experience, and preferred game complexity.
- **Coordinating sessions:** Group chats become endless threads about dates, games, and missing players.
- **Building community:** Reviews, collections, events, and conversations are scattered across disconnected platforms.

**The result:** Unplayed games, canceled sessions, and people who want to participate but don’t know where to start.

## Slide 3 — The Solution
### One home for your board gaming life.

TableTogether combines:

- **Player matching:** Discover nearby gamers with compatible interests and schedules.
- **Game-night planning:** Create events, collect RSVPs, manage seats, and send reminders.
- **Community spaces:** Join local clubs, game-specific groups, and beginner-friendly communities.
- **Game profiles:** Share collections, wish lists, session logs, and recommendations.

**From “Who wants to play?” to a full table—in one place.**

**1. Create your player profile**  
Select favorite games, preferred play styles, availability, and approximate location.

**2. Find your people**  
Discover relevant groups, hosts, and upcoming sessions.

**3. Reserve a seat**  
See game details, experience expectations, venue information, and available spots.

**4. Keep the connection**  
Log your session, follow fellow players, and schedule the next game night.

**Trust by design:** Location privacy controls, blocking and reporting, host moderation tools, and clear community standards.

- Hobbyists who host recurring sessions

- Families and casual players
- Convention communities and traveling gamers

**Launch strategy:** Focus on a small number of geographically dense communities rather than spreading users thinly across many cities.

### A dedicated social layer for an established hobby.

TableTogether sits at the intersection of:

- Tabletop entertainment
- Local social discovery
- Community management
- Event coordination

**Bottom-up market sizing**
- **TAM:** Reachable board game participants globally × potential annual revenue per user.
- **SAM:** Participants in supported languages and launch regions, plus relevant venues and clubs.
- **SOM:** Users and organizations realistically reachable through initial city launches and partnerships.

*Investor-ready market figures should be supported by current research and launch-market validation, not inferred from total board game sales.*

## Slide 7 — Competitive Landscape
### Existing tools solve pieces of the problem.

| Alternative | Core strength | TableTogether’s proposed focus |
|---|---|---|
| BoardGameGeek | Game information and enthusiast discussion | Player compatibility and local session coordination |
| Discord and group chats | Ongoing conversation | Structured discovery, RSVPs, and scheduling |
| Meetup and event platforms | Broad event discovery | Board game-specific profiles and session details |
| General social networks | Broad reach and existing connections | A focused experience centered on getting games played |

**Our differentiation:** Connect player preferences, game collections, local availability, and event participation in one workflow.

**Freemium membership**

- Premium: Advanced discovery filters, collection insights, and enhanced planning tools.

- Clearly labeled publisher promotions
- Affiliate commissions on relevant game purchases

**Proposed pricing tests:** $5–8/month for individual premium plans and $29–99/month for organizer plans.

# The Case for Wilderness Preservation

Wilderness is more than land untouched by roads or buildings. It is a living network of forests, rivers, grasslands, deserts, and mountains where natural processes still shape the world. These places support countless species, protect essential resources, and offer people a deeper connection to life beyond human development. Preserving wilderness is not simply an act of admiration for beautiful scenery; it is a commitment to ecological stability and the well-being of future generations.

One of the strongest arguments for wilderness preservation is the protection of biodiversity. Every ecosystem contains relationships among plants, animals, fungi, and microorganisms. A bird may disperse the seeds of a tree, while insects pollinate its flowers and fungi help its roots absorb nutrients. These relationships form an intricate knot of interdependence. When habitats disappear, the damage extends beyond individual species, weakening the systems that sustain life. Large, connected wilderness areas give species room to migrate, reproduce, and adapt to environmental change.

Wilderness also provides services that human communities often take for granted. Forests and wetlands help filter water, regulate its flow, and store carbon. Healthy soils absorb rainfall, while vegetation reduces erosion. Although protected landscapes cannot solve climate change alone, their preservation can prevent additional emissions and strengthen ecological resilience. Destroying these places may produce immediate profits, but it can also impose long-term costs through polluted water, declining soil quality, and increased vulnerability to disasters.

*To preserve wilderness is to recognize that the natural world has value beyond what people can extract from it.*

The benefits of wilderness are not only ecological. Wild places offer opportunities for recreation, scientific discovery, reflection, and renewal. Walking through a quiet forest or watching weather move across a mountain range can loosen the knot of daily anxiety. Such experiences remind people that their lives belong within a larger world. Access to these benefits should be broad and fair, supported by thoughtful public policies that welcome visitors while protecting sensitive habitats.

Nevertheless, wilderness preservation raises difficult questions about livelihoods, land use, and authority. Communities may depend on logging, mining, grazing, or tourism, and conservation decisions can affect their economic futures. Effective preservation therefore requires more than drawing boundaries on a map. It calls for public participation, durable funding, and support for sustainable livelihoods. It also requires respecting Indigenous peoples’ rights and knowledge. Many landscapes described as wilderness have been inhabited and stewarded by Indigenous communities for generations; protecting those places must not mean erasing that history or excluding their caretakers.

*Lasting conservation protects both ecological integrity and the dignity of the people connected to the land.*

Preservation must also respond to a changing climate. Isolated protected areas may not be enough when species need to shift their ranges. Wildlife corridors, restored habitats, and cooperation across political boundaries can help ecosystems remain connected. Responsible management may sometimes involve active measures, including controlling invasive species or restoring appropriate fire patterns. Preserving wilderness does not always mean doing nothing; it means making careful decisions that sustain natural processes rather than replacing them with short-term human priorities.

Ultimately, wilderness preservation asks society to practice restraint. Not every forest must become timber, not every river must be dammed, and not every open landscape must be developed. Some places should endure because they sustain life, hold cultural meaning, and allow future generations to encounter a world not entirely shaped for human convenience. Protecting wilderness is therefore both a practical necessity and an ethical responsibility: a promise to leave room for nature, and for the many forms of life that depend on it.

# Beyond “Hallo”: 8 Fascinating Facts About the Dutch Language

Dutch is often overshadowed by its neighbors, English and German—but it has plenty of character of its own. From tiny words that make almost anything sound cozy to compounds that seem to stretch forever, Dutch rewards a closer look.

## 1. Dutch and English Are Linguistic Cousins

*If you speak English, you already have a head start with Dutch. Both belong to the West Germanic branch of the Indo-European language family, alongside German and Frisian.*

That shared ancestry shows up in familiar-looking words:

- **water** — water
- **hand** — hand
- **appel** — apple
- **boek** — book

But watch out for false friends. Dutch **slim** usually means “smart,” while **winkel** means “shop”—not a wrinkle!

## 2. Dutch Travels Far Beyond the Netherlands

Dutch is an official language in the Netherlands, Belgium, and Suriname, as well as the Caribbean countries of Aruba, Curaçao, and Sint Maarten.

In Belgium, it is spoken primarily in Flanders and is one of Brussels’s two official languages. You’ll often hear Belgian Dutch called **Flemish**, though that label can refer to several regional varieties rather than one separate, uniform language.

Dutch is therefore not just European: its global reach reflects histories of migration, trade, and colonialism.

## 3. English Has Borrowed Some Very Dutch Words

You may use Dutch-derived vocabulary before breakfast is over. **Cookie** comes from Dutch **koekje**, meaning “little cake.”

Other English words with Dutch roots include:

- **boss**, from **baas**
- **yacht**, from **jacht**
- **landscape**, from **landschap**

These borrowings offer little glimpses of historical contact, especially through seafaring, commerce, and settlement.

## 4. Small Endings Do a Lot of Work

Dutch loves **diminutives**: word forms that suggest smallness, affection, informality, or a softened tone.

A **huis** is a house; a **huisje** is a little house. A **kop** is a cup; a **kopje** can be a small cup—or simply the ordinary word used when offering someone a cup of coffee.

There’s also a useful grammatical bonus: diminutive nouns are neuter. In the singular, they take **het**, even when the original noun takes **de**:

**de tafel** → **het tafeltje**  
the table → the little table

## 5. “Gezellig” Is Almost a Cultural Mascot

*The Dutch word **gezellig** can describe a cozy room, a lively gathering, or the pleasure of spending time with people you like. English can translate it, but the best choice—“cozy,” “convivial,” “pleasant,” or “sociable”—depends on the moment.*

A quiet evening with friends can be **gezellig**. So can a bustling café. The word often combines atmosphere with a sense of enjoyable company.

## 6. Dutch Builds Words Like LEGO

Dutch commonly joins words into compounds:

**fiets** + **bel** = **fietsbel**  
bicycle + bell = bicycle bell

A longer example is **arbeidsongeschiktheidsverzekering**: insurance against being unable to work because of illness or disability.

Such words look intimidating, but identifying the smaller building blocks makes them much easier to understand.

## 7. Two Letters Can Share a Capital

The combination **ij** is a distinctive feature of Dutch spelling. When a word beginning with it is capitalized, both letters normally become capitals:

- **ijs** → **IJs**
- **IJsselmeer**

It is generally treated as a digraph—a combination of two letters—though in some contexts it behaves rather like a single unit.

## 8. Verbs Like to Keep You Waiting

Dutch word order can surprise English speakers. In a main statement, the finite verb normally occupies the second position:

**Morgen drink ik koffie.**  
“Tomorrow I’ll drink coffee.”

Section 1

The first time Tomas saw Mara, a swallow was building a nest in the western turret above her left shoulder.
She stood in the market square, arguing with a fishmonger about the price of river trout.
The turret was no taller than a wine bottle, but it had proper battlements, narrow windows, and a weather vane shaped like a fox.
Its twin rose above her right shoulder, where a tiny blue flag snapped in a wind nobody else could feel.
Tomas stared until Mara turned toward him.
“If you’re wondering whether there are soldiers inside, the answer is only on Thursdays.”
Then she picked up her trout and walked away.

Tomas repaired clocks in a shop opposite the public fountain.
He was good with springs, patient with rust, and terrible at beginning conversations.
For three weeks, he watched Mara pass his window on her way to the bakery.
Sometimes her turrets wore frost when the street was warm.
Sometimes little bells rang inside them at noon, several minutes ahead of every clock in town.
Once, a scrap of paper floated from an arrow slit and landed against his door.
On it, in extraordinarily small handwriting, someone had written, PLEASE OIL THE DRAWBRIDGE.

He returned the note to Mara the following morning.
She read it, sighed, and pressed two fingers against her right temple.
“The east tower has been complaining all month.”
Tomas offered to look at the mechanism.
Mara considered him with the wary attention of someone accustomed to offers that concealed questions.
Then she sat on the stool beside his workbench and tilted her shoulder toward the light.
He brought out his smallest tools without asking how she had become a building.

The drawbridge needed a new pin and a drop of oil.
While Tomas worked, Mara told him she restored damaged books for the abbey library.
She liked sour cherries, disliked brass bands, and had once thrown a duke out of a reading room.
By the time the drawbridge rose smoothly, Tomas had forgotten to be astonished by the turret.
He was too busy trying to make her laugh again.
When she left, she placed a silver coin on his bench and asked whether he liked walking by the river.
Tomas said yes so quickly that she smiled all the way to the door.

Section 2

They began walking together every Tuesday evening.
Mara wore a broad scarf beneath the turrets to keep their stone foundations from chafing her shoulders.
Tomas learned to walk on her left because the eastern gargoyle spat rainwater whenever it felt overlooked.
He learned that the bells rang when she was hungry, not when it was noon.
He also learned that asking about the towers was allowed, provided he did not mistake the answer for her entire life.
“My grandmother made them,” Mara told him one evening.
“She believed a girl should never go into the world undefended.”

Her grandmother had been the royal architect and, in certain inconvenient circumstances, a witch.
When Mara was seven, bandits had come through their village during a winter famine.
The old woman built a refuge around her granddaughter with one hand and held the door shut with the other.
By morning, the bandits were gone.
The refuge had shrunk into two towers, and the grandmother had died in her chair.
Mara remembered the smell of burning rosemary more clearly than she remembered the spell.
“They were meant to keep me safe,” she said, touching a battlement.

For years, the turrets had done exactly that.
Their arrow slits flashed whenever someone approached her with a knife.
Their gates locked during fevers, and their bells woke her once when a chimney caught fire.
But lately, the stone had begun to spread.
A ridge of masonry lay beneath her collar, and on cold mornings she could barely turn her head.
Tomas asked whether she had sought help.
“Six physicians, three magicians, and a mason who suggested better drainage,” she replied.

By autumn, Tomas was in love with her.
He loved the fierce care with which she straightened torn pages, and the dreadful songs she sang while cooking.
He loved that she always gave beggars money but never pretended to know what they ought to do with it.
One night, after supper, he told her.
Mara looked down at her hands for so long that he began to apologize.
“Don’t,” she said, catching his sleeve.
“I’m trying to decide whether I can bear having something else to lose.”

Section 3

The first wall appeared across Mara’s back in November.
It was thin as a book cover and cold enough to leave frost on her nightdress.
By December, she could no longer lift her arms above her head.
People in town began offering advice in the confident voices of people who would never have to follow it.
Someone suggested that Tomas kiss her at sunrise.
Someone else suggested that Mara apologize to her grandmother’s ghost.
Mara shut the door on both of them and asked Tomas to help her find the original plans.

They searched the abbey archives for eleven evenings.
Tomas held lamps while Mara worked through boxes of brittle correspondence.
At last, inside a ledger of bridge repairs, they found a drawing of a little girl enclosed by a fortress.
The notes described a protection spell that strengthened itself whenever its bearer feared losing something.
Below that, in faded red ink, her grandmother had added a second instruction.
Mara read it twice before passing the page to Tomas.
“The bearer must retain the means to open the gates.”

There was supposed to be a key.
The drawing showed it hanging inside the western tower, just beneath the bell.
Tomas fetched his magnifying lenses and looked through an arrow slit while Mara sat very still.
He saw winding stairs, a dusty guardroom, and a narrow door held shut by a blackened spring.
Beyond the door hung something bright.
“I can reach it,” he said, “but I’ll have to take part of the roof apart.”
Mara studied her grandmother’s drawing, then asked him to bring his tools.

They worked in his shop through a night of freezing rain.
Each time Tomas loosened a stone, the turret shuddered and tried to grow another in its place.
Mara gripped the edge of the bench as mortar crept toward her throat.
“Stop if I tell you,” she said.
He promised, and kept his hands where she could see them.
When the bell began to clang, she swore at it with such force that Tomas nearly dropped his pliers.
Then the blackened spring gave way, and a small brass key fell into his palm.

Section 4

The key opened neither turret.
For a dreadful minute, they thought they had misunderstood the plans.
Then Mara felt a keyhole beneath her collarbone, where there had been only skin the day before.
Tomas set a mirror in front of her and stepped back.
She tried the key once, changed its angle, and tried again.
Something clicked inside the wall across her back.
Both drawbridges lowered, and warm air rushed through the shop, carrying the smell of rosemary.

The new stone crumbled first.
Mara bent forward as the wall broke into flakes that vanished before they touched the floor.
The ridge beneath her collar softened, and she rolled her shoulders with a startled cry.
Her original turrets remained, though their foundations no longer pressed into her skin.
For several minutes she sat turning her head from side to side.
Then she reached up to the highest shelf and took down the bottle of brandy Tomas saved for holidays.
Her hands shook so badly that he steadied the glasses while she poured.

Spring arrived late that year.
Mara returned to the library, where six months of damaged books awaited her attention.
She wore the brass key on a ribbon and opened the gates each morning before breakfast.
Sometimes she left them open all day.
Sometimes, in a crowded street or after an unsettling dream, she closed them for a while.
Tomas stopped asking whether her shoulders hurt every time she shifted in her chair.
Instead, when they went walking, he offered his arm and let her decide whether to take it.

They married in June beneath the apple trees behind the abbey.
Mara refused a veil because the western weather vane had already ruined two during fittings.
Tomas cried halfway through his vows and had to borrow her handkerchief.
When she kissed him, both turret bells rang, although she insisted afterward that she had simply been hungry.
Years later, he would still sometimes find tiny maintenance requests tucked beneath his workshop door.
He answered every one, usually with Mara leaning over his shoulder to question his estimate.
And whenever a swallow nested in the western tower, they left that window open until the young birds learned to fly.
